view of the Government’s replies : 2.3, 2.4, 8, 11.3, 14.3, 14.4, 15.4, 15.6, 15.7, 16.2, 16.3.

(iii) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government
have not been accepted by the Committee : 3.2, 6.3, 6.4, 7.2, 7.3, 9.4, 9.5, 10.2, 10.3, 10.4,
13.1, 15, 15.1, 15.3, 47.1 19.3. 19.4, 19.5,,.1916, 20:3.

(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government
have not been received: 6, 9, 9.1, 11.1.

3. The Committee will now deal with some of its recommendations on which the Action
Taken Note of the Government has not been accepted by the Committee.

Medical Education and Training
Recommendation (Para No. 3.2)

In the context of growing number of privaté medical colleges, the Committee
recommends creation of proper monitoring machinery to supervise their function. It also
empha: the need for strengthening the MCI.

Ministry’s Reply

In order to check mushroom growth of sub-standard medical colleges, the Indian
Medical Council Act, 1956, was amended vide the Indian Medical Council (Amendment)
Act, 1993,

According to amended Act, no person shall establish a medical college or no medical
college shall open new or higher courses of study (including a postgraduate course of study
or training) and no medical college shall increase its admission capacity without the previous
permission of the Central Government. Under this Act, a proposal is required to be
submitted in the prescribed format to the Central Government for opening of a new medical
college/opening of new or higher courses and for increasing the intake capacity in the
existing médical colleges. There is no report of private medical colleges being established
without the Central Government permission after the amendment of Indian Medical Council
Act, 1956. The Medical Council of India has been authorised to create necessary posts as
per their requirements to strengthen the Council.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee notes that the Department has not responded to the specific
recommendations for creation of a monitoring machinery and to strengthen the Medical
Council of India. The Committee, therefore, reiterating its earlier recommendations, desires
that a monitoring cell be created in the Medical Council of India to oversee ‘the functioning
of private medical colleges. +


2

Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM & H)
Recommendation (Para Nos. 6.3 & 6.4)

In response to the Committee’s suggestion in para 57 of its Report, given last year, to
get the Excise Duty on Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Medicines removed, the Department
stated that it had requested the Ministry of Finance on 16.1.1995 regarding removal of 10%
Excise Duty on patent proprietary Ayurvedic medicines in the current Budget and that there
has not been any response from the Finance Ministry so far, to which the Committee takes
serious exception.

The Committee feels that the matter needs urgent attention as it would be an important
step in popularising the Indian Systems of Medicine. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the new Department of ISM & H should take up this matter with the
Ministry of Finance for an early decision.

Ministry’s Reply

The ISM & H Deptt. have already follow up the matter of removal of 10%. Excise
Duty on proprietary Ayurvedic medicines with the Finance Ministry.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee takes u very serious view of the inordinate delay in getting the excise
duty removed on proprietary Ayurvedic medicines. Since the matter is reported to be
pending with the Ministry of Finance for long, the Committee desires that the case be taken
up at the Minister’s level to avoid delays.

National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur
Recommendation (Para Nos. 7.2. & 7.3)

National Institute of Ayurveda. it is said, is facing problems on several counts. There is
no Director at present; many posts in different categories are lying vacant, and no research
activity is being carried out. Lot of construction activities are going on and a major portion

of money provided is being spent on building construction. The Institute thus appears to be
in complete shambles.

The Committee, therefore, suggests that a Senior Officer of the Department be deputed
immediately to take stock of the situation und review the progress of the Institute and
prepare a report so that steps may be initiated to clear the augean stables at the earlier. The
Committee also recommends that a suitable enhancement be made in the allocation for this
Institute at the RE stage.

Ministry’s Reply

It is submitted that the post of Director has already been filled up. Action is being
taken separately to fill up other vacant posts.

Comments of the Commitee

The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the lukewarm approach of the
Department in this respect. No action has been initiated in pursuance of the Committee’s
suggestion to depute a Senior Officer to look into the functioning of the Institute. The
Committee has been given to understand that the Institute’s affiliation with the Rajasthan
University, leading to delayed commencement of Session, examination etc. are the main
factors due to which the Institute has not been functioning well. The Committee was,
however, informed that a proposal to delink it from the Rajasthan University has been
initiated. However, the Committee, while reaffirming its earlier recommendation, calls upon
the Department to make all possible efforts to set right the sorry state of affairs prevailing in
the Institute.


Mental Health
Recommendation (Para Nos. 9.4 and 9.5)

1 The Committee expresses its concern over the unsatisfactory conditions prevailing in
the Institutes/Hospitals meant for mental health care and research. The training
programme evolved by the Centre has also not picked up. The response from the State
Governments is neither forthcoming nor adequate.

The Committee feels that the need for improving the services and facilities for
treatment and training and extending them upto the district and primary health care level
can hardly be ignored. There is an imperative need for having a comprehensive plan for
tackling the mental health problems in this country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that a programme be evolved with broad thrust on improving the status of
mental health care services in our country, by involving mental hospitals, departments of
psychiatry in medical colleges. training of medical and para-medical staff and creating
awareness among the people.

Ministry’s Reply

The recommendations of the Committee have been noted. It is again submitted that a
number of Mental Institutions have been conferred autonomous status which would
definitely lead to improvement of services. Assistance to the tune of Rs. 10.00 lakhs has
been provided to the National Institute of Mental Health & Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore for
conducting training to Primary Health Physicians. The Institute has been advised to
forward the Programme of Training to all State Governments requesting them to nominate
suitable personnel for the training.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Departmént which is
conspicuously silent on the key recommendation of the Committee to. evolve a
comprehensive Plan for tackling the mental health problems in the country. Hence,
reasserting its earlier recommendation, the Committee under lines the need to seriously
consider the matter and take all possible steps to ameliorate the situation.

Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi
Recommendation (Para Nos. 10.2, 10.3 and 10.4)

The Committee is not convinced by the argument advanced by the Department for
giving much less than what was asked for by the Institute. It feels that the Department
should have ensured that the funds provided to the Institute were utilized properly. The
Committee is aware of the poor conditions obtaining in the Institute and, in fact, last year
also, in its Ninth Report, it had drawn the attention of the Department to this issue and
had recommended that a review of the functioning of Institute be conducted soon.

When asked about the action taken in this regard, the Committee was informed that
in pursuance of its recommendation, a work study of the Institute had been proposed and
the Ministry of Finance had been requested to nominate a core member from the Staff
Inspection Unit in the Study Group. As soon as the core member was nominated, the
Committee was assured, the work study would be carried out.

The Committee recommends that the Department should review thé financial
requirements of the Institute at the appropriate stage and enhance thei outlay based on its
actual needs. It also likes the Department to ensure that the Institute does utilise the fund
fully and properly. The Committee also recommends that the formalities regarding
constituting the proposed study group should be completed early and the work be started.


4

The Study group should be asked, the Committee suggests, to make concrete and positive
suggestions for bringing about radical improvements in the functioning of the Institute.
Ministry's Reply

Among other things, it is proposed to frame rules for the Management of Central
Institute of Psychiatry, for facilitating more latitude in administrative and financial matters
which will lead to further improvement in services, Director, CIP, Ranchi, is also being
asked to project requirements for its developmental needs.

This Ministry had already requested the Ministry of Finance, Deptt. of Expenditure, to
nominate a core-member from SIU Work Study Group for assessing staff requirements of
the CIP, Ranchi. The Institute has been included in their Programme for Work Study during
1995-96.

Comments of the Committee

Despite the Committee’s recommendation in its two previous reports, a review of the
functioning has not been undertaken for the reason that the Ministry of Finance had been
requested to nominate a core member from the SIU. Now since a member has been
appointed by the Ministry of Finance as revealed by the Secretary, Health. during the course
of discussion, the review should be completed as early as possible.

Drug Control
Recommendation (Para No. 13.1)

The Committee welcomes the proposal of levying and collecting cess on drugs and
recommends that necessary legal and other formalities should be completed at the earliest,
with a viewed to paving the way for setting up a Central Drug Authority in the year 1995-96.
Ministry’s Reply

The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is in the process of formulating draft
legislation for setting up of a National Drug Authority and for levying Cess on drugs and
pharmaceuticals to ensure quality control of drugs and to encourage Research and
Development in the drug sector.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is not happy with the slow progress in this regard. It, therefore,
recommends that the draft legislation may be brought before the Parliament at the earliest.
National Malaria Eradication Programme
Recommendation (Para Nos. 15, 15.1 and 15.5)

This programme is a Centrally sponsored scheme on 50:50 sharing basis with the States.
The Committee notes with concern that the Malaria situation in the country had not
improyed even after the adoption of Modified Plan of Operation (MPO) strategy from 1977.
The Committee observed from the following statistics supplied by the Department that
except in the years 1991 and 1992, the total number of cases of Malaria had gone-up over
the previous years. Similarly, deaths due to Malaria had also increased consistently, except
in the years 1984 and 1992.

The Committee does not agree with the Department’s contention that containing
malaria cases to around 2 million per year. from 1984 onwards, was in itself an indication of
the success of the programme. The aim of the programme, the Committee points out, is not
merely containment but its eradication. Even the containment theory does not hold good, as
the incidence of malaria has increased all these years. The Committee is not satisfied with
the explanation given for the outbreak of malaria in Rajasthan last year. which led to an
unsurge in deaths due to malaria in 1994.

The Committee, therefore, recommends that more funds should be provided for this
programme. It also emphasis the need for activating the administrative machinery from the
top to bottom and recommends that all out efforts be made for tackling the menace of
malaria on the level it was done during the 60s.

Ministry’s Reply
After the implementation of the Modified Plan of Operation (MPO), incidence of

Malaria came down from 6.47 million cases in 1976 to 2.18 million cases in 1989. Since then,
Malaria incidence has been contained around 2 million cases annually.

Provision for additional funds. if required, would be projected in the R.E. 1995-96. As
the programme is being impicmented through the State Governments. The State
Governments have already been asked to establish a High Powered Board on Malaria
Control under the Chairmanship of the Chief Secretary of the concerned State to coordinate
the Malaria Control Activities. address problems relating to enforcing model bye-laws in
urban area etc.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee notes with concern that no significant progress in arresting the cases of
Malaria has been made even after the implementation of the Modified Plan of operation way
back in 1977. Even the fact that it has, ever since 1989, been contained to around two
million cases, is not very encouraging. Intermittent upsurge of malaria incidence in several
parts of the country is yet another instance of failure on this front. Incidence of Malaria is
concentrated in tribal areas particularly. The Committee, therefore, desires that all out
efforts be made not only to contain but also to eradicate malaria, particularly in tribal areas.

National’ Aids Control Programme
Recommendation (Para No. 17.1)

The Committee is happy that blood bank services are being improved. The Committee
emphasises the urgent need of improving blood transfusion services and making them
foolproof so that no HIV-infected blood was given to anyone as more and more such cases
are being reported now-a-days. Disposable needles, it has been observed, are not being used
in all the hospitals/dispensaries. The Committee recommends that the usé of such disposable
syringes should be encouraged and adequate emphasis be given on surveillance and clinical
management. Increased stress should be given for voluntary blood donation.



Ministry’s Reply

The observations of the Committee have been noted and also brought to the attention
of all the State/UT Goveriments for compliance.

The Drugs and Cosmetics Act/Rules provide for compulsory testing of blood/blood
products used for transfusion purposes to be free from blood transmissible, infection, such as
Hepatitis, Syphillis and HIV, Government of India is providing ELISA Readers, HIV ‘Test
Kits and RAPID Test Kits to ull the Blood Banks in the Public Sector. Financial assistance
for laboratory technicians in each Blood Bank and for consumables is also released to State
Government every yeur. Both single use disposable needles and syringes and autoclaved
needles und syringes ure equally safe. However, there is the possibility of disposable needles
and syringes getting recycled. In view of this, guidelines on Hospital Acquired Infection
Control which inter-alia, contain instructions on proper sterlisation, autoclaving and also
destruction/disposal of heedles and syringes have been developed and circulated to all State/
UT Governments. These guidelines have been circulated once again for strict compliance.

In addition to regular surveillance, Sentinal Surveillance, atleast in two sites, is being
organised by each State Government among STH patients, ante-natal mothers and
Intravenous Drug Users. More than 2000 Doctors have been trained on clinical
management, diagnosis and infection control of HIV/AIDS. All the States have trained
Doctors.

Information, Education and Communication activities under the National AIDS Control
Programme also give emphasis on augmentation of voluntary blood donation.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee, reiterating its earlier recommendation, stresses on the need to start the
use of disposable syringes in view of the growing menace of AIDS. Simultaneously, the
Department should ensure that all the mitteriuV/equipments are provided for sterilizing the
used syringes in the dispensaries/hospnals and ensure the sterilization of syringes where
disposable syringes are not provided.

Budgetary Provisions
(Recommendations Paras 2.1—2.7)

2.1 Asked to comment on the allocation, the Department stated that certain
programmes like Rural Family Welfare Centres and Rural sub-centres would continue to be
under-funded, aggravating the problem of arrears. It would also not be possible to undertake
(i) expansion of the services required to increase accessibility and (ii) provide for
complementary requirements to improve quality.

2.2 The Committee was informed that the expansion of Rural sub-centres, which are
the grass-root level units would be adversely affected because only Rs. 190 crores have been
provided against a requirement of Rs. 300 crores for the maintenance of these sub-centres.

2.3 The Department also stated that there would-be virtually no expansion of urban
health infrastructure, although the growth of urban population is faster than rural population
due to migration. The expansion of Urban Health Posts would be possible only if additional
resources are made available. The present outlay is not sufficient even for maintaining the
existing level.

2.4 The Committee was also informed by the Secretary, that the remaining amount, out
of the total provided for 8th Plan, would not be enough for the terminal year of the plan. In
view of the submission made by the Secretary, the Committee infers that the Planning
Commission has not taken a very realistic view of the needs of the Family Welfare
Programmes which aim at arresting the alarming growth of population.

2.5 The Committee, therefore, feels that the plan outlay should be raised sufficiently, at
an appropriate stage, in order not only to sustain the existing Family Welfare Programmes

1


2

but also to take new initiatives to achieve the objectives spelt out in the Eighth Plan
Document. The Committee feels any increase in allocation in the context of growing
population would not be a bad investment.

2.6 The Committee also notes with concern that the share of Family Welfare sector,
which was 1.8% of the total public sector outlay during the 7th Plan, has been reduced to
1.5% during the 8th Plan. In view of the nature and size of the population, and a large
portion of the family welfare plans accounts for health infrastructure and services at the
grass root level, which are of vital importance for improving the lot of the poorer and
weaker sections of the society, the Committee strongly recommends that at least 3% of the
total public sector outlay should be set aside for family welfare plans.

2.7 The Committee points out that there is a keen interest among international donor
agencies to provide assistance for our population control programmes. However, this
assistance can be availed of only if a matching provision exists in the family welfare budget.
Normally, it can not be accommodated within the budget, which otherwise also is inadequate
for normal programmes without a matching step up. The Committee, therefore, feels that
there is a strong case for providing additional assistance for key areas of family welfare
programmes.

In the Eighth Plan the outlay provided is Rs. 6500.00 crores—nearly double the amount

the total Plan outlay showing thereby a step up as compared to the 1.43% which was the
actual expenditure on Family Welfare during the Seventh Plan period.

Considering the existing severe resource constraint it is not possible to further increase
the outlay for Family Welfare during the Eighth Plan period. However, from the data on
outlays and expenditure during the Eighth Plan period given below it would appear that the

Comments of the Committee

The country’s population is at the threshold of crossing 100 crores and soon it may
overtake China, the most populated country. Resources being limited, the country needs to
give top-most priority to population control programme. This much felt concern does not
reflect in the budgetary allocations. Unless population growth is controlled, the country
cannot prosper and people cannot have a comfortable living, Keeping this in mind, the
Committee recommended allocation of 3% of total Public Sector outlay for family welfare
programmes. Planning Commission should give a serious thought to this, The Committee
reiterates its earlier recommendation for higher allocation for family welfare programmes
keeping in view their importance for the overall development of the society. The
Department should again stress upon the Planning for higher allocations. Simultaneously,
the Department should make full use of the offers from international donar agencies who
are keen to assist us in the population control programmes.

Recommendation (Paras 4, 4.1 & 4.2)

4. To provide a-comprehensive Primary Health Care Service at the grass root level, a
sub-centre is established on the basis of the centre for every 5,000 population in plain areas
and one for 3,000 population in hilly and tribal areas.

4.1 The Committee notes that, as on 30th July, 1994 there were 1,31,471 sub-centres

Government of India. It also notes that a provision of Rs. 190 crores has been made for
Rural Sub-centres this year. To a question as to how the rest of the Centres are being
fundedS the Secretary stated that these centres have been set up under the Minimum Needs
Programme and are being funded by it. He also informed that no new sub-centre was
proposed to be added this year. के

4.2 The Committee is of the view that since a majority of our people live in rural and
tribal areas and these centres are peripheral health institutions providing basic health and
family welfare services to them, the decision of the Department not to add new Centres is
quite disappointing. The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious efforts be made by
the Department to provide adequate funds not only to open more sub-centres this year but

4, 4.1 & 4.2 There are 131900 sub-centres existing in the country out of which 97557

In case, State Governments wish to open additional sub-centres, they are free to open

The Committee is pained to note that no rural sub-centre was opened since -1990-91

the country cannot progress inspite of the scientific and industrial growth. The Department
should reconsider the matter and try to convince the Planning Commission of the necessity
of additional resources and allocation for expansion of the scheme.

Post Partum Programme
Recommendation (Para 6.1)

6.1 The Committee feels that for such a vital programme that too when the programme
is quite a success—a lower allocation this year is quite disturbing. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that allocation to this programme be increased, and steps be taken to further
expand it. The Committee also feels that the registration of all the births is not being done
as provided in the law, and this job may be entrusted to the local panchayats which will be
required to submit monthly reports to concerned authorities.

Ministry’s Reply

6.1 It is admitted that the allocation is less. Against Rs. 49 crores allocated for the
Scheme the likely expenditure would be Rs. 56.50 crores. If allocation is increased, the
programme can be expanded. For district level Post Partum Programme the allocation
during 1995-96 has been only Rs. 1900 lakhs and for sub-district level Post Partum
Programme Rs. 3000 lakhs. Thus the total allocation is Rs. 4900 lakhs and not Rs.4000 lakhs
as per the report. This allocation for district / sub-district level Post Partum Programme has
been static during the last three years.

The registration of births and death falls within the purview of the office of the
Registrar General of India. The Registration of Births & Deaths (RBD) Act, 1969 provides
for the appointment of registration functionaries at various levels like: (i) Registrar General,
India at national level; (ii) Chief Registrar at the State level; (iii) District Registrar at
District level; and (iv) Registrar for local areas such as Panchayat, Municipality, Municipal
Corporation or other local bodies.

The actual work of registration is carried out by a three tier hierarchy of State
Government/U.T. Administration officials drawn from one or more departments viz. the
Chief Registrar at State level, District Registrar at District level and local Registrar at
periphery level. Under the RBD Act, 1969, authority for the appointment of Chief
Registrar, District Registrar and Registrar at local area levels has been given to the State
Governments.

In rural areas the registration functionaries can be classified into Panchayats, Police,
Health, Education and Revenue. In urban areas, Health Officers or Executive Officers of
municipalities function as Registrars of Births and Deaths. The distribution of rural
Registrars ‘by type of agency is as under:-

Panchayat 11 States+1 UTT

Police Station Officer 4 States+1 UT

Village level Revenue Official 2 States+2 UTs
Community Development 2 States

Sub-Divisional /Tehsil Office 2 States+1 UT us
Primary Health Centre 3 States+1 UT v
Teachers 2 States

On the basis of Model Rules prepared by the Registrar-General, of India, various State
Governments have framed their rules which have been duly notified by them. Registration
of births in various parts of the country is being done according to the provisions of the
Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 and rules framed by the State Governments.


6

While under the 1969 Act, registration of births has been made compulsory throughout
the country, registration is still far from complete. Reasons are apathy of genera] public
towards registration, ignorance, and lack of utility of birth certificate in the persgnal life of
common citizens. For. improving the completeness of registration and increasing the
awareness if general public, the Registrar-General Office has undertaken several
promotional measures. Publicity campaigns have been launched through T.V., radio,
posters, cinema slides, printing of slogans of postal stationery etc. for promoting the
completeness of registration. In several States production of birth certificate has been made
compulsory for first school admission and entries of the name of new born in the ration
card. Inter-departmental co-ordination committees have been set up in various States.

Panchayat Officials are doing registration in a majority of the States. However,
entrusting the registration work to Panchayat does not necessarily result in improving the
registration as seen from the low registration levels in U.P. (26 per cent), Bihar (21 per
cent) and Rajasthan (22 per cent). On the other hand, there are States which have
registration officials other than those from Panchayat and yet have high levels of registration
for births e.g. Karnataka (Revenue Official—63 per cent), Punjab (Police Officials — 88 per
cent), Orissa (Health Officials—65 per cent) and Tamil Nadu (Revenue Officials—87 per
cent).

Comments of the Committee

Accepting that allocation being less and static is not sufficient. The Department should
make efforts to get higher allocations

It is disturbing to note that inspite of registration of births being compulsory under the
Act, it is far from complete in any of the States. There is no_uniform system of registration
in the States. The Centre shduld fix responsibility on one single agency, be it Panchayats or
Revenue Officials, and they should be held accountable. The Committee has noted that the
performance of those States where Panchayats have been entrusted’ with this task, is not en-
couraging. New Gram Panchayats have come up in almost all the States and they are the
most appropriate bodies to be entrusted with this responsibility. Panchayats can be made
over all In-charge under whose supervision other egencies, such as Revenue Officials, may
work.

Recommendations (Para 7.3 & 7.4)

7.3 The Committee also notes, with concern, the falling percentage of males among
acceptors of sterilisation. The Department stated that in order to motivate more men, a new

par with tubectomy.

7.3. & 7.4 Although the new UNFPA assisted No-Scalpel Vasectomy Project has been

this new method of No-Scalpel Vasectomy. Guidelines are also being issued to all States/
UTs for popularising Vasectomy and increasing involvement of males in Family Welfare
Programme. The Compensation for loss of wages (Rs. 100+) paid to the acceptors of
Vasectomy is already at par with that of the acceptors of Tubectomy under the existing
scheme. hi be
Comments of the Committee

The Committee desires that the Department should get the No-Scalpel Vasectomy
approved by the Project Implementation Committee at the earliest. Being a better method,
it needs to be given wide publicity. The Department should undertake the publicity of an
extensive scale and provide adequate trainees for the project. *

Involvement of Non-Governmental Organisations Recommendation (Para 11.1)
Recommendation (Para 1.1)

11.1 Keeping in view the nature and magnitude of population control programme, the
Committee feels that the involvement of NGOs to supplement the Governmental efforts is
crucial that any let up in this regard would prove to be detrimental.. The Committee,

therefore, recommends that an in-depth study should be undertaken by the Department so
as to find out the reasons for the reluctance of NGO to take up family welfare programmes.
Ministry’s Reply

11.1 The Government is conscious of the importance of involvement of NGOs in the
family welfare programme. Several steps have been taken during the last 2-3 years to step up
NGOs’ involvement in the programme by devising new and attractive model . schemes,
organising regional/State level and national level meetings with prominent NGOs, State
Government functionaries*to educate and motivate them to work for the family welfare
programme. As a result of these efforts as large number of organisations in the country have
come up for taking up projects under the various schemes. Seven large and well established


8

organisations have been recognised as Mother Units and given power to support 50 NGOs in
their area. An imprest of Rs. 10 lakhs has been placed at their disposal from which grant on
approved projects can be released to the smaller NGOs and replenished from the
Department of Family Welfare so that the imprest amount always remains at Rs. 10 lakhs.
In the State also State SCOVA Committees have been set up and they have been given
powers to sanction projects upto Rs. 10 lakhs per project.

As a result of these efforts the Department of Family Welfare has been able to upgrade
the level of funding support to NGOs from Rs. 3.29 crores in 1990-91 to Rs. 16.30 crores in
1994-95. The number of NGOs supported has also gone up from 91 in 1990-91 to 831 in

Department of Family Welfare. Similarly there are indications that a large number of
projects are being received by the State SCOVA Committees and Mother Unit
Organisations. There would, therefore, be no dearth of NGOs working for the family
welfare programme in the country in the near future.

The Department of Family Welfare has ordered mid-term evaluation of projects
sanctioned under the model schemes during 1993-94 to know the result of the schemes and

The Committee has been given to understand that a mid-term evaluation of projects
sanctioned under the model scheme during 1993-94 has been completed. The Committee

Recommendation (Para 6)

6. Besides providing ante-natal, natal and post-natal services to expectant mothers, this
programme also provides family planning services. In other words, it is a maternity centred
hospital-based approach to Family Welfare Programme. It covers 550 Post Partum Centres
at the District Levei hospitals and 1012 centres at the Sub-district level hospitals. This year a
provision of Rs. 40 crores has been made, which shows a slight reduction over the last year.
The Department stated that it is due to the fact that the component of de-canalisation has
been excluded from the programme.


Ministry’s Reply

No action
Sterilisation Beds
Recommendation (Paras 7 & 7.1)

7.. A scheme for reservation of sterilisation beds in hospitals and nursing homes for
providing facility for tubectomy operations was felt necessary as the beds for such cases were
not readily available. At present, a total of 2797 beds are available. A maintenance grant of
Rs. 3,000 per bed per annum is paid to each institution provided they have achieved 75/60
tubectomies per annum.

7.1 An allocation of Rs. 1 crore has been made this year. The Department claims that
the programme is quite a success, and 1,05,269 tubectomies were performed during 1993-94
over 58 tubectomies per bed per annum.

Ministry’s Reply
No action
Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives

Recommendation (Paras 8 and 8.1, 8.2)

8. The budget allocation for free distribution of contraceptives has been reduced from
Rs. 76 crores in 1994-95 to Rs. 69 crores in 1995-96. To a specific question regarding the
reduced allocation, the Department stated that earlier targets of contraceptive users were
being fixed by the Department in consultation with the States and supplies used to be
dispatched accordingly. In order to reduce wastage from this year onwards, the States have
been requested to work out their requirements in this regard and supplies will be made
accordingly.

8.1 The Department stated in the performance budget, that greater thrust was being laid
on spacing method for younger couples and there was a likelihood of increase in the total
demand for conventional contraceptives.

8.2 The Committee hopes that the increase in requirement of contraceptives will be met
by the Department despite a reduced allocation.

Ministry’s Reply

8, 8.1 & 8.2: During 1995-96 no targets for Free Distribution of condoms have been set
by Deptt. of Family Welfare. Supply of condom stocks to the States will be on the basis of
demand projected by the States. This will lead to significant reduction in wastages, but there
will be no problem in meeting all genuine requirements projected by the States.

Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
Recommendation (Para-9)

9. IEC activities are carried out to achieve wider publicity for family welfare methods.
A sum of Rs. 34.46 crores has been allocated this year. The Department proposes to
establish IEC Bureaus at State level, so that local-specific communication material can be
prepared. It also proposes to establish Population Awareness Units through Nehru Yuvak
Kendra Sangathan and Mahila Mandals by involving the youth and women respectively.

Ministry’s Reply
No action


Research & Evaluation
Recommendation (Paras 10 & 10.1)

10. The allocation for Research & Evaluation has been reduced from Rs. 16.59 crores in
B.E. 1994-95, to Rs. 15.79 crores in 1995-96. For Indian Council for Medical Research (ICMR),
the provision has been reduced from Rs. 9 crores to Rs. 7.5 crores. Explaining the reason for
reduction in the provision to ICMR, the Secretary stated that ICMR was given grants-in-aid on
a year to year basis for undertaking research in contraceptive technology by involving 33 Human
Reproduction Reseach Centres (HRRC), and this year the Department is proposing to establish
14 more HRRCs. Another reason is that out of the 33 HRRCs established so far, only 23 have
agreed to implement the district project evolved by the ICMR and the rest opted out of it since it
was voluntary.

10.1 The Committee is of the opinion that the research and evaluation activities are very
crucial for developing new techniques of population control. It also feels that the allocation
made is not adequate even for sustaining the ongoing programmes. The Committee therefore.
recommends that allocations for research activities should be raised suitably. The Committee
also feels, that the Department should take adequate measures to persuade the remaining
HRRCs also to accept the district projects which are basically meant for improving the quality of
family planning services at the district level.

Ministry's Reply

10 & 10.1 The allocation of grant to Indian Council of Medical Research for various
research activities during the current year is 750 lakhs as against 723 lakhs during 1994-95.

The working and progress made in the District Project by HRRCs was reviewed by
Secretary (FW) and the project was dropped from six HRRCs because of poor performance by
HRRCvs/specific request from HRRCs to terminate the district project.

Involvement of Non-Governmental Organisations
Recommendations (Paras 11 & 13)

11. A sum of Rs. 8.5 crores has been provided for the year 1995-96 under this Head. The

He however, accepted that more of that were coming forward now and their number had
increased considerably. The Secretary admitted that the present level of allocation would not be
adequate to meet the requirement in this regard.

Area Development Project
Recommendation (Para 13)
13. Area Development Projects have been taken up with financial assistance from external

agencies in 15 States and in the National Capital Territory of Delhi to improve health and family
welfare delivery system. It is noted that its outlay has been kept at the level of the year 1994-95.

Ministry’s Reply
No action

Recommendation (Paras 19 & 19.1)

19. On the question of progress made in framing the Rules and the Constitution of the
proposed Central Supervisory Board with regard to implementation of the Pre-natal Diagnostic

24

19 & 19.1 The constitution of the Central Supervisory Board under the Pre-Natai

Recommendation (Para 21)

21. In the process of implementation of various programmes / schemes relating to family
welfare, a vast network of institutions for the delivery of health and family welfare services
have come up in our country. The quality of service, which varies markedly from State to
State, the Committee feels is far from satisfactory. The outreach is insufficient, particularly

improving the quality and outreach of services at the earliest.

22. It appears to the Committee that keeping in view the general constraint of

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, do hereby present the Fourth· Report of the Committee on the National Health 
Programme s of the Department of Health (Ministry of Health & Family Welfare). 
The Committee considered various documents and papers received from the Department of 
Health and also heard its Secretary and other officials to elicit further information at its meetings 
held on the lOth & 11th June, 1993. 
The details of the working, targets, achievements, allocations and expe nditur e regarding 
major Nationa l Health Programmes of the Department viz. National Malaria Eradication 
Programme; Kala-azar; National Filaria Control Progr amme; Nationa l Lepr0sy Eradicat ion 
Programme; National Programme for Co'1trol of Blindness and National AIDS Control 
Programme were discussed by the Committee and have been included in the Report. 
The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on the 16th December, 
1993.

An Overview 
1. 'Health is Wealth' is a well-known proverb and it is an axiomatic fact that only healthy 
citizens can make a nation prosperous and healthy. Health plays a vital role in the making of a 
nation great and strong. Development and maintenance of good health is not only a personal or 
an individual effort but a Welfare State also plays a very important role in it. 
2. It is expressly mentioned in our Constitution in Article 47, which relates to the Directive 
Principles of State Policy, that 'The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the 
standard of living of its people an~ the improvement of public health among its primary duties ... ' 
The improvement of health and ritilrition on national basis is the respon sibility of the Central 
Council of Health. Since the inception of planning process in 1952, various health programmes 
have been introduced in the country. In pursuance of its commitment, Government also 
formulated a national Policy on Health in 1983. 
3. But, the dimensions that health problems have acquired in our country are really complex 
and alarming. Majority of diseases people suffer from are poverty-related , while some have their 
origin in the utter Jack of cleanliness and awareness or consciousness towards health. Rapid 
increase in environmental pollution , increasing population, cropping up of new diseases like 
AIDS and cancer are some of the challenges that the nation is facing today. To fight on all these 
fronts simultaneously is, of course, a formidable task, particularly when the resources at hand are 
limited. 
4. As per World Bank estimates, in India only 1.3% of the Gross Domestic Product is spent 
on health which is perhaps the lowest amongst the developing countries. It is flabbergasting to 
f~rther note that the alloca tion has shown a gradual diminishing trend in the successive Five Y car 
Plans. For instance, 3.3% of the total outlay in the First Five Year Plan has come down to a 
dismal 2:74% during the Eighth Five Year Plan. In the face of the financial constraints foreign 
assistance was sought. Some traditional diseases like Leprosy, Tuberculosis, Malaria, Blindness, 
~tc. still persist affecting the majority of our population. In such a situation, it is to be seen if 
Government's commitment to attain the goal of health for all by 2000 A.D. could possibly be 
fulfilled. 
5. World Bank assistance to the scale of 100 to 200 million dollars per year has been cleared 
for Health sector throughout the Eighth Five Year Plan. The first project taken up under this 
project is the AIDS Control Programme. A<>sistance is also expected for Leprosy and Blindness 
Control Programmes. 
6. In an effort to fight the menace of major diseases Government is implementing various 
National Health Programmes. The Committee had detailed deliberations on some of them 
namely; National Malaria Eradication Programme; Kala-azar; National Filaria Control Prog­
ramme; National Leprosy Eradication Programme; National Programm e for Contro l of Blindness 
and the National AIDS Control Jirogramme . 

I. National Malaria Eradication Programme 
7. It is estimated that at the time of country's Independence in 1947, there were over 75 
million malaria cases and about one million deaths had occured due to it. For its control, a 
national strategy was formulated in the year 1953. DDT proved to be a very effective insecticide 
and a great success was achieved in controlling this disesase. Encouraged by this initial success, 
the National Malaria Control was renamed as 'National Malaria Eradication Programme ' in the 
year 1958. By the year 1965, the incidence of malaria witnessed a downward trend, with nil 
mortality rat e which was, in itself, a great achievement. But this success was short-lived as in the 
mid-seventies recurrence of malaria was visible. There was a sharp increase in the number of 
reported malaria cases to the tune of 6.47 million per year. The strategy was revised once again 
named Modified Plan of Operation (MPO) ·with the objective of elimination of mortality rate, 
effective control of malaria and maintaining the gains achieved so far in its eradication. The 
objectives were sought to be achieved by prompt case- detection through active and passive 
surveillance and vector control by residual insecticidal spraying. 
8. Since 1984, the incidence of malaria has stabi lized at around 2 million cases per year. It is 
reported that during the year 1991, there were 1.81 million positive cases of malaria and around 
400 deaths. During the year 1992, there were approximately 1.4 million reported malaria cases. 
Though tribals constitute only 8% of the total population, yet they account for over 30% of the 
malaria cases and 60% of the deaths on account of P. Falciparum. Similarly, there was a sharp 
increase in the number of cases detected in urban slums from 1,39,057 in 1989 to 2,11,890 in 
1991. Studies and surveys conducted in this regard have shown the presence of resistance to DDT 
and a combination of anti-malaria insecticides. 
9. There are Seven States in the country namely, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, 
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan which are more vulnerable and most of the malaria 
deaths have occured there. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare for the year 1992-93, Malaria cases during the last five years indicated that in the year 
1988, ther( have been 1.85 million cases with 0.68 million P. Falciparum cases and 209 deaths. In 
1989, there were 2.05 malaria cases with 0.76 million P. Falciparum cases and 268 deaths, in 1990 
out of the 2.02 million malaria cases there have been 0.75 million P. Falciparum cases with 353 
deaths, in 1991 out of 2.11 million malaria cases there were 0.91 million P. Falciparum cases with 
421 deaths and in 1992, there were 1.42 million cases with 0.45 million P. Falciparum cases and 
246 deaths. 
10. The National Malaria Eradication Programme is being implemented as a centrally 
sponsored category-11 on a 50:50 cost sharing basis between the States and the Central 
Government. Under this Programme, the Central Government meet s the cost of entire quantity 
of DDT and partially of BHC and Malathion, antimalaria drugs like Chloroquine, Primaquine 
and Pyrenthamine, etc. The State Governments are expected to meet the expenditure on staff 
and other operational costs for successful implementation of the Programme. 
11. During his oral evidence tendered before the Committee , the Secretary, Department of 
Health , informed that malaria has taken an endemic turn because of the fact that the health 
infrastructure in the most affected States is'ex tremely weak. The Dcptt. has also reali sed that the 
tribal and hilly areas where malaria infection cases are high, have to be dealt with on a different 
footing from the rest of the country. Fifty per cent share of the States has to be reviewed and the 

Central Government is thinking to have the central scheme implemented by taking assistance 
from World Bank to fight this menance. Keeping this in view, it is proposed to intensify the 
efforts for the full containment of malaria during the Eighth Five Year Plan. Accordingly, major 
attention is proposed to be given to the tribal sub-plan areas of Seven States of Andhra Pradesh, 
Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan, the urban population and 
population living in the project areas and rest of the country. This control strategy is a balanced 
mixture of preventive and curative measures for elective spraying for vector control, larviciding 
and source reduction in urban areas and early detection and treatment. 
12. During his oral evidence tendered before the Committee, the Secretary, Department of 
Health, informed that they had achieved a great initial success in controlling malaria, but when 
the incidence reached a figure of 1,00,000 in the entire country in the seventies, they liad a 
rebound and the incidence rose to about 6.5 million. Thereafter, the programme was started in 
1977 and they were able to bring this figure down to 2 million in 1984. After that, this figure has 
more or less ramained stable. It means there has been n0 further improvement after 1984. This 
was due to a very high level of infection in the tribal areas of North-East. The migrant labour 
iorce from these areas going to different parts of the country also contributes to the spread of 
Malaria. A lot of on going construction activities contribute to the cause of stagnation of water 
and pollute environment leading to breeding of mosquitoes, hence the incidence of malaria. 
13. The Committee was informed that for this purpose, a sum of Rs. 86 corres was spent 
during the year 1991-92. In 1992-93, Rs. 65 crores were allocated for malaria control programme 
which also included other vector diseases like Kala-azar and Filaria. Now, this amount has been 
increased to Rs. 87 crores for procuring insecticides, larvicides and drugs. For the year 1993-94, a 
sum of Rs. 110 crores has been allotted. It is also proposed to provide 100% Central assistance to 
the North Eastern States and the tribal sub-plan areas. For the tribal areas, it is also proposed to 
mobilise resourc es from the World Bank as well. 
14. The Committee was informed that there was mainly three reasons for the resurgence of 
malaria, namely:-
(i) Administrative reasons-complacency shown by the administration after getting some 
initial success. 
(ii) Technical reasons-
(a) Mosquitoes became immune to many insecticides and the insecticides which were 
very effective in the past became ineffective; 
(b) the parasites have been irresistable to certain drugs; 
(c) New drugs were tried out which also contributed in non-effectiveness of the 
programme to some extent. 
(iii) Financial reasons- The programme was integrated into the Primary Health Centres after 
getting initial success in the sixties. The Primary Health Centres being very busy in their 
own programmes, could . not provide attention and time which was very necessary for 
controlling malaria. Even financial allocation required for filling up the posts which were 
available in the sub-centres for eradication of malaria remained unfilled; the supply of 
PLO, etc. was not available because of financial constraints. All these factors 
contributed to the failure of the programme. Even financial allocations were reduced. 

Kala-Azar 
15. Kala-azar is another deadly disease which has become a serious Public Health Problem in 
Bihar and West Bengal. It is observed that after its resurgence in Bihar in early 70s, the disease 
has spread over from 4 districts to adjoining areas and now 30 districts in Bihar and 9 districts in 
West Bengal are the most affected. This estimate is based on cases reported in Government 
hospitals only. Some cases go to private practitioners and thus remain unreported. The disease is 
on the increase and has assumed serious dimensions in the above two States. 
16. According to the estimates, there were 14079 Kala-azar cases in the year 1986 with 47 
deaths and in West-Bengal there were 3718 cases with 25 deaths in the same year. There has 
be~n a rap id increase both in its incidence as weB as deaths in Bihar. In the year 1989, there 
were 30903 cases with 477 deaths in Bihar and 3575 cases with 20 deaths in West Bengal. In t~e 
year 1992 there were 66959 Kala-azar cases in Bihar with 1266 deaths (provisional upto October). 
So there has been alarming increase, both in the incidence and the death cases in Bihar which 
requires immediate remedial steps. 
17. Organised control measures have been initiated to control Kala-azar. Upto 1990-91, 
financial assistance for its control was being provided by the Central Government out of the 
NMEP budget provisions. However, separate funds amounting to Rs. 4.06 crores were madt: 
available during 1990-91 for control of this disease in Bihar and West Bengal. 
18. The Committee was informed that in order to check the menace, efforts are being made 
for interruption of transmission, for reducing vector population by undertaking indoor residual 
insecticidal spray twice annually. Early diagnosis and treatment of Kala-azar cases and providing 
health education for community awareness, are also being undertaken in this connection. 
19. The Committee was also informed that in view of the financial constrai nts, the Central 
Government decided to meet the total cost of medicines and insecticides for Kala-azar control in 
Bihar. Under the district action plan development, State Governments have agreed to deploy 
exclusive infrastructure for Kala-azar control and adequate material with strict superv ision, 
monitoring and evaluation. The concept of making different functionarie s at various levels 
responsible and accountable for success of the programme is likely to make a good impact on 
reduction of the incidence of Kala-azar. 
20. The Central Government is providing insecticides and imported anti Kala-azar drug i.e. 
Pentamidine Isothionate to the West Bengal Government. The Central Government has also 
provided assistance to the Bihar Government in cash and kind during the last two years i.e. in 
1990-91 and 1991-92, to the tune of Rs. 389.49 and Rs. 1535.99, respectively. 
21. A budget provision of Rs. 1500.00 lakhs has been made to provide material assistance for 
Kala-azar control. However, in view of the seriousness of the problem, commitment of the 
Central Government to ensure availability of material for effective control, a Revised Estimates 
for Rs. 2376.55 lakh has been proposed to meet the cost of insecticides and anti Kala-azar drugs. 
22. In addition UNICEF assistance of Rs. 15.55 lakh had been provided for 1990-91 to the 
State Governments for public information, education, communication activities and orientation 
training of medical professionals. UNICEF is providing assistance on continuing basis directly to 
the State Government of Bihar. Material assistance including the insecticides, DDT and the 
imported drug Pentamidine lsothionate is also provided. 

National Filaria Control Programme 
23. Filaria, like Malaria is also a deadly disease which has become a major health problem in 
our country. The disease has been prevalent throughout India except the States of Jammu & 
Kashmir, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh. ~liwram, Meghalaya, Tripura, Manipur, Rajasthan, 
Arunachal Pradesh. Delhi, Chandig~uh . f L .. :yana, Sikkim & Nagaland. Present estimates indicate 
that about 389 million people are li\·,ng in 175 endemic districts of which about 103 million are 
living in urban areas and the rest in rural areas. 
24. In order to control this disease, the National Filaria Control Programme was taken up in 
the year 1955 with the following action plan:-
(i) Delimitation of the problem in hither-to unsurveyed area; 
(ii) Control in Urban Areas through : 
a) Recurrent anti-larval measures; and 
b) Antiparasitic measure~. 
25. For this purpose about 206 Central Units, 27 Survey Units and 195 Clinks are working in 
the country. About 43.43 million people in urban areas are being protected through anti-larval 
measures by 206 control units and 195 clinics are giving treatment with Diethy I Uarbanarine to 
clinical cases and microfilaria. 
26. During the course of his oral evidence tendered before the Committee, the Secretary, 
Department of Health informed that efforts made in this connection have shown remarkable 
results . It is observed that about 73 per cent of the towns in microfilaria rate and about 69 per 
cent of towns in the disease rates where control measures are in operation for more than five 
years. have shown marked reduction in the filaria cases. 
Monitoring

Programme and this organisation has got a good number of people spread all over the country. In 
addition to this, there are about 17 Regional Directors of Health posted in different States. 
Observations I recommendations

eradication and control of malaria, resu lting in resurgence of malaria cases, especially after 
achieving initial success to a great extent during the fifties and the sixties. 
29. The Committee feels th;Jt a~sistance of World Bank be obtained expeditiously and new 
methods and technology should be useJ for the purpose. 
30. The Committee recommends that State Governments should be asked to be more 
vigilant, prompt, to strengthen the infrastructure including adequate staff anJ to make it 
obligatory for the private practitioner<: 10 report all the ca<;es to the authorities concerned. 
Malaria Research Centres should be provided requisite infrasrntcttJrc and staff to act as watch­
clogs. 
31. The Committee observes that the allocations for .\l daria are combined with the 
allocations for filaria and Kala-azar, which means that when there is an increase in filaria and 
Kala-azar part of allocations may be accordingly shifted to these areas, reducing the actual 
allocation for mahuia. The Committee recommends separate allocations for all the three wings

of all three diseases having common aiiocai1ons . it is quite dear tiw L rhae bas been no actual 

increase in funds for anti-malaria programme in spite of the fact that the number of malaria cases 
have not come down since 1984. Not only that, there has been an increase in malaria cases, 
particularly cases of Malaria falciparum in tribal areas and in urban slums. The fact that majority 
of deaths from malaria being in tribal areas (60% of total cases) was found shocking by 
Committee. It is recommended that the recently-cleared proposal of making malaria eradication 
programme in tribal and other malaria-prone areas where health service is weak a 100% 
centrally-sponsored Scheme should be immediately implemented. Regular monitoring must also 
be done through cooperation with State Governments and local bodies. 
32. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the shortage of some effective and 
potent medicines to cure malaria particularly P. Falciparum and recommends that steps should be 
taken to ensure that the requisite medicines arc easily available in all the Hospitals/Dispensaries 
and in the open market. Government should also supply such medicines under National Malaria 
Eradication Programme to all the States so that all the State Government Hospitals could have 
the medicine. Arrangements should also be made to supply these medicines through Mobile 
dispensaries in the areas most affected by Malaria. Regular spray in the affected areas should also 
be undertaken. Inpregnated bed nets duly dipped in synthetic chemicals which not only kill the 
mosquitoes but also acts a repellent be provided wherever possible. 
33. As per the annual report (1992-93) of the Ministry of Health &. family Welfare, budget 
provisions and expenditure, both in cash and kind, is not adequate. Instead of increase, there has 
been decrease both in the allocations and the actual expenditure incurred on filaria Eradication 
Programmes. 
34. The Committee recommends that adequate funds, separate from the Malaria Eradication 
Programme, may be provided for controVEradication of Filaria and Kala-azar. 
35. The Committee also recommends that concerted efforts should be made to use new 
techniques and no laxity be shown in this regard. The Committee also recommends that both 
urban and rural areas be covered under Filaria Eradication Programme and awareness 
Programme should be given wide publicity through print and electronic media. Adequate supply 
of anti-filaria drugs in hospitals, dispensaries and in the open market be ensured apart from the 
usual spraying. 
II. National Leprosy Eradication Programme 
36. India has a very high rate of incidence of leprosy, which is widespread all over the 
country, and is one of the major health problems. 
37. The magnitude of the disease can be judged by the fact that as per the Ministry's Annual 
Report (1992-93), out of 10 million cases of leprosy in the world, 2.5 million are estimated to be 
found in India. The prevalance rate of leprosy exists above 5 per 1000 population in 201 districts 
out of 468 districts and about 15% of the leprosy sufferers arc children below 15 years of age. 
38. The leprosy control Programme, which was in existence since 1955, was given priority 
and redesignated as National Leprosy Eradication Programme in 1983. It is one of the centrally 
sponsored Health Schemes financed 100% by the Central government and implemented through 
State governments. 
39. During the course of his oral evidence tendered by the Secretary, Department of Health, 
the Committee was informed that the programme has been launched in 135 districts which are 
considered endemic i.e. where the prevalence rate is more than 5 per thousand. The Programme 
remains to be launched in 66 other districts which are in the same category. Then 

there are 77 other districts which are moderately endemic i.e. having a prevalance rate of 2 to 5 
per thousand. If these 143 districts are covered over and above 135 districts that are already 
covered then 95% of the leprosy patil·nts will be covered. 
40. The Committee was also informed that in the last 5-6 years, since the introduction of 
Multi-drug Therapy there has been a major breakthrough in bringing down the incidence of 
leprosy as out of estimated 4 million cases in 1981, the number has come down to 1.4 million by 
the end of february, 1993. Wherever the Multi-drug Therapy Programme has been in operation 
for more than 5 years, there is 80% reduction in incidence. 
41. The Secretary of the Health department stated that the programme has produced 
dramatic results and it is expected that leprosy would be eliminated from the country by the turn 
of the century, i.e. when the prevalence rate will be below 1 per 10,000 population. 
42. The Secretary of the department admitted that in an effort to cure more and more cases 
sufficient attention had not been paid to rehabilitation and reconstructive surgery and to help the 
patients lead a normal life after they are cured. 
43. Therefore, it is very necessary to have centres of reconstructive smgery and rehabilitation 
and a sustained health eduction campaign to make people understand that the patients who are 
cured or have undergone treatment for the disease arc absolutely safe and infection free. 
44. The Committee was informed that under the programme of major reconstructive surgery 
there is no plan to create new institutions instead under the world Bank project institutes where 
reconstructive surgery is available will be revamped and provided with equipments and appliances 
free of cost. 
45. These institutes will also be provided Rs. 250CY- for each major surgery and package of 
services which include full cost of operation service, OPD and total care of the patient. If an 
institute is not available within a district then the patient will be referred to any such institute 
established in a nearby district. In that case, the amount will be Rs. 250()1.. plus the 
reimbursement of travel expenses of the patient. 
46. It was informed that there are district Leprosy Officers in 105 districts in which Multi­
drug Therapy Programme has been taken up and also there is one doctor for every 4-5 lakhs of 
population. To ensure that the programme reaches every village there are village level workers 
for every 20,000 population who are supposed to go around and find out the cases and see that 
the services reach them for their treatment. 
47. The Secretary conceded that some posts of doctors are lying vacant in some districts and 
the State Governments have been urged to fill them up. 
48. There arc also District Leprosy Societies in all the districts where the programme has 
been taken-up. In the societies there are local representatives, members of Legislatures, 
panchayats etc. with whom various aspects of the programme are discussed. 
49. As regard role of Voluntary organisations it was informed that out of about 285 
voluntary organisations, 55 are receiving assistance from Central Government. The grants-in-aid 
are given under the Survey, Education and Treatment (S.E.T) Scheme and are released through 
the State Governments. 
50. The performance of the voluntary organisations are being closely monitored by the 
Central Government and also by the State Governments themselves. However, the Secretary 
admitted that it is possible that some voluntary organisations may not be performing upto the 
expectations but by and large they are doing commendable work. It was also informed that there

done extremely good work.

Rs. 140.00 crores as agamst actual expenditure of Rs. 40.00 crores during the Sixth Plan (1980-
85) and Rs. 85.82 crores during Seventh Plan (1985-90) The expediture for the 8th Five Year

Observations/recommendations 
1. The reported data has been validakd. 
2. The progress of programme is slow in littJr Pradr~h. Madhya Pradesh. Bihar. Oris;;a 
and West Bengal. 
3. A good number of posts of .Medical Officers. Non-t\1edical Supervisors are vacant in 
some states. Such vacancies are 20% to 30''l'o in Uttar Pradesh. Madhya Pradesh. Bihar

4. There is need for further toning up of logistic arrangements i.e. drugs. vehicle'i and

5. Temporary Hospitalization wards are not being utilised to their capacity. 
6. There is need to further tone-up the training acti\ ities. 
7. M.D.T . has been found to he very effective. 
54. The Committee appreciates the optimism of the Mini~try thJt they will be uble to 
eliminate leprosy from the country by the turn of the century and hopes that th<.. Ministry will

55. The Committee also hopes that the Ministry will learn k~son from their mistakes in 
Malar ia Eradication Programme and will not repeat them in this pt ogramme <;nC. recommends 
that foolp roof steps be taken not only t.)r the elimination of the leprosy hut also for rehabilitation

56. The Committee reco mmends that M.D.T. programme, which has produced dramatic 
results, be expanded to such an ex tent that all the distnct s of the country whe re the prevalence 
rate of leprosy is more than 2 per 1000 population and pockets of districts which have endemic 
leprosy , are brought under it immediately. The Committee also recommend s that rural and 
backward areas which have endemic leprosy be given special attention. 

57. The Committee expresses its deep anguish over the fact that Department has done 
almost nothing for so many years for the rehabilitation of the patients which virtually negates the 
objective of the programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that rehabilitation and 
reconstructive surgery be given utmost priority and centres of reconstructive surgery and 
rehabilitation be opened in all the districts where prevalence rate is more than 2 per 1000 
population. 
58. The Committee takes strong exception to the approach of the Department to treat cases 
in which disease starts eating up fingers and nose, as burn put cases for whom nothing much can 
be done except rehabilitation to a limited extent. 
59. The Committee is of the view that if the explanation of the Department is accepted no 
treatment is to be provided to the advance cases of AIDS and Cancer as they are not curable. 
The Committee feels that no case is a burn out case and every patient deserves the best 
treatment and rehabilitation even if he cannot be cured. 
60. The Committee, therefore, recommends that for the so called burnt out cases more 
humanistic approach be adopted and they be provided best possible treatment and he kept in the 
hospitals as long as it is required. 
61. The Committee also recommends that some scheme be formulated for the poor patients 
who are living on the river banks of religious places, begging on the streets or living in isolated 
places for whom even their families do not care and they may be provided food, clothing, shelter 
and all other medical attention. 
62. The Committee is not convinced with the claim made by the Secretary during the course 
of his oral evidence that they have one doctor for every 4 to 5 Jakhs of population and 
recommends that it should be ensured that there are doctors for every 4-5 lakhs of population 
and also recommends that Committee be informed of number of doctors in position in each 
district. 
63. The Committee fails to understand the rationale for having District Leprosy Officers in 
105 districts only when the programme has been launched in 135 districts. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that post of District Leprosy Offi.;ers be immediately created in remaining 
30 districts and also recommends that District Leprosy Officers be appointed in all the districts of 
the country, in phases, where the prevalence rate is more than 2 per 1000 population. The 
Committee is of the considered view that only doctors as District Leprosy Officer can properly 
monitor the progress of programme and recommends that only medical men be appointed as 
District Leprosy Officers. 
64. The Committee also recommends that wherever the post of District Leprosy Officer is 
vacant it should be immediately filled up and it should also be ensured that posts of District 
Leprosy Officers are not kept vacant for long durations. In case it is not possible to fill up the 
post for some reasons the alternative arrangements be made. 
65. The Committee feels that budget allocation of Rs. 35.00 crores for NLEP for the year 
1993-94 is inadequate and it should have been increased substantially keeping in view the 
importance of the programme arid rate of inflation, irrespective of the fact that World Bank grant 
worth Rs. 68 crores was expected to be released from August, 1994. In the course of oral 
evidence before the Committee, the Health Secretary said that refampicin, needed for both 
leprosy and tuberculosis, is now likely to be produced in the country from the basic stage. This 
would lead to the reduction of the cost of Refampicin, which is a costly drug now. The 
Committee thinks that instead of the price of drugs being primarily within the purview of the 

Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Health Ministry be also involved in this particularly in the 
case of basic drugs needed for national programmes. 
III. National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) 
66. Eye is the most beautiful and invaluable gift of nature. Without eyes world is nothing but 
darkness. India being the second most populous country in the world, has at present 14 per 
thousand cases of blindnes s. Government in its first effort to meet the backlog of blindness on a 
national scale, launched a National Programme for Trachorma Control in 1963. This Programme 
was subsequently merged into the National Programme for control of Visual impairment and 
prevention of blindness which was re-named in 1976 as National Programme for Control of 
Blindness (NPCB). Thi s is 100% a Central Government sponsored scheme. 
67. As per the evaluation of blindness done by All India Survey 1988-89, cataract is found to 
be responsible for 81% of blindness in India. 
68. National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCll ) aims at providing intensive health 
education for eye care through the mass media and extension education methods; extension of 
ophthalmic servic es in rural areas through mobile units and eye camps and establishment of

claims that it is engaged in the control of blindness since 1963 but the Committee is surprised to

therefore, recommends that there should not be any let up in the efforts to achieve the target of 
reducing the blindness from the present 14 per thousand to 3 per thousand by the turn of the 
century i.e. 2000 A.D. 
70. The Secretary, Dcpa1tment of Health, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, in his oral 
evidence tendered bef0re the Committee, has stated that at least two million people are being 
added every year to the number of persons requiring cataract operations whereas the 
performance has been to the tune of 1.5 million operations per year. In other words at least 
50,000 people are being added to the list of patients requiring cataract surgery every year. 
71. The Committee takes it seriously that the achievement rate of cataract operations is 
declining steadily. For instance, in the year 1990-91, the percentage of achievement for cataract 

operations was 92.53% but in the year 1991-92 it was only 73.47% and in 1992-93 it is 
expected still to go down as against the target of 20.00 lakhs, only 12.25 lakh operations have 
been performed till February, 1993. Therefore, this is a matter of great concern and anxiety. 
72. The Committee strongly recommends that Government should find out the reasons of 
this fall in the cataract operations and devise some programmes so that more and more 
cataract operations can be performed at a greater speed and if not more, at least targets fixed 
should be achieved every year. The Committee also puts a word of caution that in its urge to 
achieve the targets , Government should ensure that no quacks are used in such operations 
and that the number of casualities should be eliminated completely. It should also be ensured 
that post-operations care should be given high priority and benefits given to the poor families 
undergoing such operations should reach them immediately such as grant of Rupees Sixty for 
spectacles and the like. 
73. The Committee is surprised to find that no foolproof method has been adopted in 
calculating the cataract operations done by the private and non-Government organisations 
(NGOs) and recommends that supply of information to the PHC or CHO at the district level 
should be made mandatory for all such organisations engaged in the cataract operations. 
74. The Secretary , Department of Health informed the Committee that corneal blindness 
is not a major reason for blind nor a contributory factor. But, the Committee feels that there 
is a need to set up eye-banks in the country and therefore recommends that Government 
should persue, educate and encourage people through mass media to donate eyes voluntarily 
on a large scale. Simultaneously, Government should also develop adequate infrastructu re and 
facilities in order to successfully procure the eye of each and every donor. 
75. Voluntary Organisations play a significant role to make Nation~! Programm e for 
Control of Blindness (NPCB) , successful, especially in t he field of Education, Prevention, 
Rehabilitation and Surgical services, etc. Government have been giving emphasis in the recent 
past to form District Blindness Contr ol Societies in all the States and Union Territori es which 
are to be registered under the Societies Registration A ct of 1860, under the control of Deputy 
Commissioneli'District Magistrate by involving voluntar y organisations of the area and raising 
funds from local sources. In this connection , t he District Ophthalmic Surgeon is the Member 
Secretary of the Society apart from the repr esentatives of the local and voluntary organisations 
and as per the oral evidence tendered before the Committee by the Secretary, Deptt. of 
Health 174 such societies have been formed so far and are functioning. 
76. The Committee feels that it is a very good step taken by Government in order to 
achieve targets fixed for cataract operations and making National Programme for Contr ol of 
Blindness a success and recommends that a mechanism may be evolved to hold meetings of 
such societies at least once in three months and all concerned should be asked to attend the 
meetings and also monitor the cataract operations performed in their district invariably. The 
Committee also recommends that concerted efforts should be made to form such societies in 
all the remaining distircts all over the country as soon as possible. 
77. As per the Annual Report of the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare for the year 
1992-93 funds allocations under Eighth Plan for the National Programme for Control of
