AN OVERVIEW 
The Ministry of Human Resource Development was set up in 1985 with the objective of 
integrating efforts towards the development of human potential in the areas of Education, 
Women & Child Development, Art, Culture, Youth Affairs & Sports. The Department of 
Education is an important constituent of this Ministry. During 1993-94 a budget provision of 
Rs. 2159.33 crores was made available for education in the Central Sector. This was increased to 
Rs. 2192 crores in the Revised Estimate 1993-94. 
2. There are a large number of subordinate offices and autonomous organisations under the 
Department which are engaged in carrying out the activities and programmes of the Department. 
They include, among others, the Directorate of Adult Education, National Council of 
Educational Research & Training (NCERT), National Institute of Educational Planning & 
Administration (NIEPA), University Grants Commission (UGC), Indian Council of Social 
Science Research (ICSSR), Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), the Navodaya Vidyalaya 
Samiti (NVS), the Central Board of Secondary Education, the National Book Trust, Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Regional Engineering Colleges. 
3. The National Policy on Education, 1986 has been instrumental in laying down the 
priorities in education at the national level. Elementary Education has been getting the highest 
priority in the educational sector, to accelerate the pace for achieving Universal Elementary 
Education by the end of this Century. The Operation Black Board scheme, launched in 1987-88, 
aims at bringing about significant improvement in the provision of facilities in primary schools. 
This is expected to improve retention of children in primary schools. 
4. The programme of Non-Formal Education aims at bringing education to working children, 
girls and children living in habitations which are not covered by formal schools. NFE is envisaged 
as an alternative strategy for formal education and plays a complementary role in achieving 
Universal Elementary Education by covering drop-outs or those who have not enrolled for one 
reason or the another. 
5. The Adult Education programme provides basic functional educational skills for those who 
could not avail the opportunities for education through formal and non-formal schools. The 
Technology Mission for Literacy, set up in 1988 with the aim of covering the total area, has 
achieved success in the southern, eastern and western regions and the focus has now shifted to 
the Hindi speaking States which have a low percentage of literacy. 
6. The Department is giving serious attention to achieving Education for All, and its 
endeavours towards this end found mention during the "Education for All Summit" of 9 populous 
countries of the world, held in 'New Delhi' in December, 1993. As a result of these endeavours, 
the resource allocation to education is expected to be increased from the existing 3.2% to 6% of 
the GNP from the 9th Plan. 
7. In the school education field, there are 796 Kendriya Vidyalayas, including three 
Vidyalayas in foreign countries. These are opened in areas with a sizeable concentration of 
Central Government employees. 
8. The Navodaya Vidyalayas scheme, launched in 1985, provides good quality education to 
talented children predominantly from rural areas. There are 321 Schools which are residential and 
offer education free of charge for all students. 
9. In the area of Vocational Education, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme was started in 1988 
with the main objective of providing diversification of educational opportunities to enhance 
individual employability. Vocational courses, mainly in the areas of Agriculture, Business & 
Commerce, Engineering & Technology, Health and Para Medical, Humanities and Home 
Science, are introduced at the +2 level in schools selected by the State Governments. So far, 

Vocational Sections have been sanctioned in 5,588 schools creating a capacity for diversification 
of 7.96 lakh students. 
10. The scheme of pre-vocational education has also been launched at the lower secondary 
stage in 1993-94 with the objective of imparting simple marketable skills to students in classes IX 
and X. 
11. The Department of Education has been seeking bilateral and multilateral assistance from 
international agencies so that additional resources may be available for educational programmes. 
Some new projects have been started in the last few years such as Mahila Samakhya Project in 
four States with the assistance of Netherlands; Andhra Pradesh Primary School Project with UK 
assistance; Lok Jumbish Project in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA; Shiksha Karmi Project 
in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA and Bihar Education Project with UNICEF assistance. 
12. In the Higher Education Sector, the University Grants Commission is concerned with 
promotion and coordination of university education and determination and maintenance of 
standards of teaching, examination and research in universities. The total number of Universities 
in 1993-94 was 189 with 7938 Colleges and a student enrolment of 48.05 Jakhs. A new Central 
University is also being set up in Tezpur to increase the facilities for higher education in the 
North-Eastern Region. 
13. In the Technical Education field, 5 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have been 
established to provide instruction and research in some branches of Engineering and Technology, 
Science and Arts for advancement of learning. These Institutes are imparting education at the 
undergraduate, postgraduate and research level, in addition to sponsoring research and they are 
fully funded by the Central Government. One more liT is proposed to be set up in Assam. 
14. The Regional Engineering Colleges have been set up to enable the country to meet the 
growing requirement of trained technical manpower. There are 17 Regional Engineering Colleges 
which offer First Degree Programmes in Engineering and Technology, out of which 14 have 
facilities for postgraduate and Doctoral programmes and also conduct research. 
REPORT 
15. Human Resource Development is of paramount importance for the progress of the 
country and education is one of the most important components in this regard. Though we are 
committed to achieve the objective of Education for All (EFA) by 2000 but increasing population 
and limited resources at hand are the two obstacles in the way of achieving this goal. 
16. At present, Budget outlay for Education is 3.2% of the (Gross Domestic Product) GDP 
and the Department of Education has assured that from 9th Plan onwards the outlay will be 6% 
of the GDP. 
17. The Committee welcomes the decision of the Government that Education will get an 
allocation of 6% of GDP. The Committee also hopes that there would be reflection of this decision 
in the Budget Estimates of the year 1995-96 and of subsequent years. 
18. Revised Budget Estimates for 1993-94 of the Deptt. of Education is Rs. 2192 crores. There 
has been a 10% increase in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 over the previous year at Rs. 2423.6 
crores, out of which Rs. 1548.3 crores have been provided for planned expenditure and the rest of 
Rs. 875.3 crores is earmarked for Non-Plan expenditure. 
19. Secondary and Physical Education have been allocated 24.3% of the Budget Estimates of 
Educationl Deptt. and 24.2% of the funds of the Deptt. have been provided for University and 
Higher Education. Elementary and Technical Education have been provided 21.6% and 18% 
respectively of the funds for 1994-95. 
20. The Secretary, Deptt. of Education, in his oral evidence before the Committee has stated 

that the major thrust of the budget is on Elementary Educatiofi) with the objective of achieving 
education for all by 2000, decentralisation of educational administration and review of all these 
programmes quarterly, by a group of Chief Ministers. 
Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Department of Education 
21. Department of Education is running about a dozen schemes, but the Committee took up 
for consideration only some of the major ones, which have been stated in brief in the following 
paragraphs, alongwith the Committee's observations/recommendations thereon. 
I 
Elementary Education 
22. Article 45 of the Constitution of India provides for free and Compulsory Education for 
all children below the age of 14 years. It was expected that by the year 1995, India would achieve 
Universal Elementary Education. However, there is still 153 million children, as on March, 1991, 
in the age group of 6-14 who are yet to be covered under the scheme. They constitute 18 per 
cent of the total population of the country. The Committee hopes that by the end of this century 
this backlog will be covered and total universal Elementary Education will be achieved. 
23. The Revised Budget Estimate for 1993-94 for Elementary Education is Rs. 443.7 crores. 
In Budget Estimate for, 1994-95, has been given Rs. 523.86 crores for Elementary Education. 
24. While the Committee takes note of this increase in allocation for Elementary Education, it 
feels that in view of the rising prices, the increase in real terms, is not substantial. 
25. The Committee feels that the Deptt. may take steps to decentralise Elementary Education 
and take help of Panchayati Raj institutions for proper monitoring and implementation of the 
Scheme. 
Operation Blackboard 
26. In the Eighth Plan it has been provided that the Scheme would continue and a third 
teacher and a third room would be added to primary schools wherever enrollment exceeds 100 
students. Thirty per cent of such schools would be covered in the said plan. Besides these, 
Operation Blackboard would cover 10 per cent of upper primary schools during the last two years 
of the Plan.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Fiftieth Report of the Committee on the Netaji
Bhawan, Calcutta.

2. A Study Group of the Departmental-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development visited Netaji Bhawan, Calcutta on 10th October, 1996 to
have a first-hand information on the activities of Netaji Research Bureau engaged in the task
of study, research and enquiry about Netaji’s life of profound experience and super-human
struggle and all round development of Netaji Bhawan. A list of Members who visited Netaji
Bhawan is enclosed as Annexure.

3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same on the 27th

REPORT

1. NETAJI BHAWAN, Calcutta, the ancestral house of Subhas Chandra Bose was
dedicated to the nation on 23rd January, 1947 by Sarat Chandra Bose. The Netaji Museum,
established in 1961 by Netaji Research Bureau, is a full-fledged biographical museum of vast
material on the life of Netaji collected from all parts of the world. Thi: museum is a store
house of inspiration and enlightenment for the people of this country.

2. Netaji Bhawan, with its traditional pillars and porticos, gives the appearance of a
typical early 20th century Bengali residential house. A marble plague, bearing the name of
IN Bose, Netaji’s father, decorates the front entrance. A fine profile of Netaji’s face draws
the attention of the visitors at the entrance gate. In the main portico stands a replica in red
stone of the stately ILN.A. Martyrs Memorial Column with the I.N.A. motto inscribed on it.

3. On the top floor of the Netaji Bhawan, Netaji’s cot, clock, clothes, shoes and Gita
have been preserved in the room where Netaji used to stay. Netaji's office-room during the
period of his Congress Presidentship is still painted in the hues of the Indian tricolour. His
working-desk, revolving chair, book-almirahs, etc. are preserved in-tact. The Netaji Bhawan
contains a treasure of numerous photographs, documents and articles relating to Netaji’s life.
The uniform donned by Netaji as G.O.C. of the Volunteer Corps at Calcutta in 1928, his
original passport and some rare antiques brought by him from Burma are among the
valuable exhibits. Warm clothings used by Netaji in Europe are kept in a show-case. Postage
stamps printed by Free India Centre, Azad Hind journals and Hindusthani translations of
German military texts are some of the interesting things to be seen.

4. The Freedom Library with marvellous collections of books on India’s Freedom
Struggle forms an integral part of the Museum. Books, periodicals and documents are being
collected to cover the entire freedom movement of India since 1857. The archives of the
Bureau consist of almost all published works of and on Netaji in various languages, a large
collection of letters covering his entire life, an extensive compilation of his speeches and
writing and journals, newspapers and other source material relating to Netaji. A scheme of
publishing Netaji’s work has been taken up by the Netaji Research Bureau with the
assistance of the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Education,
Government of India and nine such volumes have already been released. The remaining
volumes should also be completed before the commencement of Netaji Centenary Celebra-
tion year, i.e. 1997 which also happens to be the 500 year of India’s Independence or at
least efforts should be made to publish rest of the volumes during the centenary year.

5. Modern microfilm reader has since been installed in the Library and relevant
documents have been obtained in microfilm from other organisations and countries,
particularly from German and Japanese foreign offices. Films and voice and music tapes also
constitute part of the archives. The Bureau has also made one documentary film on Netaji
which was shown to the Committee at the time of its visit. The Committee was informed
that film shows, specially historical documentary on Netaji and the Indian struggle for
freedom are regular feature of the programmes of Netaji Museum.

6. The Committee was also informed that Netaji Research Bureau has, through the
years, planned and executed on scientific lines the all round development of Netaji Bhawan.
The rich museum, library and archives are recognised as the first and one of the best of their
kinds. In short, Netaji Research Bureau has grown up to be an impressive National Institute
of History and Politics.

7. The Committee was informed that Netaji Research Bureau plans to celebrate Netaji
Subhas Chandra Bose Centenary in a befitting manner. As part of the centenary
celebrations, Netaji Research Bureau plans to create Netaji Museum a unique institution of
international importance as a living and permanent memorial to Netaji Subhas Chandra
Bose. The Institution will consist of a Historical Research Organisation, a research oriented
centre for academics and traditionals in economics, politics, sociology, education, health,
environment, etc. and a broad-based cultural centre. Netaji Bhawan will, thus become a
beaconlight for India’s triumphal entry into the twenty first century.

8. While planning for development and modernisation of Netaji Bhawan Complex, a
total view has been taken of reinforcing and developing the old historical building without
interfering with its traditional character and constructing a contemporary building
complementing the existing structure and in harmony with it. The Complex will become a
unique, structurally attractive and eminently functional place. In brief, the development
programme of Netaji Bhawan Complex will include modernisation of Netaji Museum,
upgradation of Netaji archives, expansion of freedom library and automisation of library
services and other ancilliary works. Netaji Research Bureau expects the Government of
India to wholeheartdly contribute and extend financial support in the fulfilment of the
programme of development for Netaji Centenary.

9. The Parliamentry Committee was given to understand that the former Prime Minister
of India had visited Netaji Bhawan Complex at Calcutta and assured to give financial grant
of Rs. 12 crores (Approx.) for the upgradation and development of Netaji Bhawan. Even
the present Prime Minister, while visiting Netaji Bhawan on 14th July, 1996 reiterated that
the commitments made by the previous Government will be honoured. The Parliamentary
Committee -was, however, distressed to note that despite the commitments made by the two
Prime Ministers, Netaji Museum has not received any financial support from the
Government of India so far. The Committee in its 43rd Report on Demand for Grants
1996-97 had also asked the Department of Culture to act fast in consultation with Ministry of
Finance and Prime Minister Office. It is unfortunate that the Department of Culture has not
moved thus far. The Committee fully supports the developmental plans of Netaji Bhawan
and strongly recommends the Government of India to extend the necessary financial support
as per the commitments already made so that Netaji’s Museum could be developed and
strengthened as a monument of national importance in the year of Centenary celebrations of
Netaji. The Committee strongly recommends that the commitments made by the two P.Ms.
should get reflected in the RE for the year 1996-97 because of the centenary year starting in
January, 1997.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The origin of the National Library, Calcutta can be traced back to March, 1836
when the Calcutta Public Library was opened to the public at 30, Esplanade Row, Calcutta.
Subsequently the Calcutta Public Library was merged with the Imperial Library and offered
to the public in January, 1903. The National Library came into being in 1948 with the
passing of the Imperial Library (Change of Name) Act 1948.

1.2. The National Library, Calcutta is the biggest library in the country with the
collection of about 2.4 million volumes, besides journals, periodicals and palm-leafs etc. It
was declared as an Institution of National importance as enshrined in Article 62 of the 7th
Schedule of the Union List of the Constitution of India. At present the National Library is
housed in three separate buildings with a separate preservation laboratory, spread over 30
acres of land in the compound namely “Belvedere”, a French name meaning beautiful
garden within the heart of Calcutta City.

1.3. The National Library serves as the permanent repository of all reading and
information material produced in India as well as all printed material written by Indians and
concerning India written by foreigners, wherever published and in whichever language. The
National Library is the recipient of all material published in India, under the Delivery of
Books Act, 1954 as amended in 1956. The Library has an Exchange Programme with 225
institutions in 95 countries under the Cultural Exchange Programme of the Government of
India
II. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

The following are the basic aims and objectives of the National Library:

(i) Acquisition and conservation of all significant printed material produced in the
country to the exclusion of ephemera; ;

(ii) Collection of printed material concerning the country wherever it is published and
also acquisition of a photographic record of such material that is not available
within the country; ,

(iii) Acquisition and conservation of manuscripts of national importance;

(iv) Planned acquisition of foreign material required by the country;

(v) Rendering of bibliographical and documentation services of retrospective material,
both general and specialised;

(vi) Acting as a referral centre purveying full and accurate knowledge of all sources
and bibliographical information and participation in international bibliographical
activities;

(vii) Provision of photocopying and reprographic services; and

(viii) Acting as the centre for international book exchange and international loan.
गा, ACTIVITIES OF THE NATIONAL LIBRARY

(a) Collection .building and collection organisation programme: This is a major

programme which is looked after by the Acquisition and Processing: Divisions of the Library.

‘ In order to manage different activities, there are separate divisions like, Book Selection

Division for purchase and receipt of English books, English Serials Division, Indian
Language Division etc.

(b) Reader’s Service (including Bibliographic Services Programme: The National Library

2610/ RS/ F—3-A.



2

renders services to its readers from different parts of India and abroad on 362 days in a year.
It is closed on 3 national holidays (26th January, 15th August and 2nd October). Throughout
the year the service sections remain open from 9.00 a.m. to 8.00 p.m. on working days and
from 9.30 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. on holidays. On an average, 1000 readers are served everyday.
The Library acts as the main bibliographic centre of India. The Indian National Bibliography
is published on the basis of the receipts under the Delivery of Books Act. The Library also
shoulders responsibility of current and retrospective bibliography on Indology and other
subjects. The Committee observes that the referral centre which is a part of the bibliographic
services is not sufficiently equipped with the retrieval services such as subject index of
articles published in journals, subject search and bibliographic assistance etc. and necessary
steps are required to be taken in this regard

(c) Conservation of Library Materials Programme: In order to conserve library material,
a small repair unit was started in 1957 which has Preservation Division, Laboratory Division
and Reprography Division. The Committee is of the view that this is inadequate and needs
to be further strengthened.

(d) Modernisation: In order to implement the automation programme, the Library
introduced Anglo American Cataloging Rules, 2 (AACR 2) as the first step towards
modernisation of its operations. This rule is a cataloguing code which is a standardised
cataloguing format and is internationally accepted for automated systems. It has taken up
the standardisation of diagritical marks [special marks attached to alphabets (Roman script)
for transliteration from Indian Scripts] for romanisation of Perso-Arabic scripts through
automation system and has also developed a standardisation chart of diacritical marks for
automated bibliographic services in different languages. The Committee feels that the
Library should complete the computer.cataloguing of books and manuscripts without further
delay.

3.1. The Committee feels that in view of the latest developments in technology brought
out in the Library system all over the world, the National Library, Calcutta should also
adapt itself with the changing needs in order to perform its functions properly and
expeditiously. Hence it should acquire the modern software and communication technology
available in these fields and it should’ establish a site on INTERNET and it may be
connected through INTERNET service with all the leading libraries, educational centers and
research-oriented institutes of the world for a speedy and effective exchange programme.
The Committee is of the view that the Library may also examine a proposal to provide this
facility free to the schools and edcuational institutions which have received the Bibliographic
Data Base Project under MPLADS.

IV. BHASA BHAWAN

4.1. The present accommodation available in the National Library is not able to cope
with the various activities of the labrary including preservation of age old books, other
valuable articles and documentation of various new collections etc. The shortage of space
has adversely affected the functioning of the library. In. order to overcome this problem, a
Master Plan has been sanctioned which includes construction of a massive building called
“Bhasa Bhavan” with most modern facilities matching international standards. It would be
equipped with latest software and communication technology including Closed Circuit
Television (CCTV)

4.2. The foundation stone of ‘Bhasa Bhawan’ was laid on the 7th April, 1989 by late
Shri Rajiv Gandhi, the then Prime Minister of India. Originally the estimated cost of the
project in February 1989 was Rs. 35.34 crores. The Administrative approval and expenditure
sanction for Rs. 41.57 crores was issued by the Department of Culture only in January, 1993

approval and sanction for the expenditure. This inordinate delay must have resulted in cost
escalation for which the Department of Culture owes an explanation. The Secretary and the
Joint Secretary, Department of Culture were summoned by the Chairman, HRD, on 16th
December, 1996 to clarify the reasons for delay in according the administrative approval for
this expenditure. Even’ they were not in a position to clarify the precise reasons for this
delay. The Committee takes a serious note of this delay and recommends that the
Department should look into the matter and fix responsibility not only for causing delays but
also for cost escalation. The Department should also look into as to whether the tender
documents contained a clause for providing escalation of the estimate which is very relevant
for fixing the responsibility on the previous contractor. The Committee feels that barring
some additional items in the second tender, if any, rest of the increase in the cost should be
borne by the previous contractor.

complete by Decemeber 2000 A.D. at a revised cost of Rs. 60.46 crores.The tender for the

processing of the tender was further delayed, The stay order was got vacated in the month

foundation was started in February, 1995. The test pile was started in March, 1995 and

5.1, The Committee noticed that the existing buildings of the library are in a very bad
shape. There are complaints of water seepage and leakage of roofs. In view of its historical
importance, the buildings require special repairs and civil maintenance. The Committee was
also informed that proper maintenance of electric installations, pumps, lifts, etc. could not
be done for the last three years due to paucity of funds. The Committee is constrained to
note that the C.P.W.D has failed to discharge its responsibilities of proper upkeep and
maintenance of the buildings and thus owe an explanation in this regard. The Committee,
therefore, feels that the Department of Culture should impress upon the Ministry of Urban
Affairs and Employment to direct the C.P.W.D to carry out the necessary repairs and
other maintenance works at regular intervals to avoid further decay of this historical
building. :

5.4. The Committee also found that most of the work charged employees are being paid
their wages form the non-plan budgetary allocation meant for National Library and that too
without performing any job. The Committee further learnt that this practice has been going
on for the last twenty years without any check form the Department of Culture. This
appears to be irregular. The payment of wages to the work charged employees should have
been made from the budgetary alloction of C.P.W.D given by the Ministry of Urban Affairs
and Employment. The Secretary and the Joint Secretary, Department of Culture informed
the Chairman, HRD on 16th December, 1996 that this practice has been going on for the
last twenty years. The Committee takes a serious note of this lapse and recommends that the
responsibility should be fixed on the lapse of such an irregular practice. Since this
irregulaity was discovered by the Committee, the Department of Culture may apprise the
Committee within two monts about the action taken thereon. (

5.5. The Committee, therefore, feels that the budgetary, alloction meant for National
Libarary should not be used for the payment of wages to the work charged employees
engaged by C.P.W.D. This is particularly so as the library is already starved of funds. The
Committee, also recommends that the dues.of CPWD should be settled immediately. Since
the Libarary is badly in need of maintenance and special repairs in view of its historical and
architectural design, the Department should properly work out its requirement of funds and
project it before the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission.so as to ensure adequate
and timely availability of funds. The Committee observes with concern that, at present there
is a mismatch between Plan and Non-plan expenditure which needs to be rectified. The
Committee also observes that apparently there is a lack of total perspective planning and the
planning appears to be piecemeal. The Committee, therefore recommends that a
comprehensive plan may be prepared with project work alongwith the detailed budgetary
needs for meeting the requirements of National Library. The Committee also desires that
the C.P.W.D. may examine the problems of absorption of the work charged employees and
consider their demands sympathetically.

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1. The National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur was established on 7th February, 1976 as
an Autonomous Body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by taking over the
erstwhile Government Ayurvedic College, Jaipur. The Institute complex is spread over in an
area of 13 acres of land situated within the walled city. The activities of the Institute are
controlled and managed by the following 3 Standing Committees:

1. Governing Body

2. Finance Committee

3. Scientific Advisory Committee.

Il. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

2. The NIA is an apex Institute of Ayurveda engaged in teaching, research and health

care. The main objectives for which the Institute is established are as follows:

1. To promote the growth and development of Ayurveda;

2. To produce graduates and post-graduates in all branches of Ayurveda;

3. To conduct research on various aspects of Ayurveda;

4. To provide medical care through Ayurvedic System of Medicine to the suffering
humanity;

5. To provide and assist in providing services and facilities of the highest order for
research, evaluation, training, consultation and guidance to Ayurvedic System of
Medicine;

6. To conduct experiments and develop patterns of teaching in under-graduate and
post-graduate education in all branches of Ayurveda.

या. INFRASTRUCTURE

3. The Institute has Academic Block, Hospital Block, Hostels for Boys and Girls,

5.2 The Committee views this with great concern, The Committee is not in a position to
understand as to how the training courses and the hospital are being run with such a large
number of posts lying vacant, on both teaching and non-teaching side. Now since the rules
have already been modified, there should not be any difficulty in recruiting the staff as per
the requirement. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that immediate steps may
be taken to fill up all the sanctioned posts. The additional posts may also be sanctioned as
per requirement

VI. TEACHING ACTIVITIES

6.1 The Committee has noted that the Under-graduate course of Ayurved-acharya
(B.A.M.S.) is spread over to 44 years of the main course and one year of Internship. 60
students are admitted each year. Admission is made after conducting a pre-Ayurveda Test.
The Committee was informed that upto 1989 the Test was conducted by the Institute on All-
India basis and from 1990 onwards, the University of Rajasthan is conducting it. The
Committee is, however, constrained to note that during the years 1993 to 1995, no admission
was made because the University did not conduct the Test. While, the University wanted to
admit the students with the oriental Sanskrit course of ‘Upadhyaya’, the CCIM insisted on
admitting students with Biological Sciences at 10+2. The case went upto the Supreme Court
and the Supreme Court held that the CCIM regulations should only be adopted. It is
unfortunate that on such a small issue the whole admission process was stopped and the
admissions could not be held for 3 years. The Committee hopes that this would not recur
again.

6.2 The Committee was given to understand that the students are admitted in the course
practically from Rajasthan and nearby areas and. there is no National Character as such. The
Committee also regrets to note that the Institute is functioning as one of the local Ayurvedic
Colleges. The Syllabus, and Curriculum are also not of high standards. This is compounded
by the large number of teaching posts lying vacant and the sub-standard teaching being
imparted. Another problem which is also of a great concern is that examinations are not
conducted as per schedule, as a result of which, the 54 years course is stretched over to 7 or
8 years. When the Vice-Chancellor of Rajasthan University was asked about the affiliation
itute, he informed that the affiliation for the graduation course was granted about
ago, initially on a provisional basis for a few years and thereafter on a permanent

is. The Committee feels that with so many problems afflicting the Institute and due to
lack of basic facilities such as sufficient teaching faculty and equipment, the Institute cannot
impart education of the standard expected of a national institute. The Institute should first
set itself right including provision of the basic facilities before admitting students in future,
starting with the next academic year itself. The Department of ISM&H should also make
necessary endeavours in this regard. Otherwise, with the present sub-standard education
being imparted in the Institute, the products of the Institute cannot be expected to give a
better treatment to the patients.

6.3 The Committee has also noted that Post-Graduation Courses are offered in
9 Departments with an intake capacity of 5 in each Department. For the first time, the P.G.
course was started in one Department in 1971. Later on, in 1981 five Departments, in 1987
one Department and in 1988 two Departments started the P.G. courses.

6.4 During the course of the visit of the Committee to the Institute, the Committee held
dis ons with the Vice-Chancellor, Rajasthan University alongwith the Director, NIA and
the Joint Secretary, Department of ISM&H. During the visit, the Vice-Chancellor informed
the Committee that the Rajasthan University did not grant any affiliation to the Post
Graduate course. However, the Department of ISM&H later informed the Committee that



4

affiliation was granted to the P.G. courses from the respective years when the courses were
started. In view of the condtradictory statements given by the Vice-Chancellor and the
Department, the Chairman again sought clarifications from the Vice-Chancellor, Rajasthan
University and the Secretary, Department of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy
on the 4th January, 1997.

6.5 The Vice-Chancellor of gthe Rajasthan University while clarifying the position
corrected his earlier statement and informed that the University has granted provisional
affiliation. He further stated that the provisional affiliation is reviewed after five years and if
found satisfactory, permanent affiliation is granted. He further informed the Committee that
even though a regular review is not undertaken every year, yet if the performance is found
unsatisfactory or in case any complaints are received, the provisional affiliation can be
withdrawn. The Director of the Institute informed the Committee that the degree given is
not recognised by the Central Council of Indian Medicines.

6.6 The Committee expresses its concern over the unsatisfactory state of affairs prevailing
in the Institute and the casual approach shown towards the important aspect of affiliation of
the Institute with the University by all the concerned authorities i.e. the National Institute of
Ayurveda, the Department of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy; and last but
not least the Central Council of Indian Medicines (CCIM). The Committee takes a very
serious note and observes that the Department of ISM & H and the CCIM, have totally
neglected the Institute all these years. Even though the CCIM is supposed to review the
functioning of the Institute every year, it does not appear to have taken any measures to
improve the academic standard of the Institute, for recruitment of staff and for overall
improvement. The Committee takes a strong objection to the casual approach adopted by
CCIM towards the NIA, Jaipur, particularly when it has not so far recognised the degrees
given by the Institute and has thus put a blind eye to the fact that examinations are being
held regularly. After the CCIM has reviewed, the Committee is not able to understand as to
why they did not insist on maintaining certain standards. Any deficiency found should have
been brought to the notice of the Institute and within a given time limit the infrastructural
deficiency should have been made good. The Five year rule may be the University’s concern
but for granting provisional affiliation also it is the bounden duty of the CCIM to see that
the deficiency has been made good within the stipulated time laid down by it.

6.7 Even though the first P.G. Course was started in 1971 and the Rajasthan University is
supposed to review it after five years, it does not appear to have reviewed the provisional
affiliation so far. To a specific query, the Vice-Chancellor, could not clarify the position
relating to the conditions laid down by the University for granting provisional affiliation. In
fact the Committee does not see any logic as to why the affiliation is reviewed after five
years. The University should take a final decision in the matter immediately and if the
Institute meets all the requirements, the affiliation should be granted without further loss of
time as it directly affects the future career of students enrolled in the Institute for P.G.
courses,

6.8 The CCIM should also conduct its own review and find out the necessary requirements
that are to be met and should take appropriate steps at the earliest. The Department of ISM
& H should not leave any efforts for improving the performance of the Institute and to meet
all the requirements for Graduation and Post-Graduation Courses. The Committee would:
very much like that the responsibility should be fixed for not making any effects for getting
permanent affiliation for the Post Graduation Courses of the Institute to the Rajasthan
University even though the first Post Graduation Course was started in 1971. The
Department should give a compliance report to the Committee within two months.



6.9 The Committee is also constrained to note that national character has not yet been
developed in the Institute. Majority of the teaching staff are taken over employees of the
erstwhile Government Ayurvedic College who do not possess the required qualifications. The
teachers as well as the students have developed the habit of evading classes due to which there is
difficulty in conducting classes regularly. The Committee feels that the things should no longer
be allowed to continue in this manner. A total over-hauling of the functioning is required. The
immediate step should be to appoint the required staff.

6.10 The Director also stated that the Institute has applied to the Rajasthan University for
autonomy. This would enable the Institute to hold examinations on its own from all over the
country and give a national character, he added. He also stated that the autonomy would also
help in improving academic performance. But the Committee has got its own doubts on this.
When the Institute is not able to function well under the control of the University, then it cannot
be expected to improve its functioning without University’s supervision. The Committee,
however, not only agrees that the Institute should reach the level of autonomous Institution but
also expects it to attain the deemed university status. But at present, the Institute is not in a
position to do either. Firstly, it is required to be set right. For this, the Director of the NIA, the
Vice-Chancellor of Rajasthan University and the representatives of the Department of ISM &
H should sit together, discuss the problems and find solutions. The question of autonomy can be
considered after an year or two when the Institute starts functioning with adequate teaching
staff.

VII. PHARMACY

7.1 The Institute has a Pharmacy having modern as well as conventional equipments and
instruments. It is engaged in the manufacture of medicines for research mostly for IPD and
OPD. When asked to comment on the scope of large-scale and commercial manufacture of
medicines, it was clarified that the Pharmacy has a good scope to manufacture more medicines if
the vacant posts are filled up. The Committee feels that there is a tremendous demand for
Ayurvedic medicines in the country. This potential can be tapped well if the medicines are
produced to the maximum capacity. The Committee reiterates the recommendation made in the
preceding paragraphs to fill up vacancies at the earliest as the rules have already been modified.
The Director also informed the Committee that the Institute would start a herbal garden if the
State Government of Rajasthan provides land. The Committee recommends that the
Department of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy may take up the matter with the
State Government in this regard.

VIII. RESEARCH

8.1 The Committee views with concern to note that no research activity worth mentioning is
undertaken in the Institute. The presently available faculty members are not tuned to the work
culture expected in such an Institution of national importance. Research work is undertaken in a
very few areas such as Sciatica, Neuralgia etc. with Agni Karma. Considerable work on Fistula
and Piles with the use of Ksharasutra has been done by an Associate Professor of the Institute
for which he was awarded many Merit Certificates including one by the Governor of Rajasthan.
The Director of the Institute also informed the Committee that the research work being
undertaken in the Institute is not of the standard of a National Institute. Efforts are, therefore,
required to be made to uplift the Institute to the status and level to which it is ordained for and
to enable it to achieve its objectives. The Allopathic medicines are becoming very costly day-by-
day, besides giving side-effects. Improving the research activities is all the more necessary in
view of the Post Graduation and Ph.D. Courses being run in the Institute. The Institute should
therefore, rise to the occasion and prove the effectiveness of Ayurvedic medicines, old and
newly invented, through its research so that people look towards Ayurveda.


ati ti

IX. PATIENT CARE ACTIVITIES

9.1 The Institute has 2 Hospitals having a capacity of 200 beds at present. Since the
inception of the Institute, 6.34 lakh patients (medicine days) have been treated for various
diseases. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the average occupancy is only
about 63%.

9.2 The turn out of patients in the Hospital is comparatively low. The Committee is of the
view that the mishandling of the Institute on all fronts is the main reason for this. All-out
efforts are, therefore, required to be taken to reverse the trend and to make the Institute a
real National Institute in trué sense of the term. With the revised recruitment rules, it is
expected that the Institute will get better talent and with that, the Hospital will improve
qualitatively. Confidence among the people is also required to be increased on the
effectiveness of the treatment in the Institute so that people in large numbers come to the
Institute for treatment.

X. GOVERNING BODY

10.1 The Committee is constrained to learn that the Governing Body of the Institute has
not been able to meet for the last six years. The last meeting was held on 23.9.90 after
which the Governing Body could not meet. The reasons given for not having regular
meetings of the Governing Body is that the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare
who happens to be the ex-officio President of the National Institute of Ayurveda, is not able
to give time for convening regular meetings of the Governing Body due to his pre-
occupation. In making the Minister of Health as the President of the Governing Body, the
idea must have been to take full advantage of his presence for taking the decisions on the
problems/issues confronting the Institute but the fact that the Governing Body has not been
able to meet for a number of years, has frustrated the very purpose. Since the Governing
Body is the main forum for decision-making and review of the work, many issues and
problems relating to the efficient functioning of the Institute have been lying unresolved all
these years. When the Committee sought to know the action being taken in this regard, the
representative of Department of ISM & H informed that efforts are being made to amend
the bye-laws to ensure regular meetings of the Governing Body. The Department of ISM &
H is squarely responsible for not holding regular meetings of the Governing Body and for
allowing the Institute to deteriorate to the present level. The Committee takes a strong
exception to this attitude of the Department (Department of ISM & H now and Department
of Health earlier). The Committee strongly recommends that immediate meeting to resolve
all pending problems, should be called. The Committee also recommends that the rules and
bye-laws of the Governing Body should be amended so as to make provision for
appointment of a person, other than the Minister of Health, as Chairman of the Governing
Body, who is high enough in the hierarchy to take prompt decisions.

XI. BUDGET
11.1 The allocations made for the Institution during the last three years are as under:—

lakhs was reduced to Rs. 170 lakhs in R.E. on Plan side. On this the Department have
stated that the reduction at the R.E. stage was mainly due to slow construction. The
Committee takes a very serious view of the slow pace of construction activities going on in
the Institute. This, the Committee feels is mainly due to lack of any monitoring on the.
construction activities. The construction activities going on in the Institute are for a Boys
Hostel, Over head Water Tank, Kitchen Block etc. The Committee desires that there shall
be a regular monitoring of the construction work. As already suggested earlier, the
Department may grant additional funds to the Institute for acquiring necessary modern
equipments.

11.2 The Committee has also noted that the Institute is in the practice of depositing in
the Bank as FDRs, certain amount meant for construction work. When the Committee
sought clarification on this, the representative of the Department of ISM&H stated that the
grants are given by the Department to the Institute, using the State P.W.D. as an agency to
carry out construction work. The Institute has a Finance Committee chaired by the
Secretary, the Department of ISM&H and the Finance Committee took a decision that since
the P.W.D. was taking a long time in completing the works, the amount should be given to
the P.W.D. in instalments, spread over a period of time. He also stated that the funds are
released as and when the P.W.D. require. In accordance with this decision, grants which are
given to the Institution were deposited as FDRs in the name of Executive Engineer and as
and when they required funds, the funds are released, it was added. The Committee feels
that it is an irregular practice which cannot be allowed in a Government Department. Even
if the funds lapse on the completion of the financial year, it is the responsibility of the Union
Department to allocate the required funds in the next financial year. The Committee,
therefore, desires that the Department may look into this in the light of the financial rules
and take necessary action accordingly.

11.3. The Committee was surprised to find that different methods were being followed
in the case of committed expenditure of the previous plan. According to the understanding
of the Committee, committed expenditure will not get reflected in any shape or form in the
subsequent plan. What is termed as a non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan becomes
relevant only to the expenditure of new non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan period.
This applies in the case of both autonomous as well as deemed university institutions. In
order to get further clarification in the matter the Secretary and the Financial Adviser of the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare were specially called to clarify as to whether this
view of the Committee is correct or not. The Secretary could not come because of illness.
The Financial Adviser appeared before the Chairman and he confirmed that the non-plan
committed expenditure of the previous plan should not get reflected into the non-plan
expenditure of the subsequent plan. He also confirmed that they are not making any
distinction between the Government institution and other autonomous and deemed
university institutions which naturally means that the confusion which is prevailing in some
of institutions in treating committed expenditure as part of the new non-plan expenditure
should be clarified by the department concerned to all the institutions in the country so that
there should be uniformity in matters of procedure of not including the committed non-plan
expenditure. in the subsequent plan’s non-plan expenditure.

11.4. The Committee also noticed that in some of the institutions where vacancies were
available, there were utilising the funds’ meant for vacancies, for the purpose of non-plan
expenditure, which according to the Committee is not a desirable feature. Plan money can
not be diverted for non-plan side or even the non-plan expenditure should not have any
element of the scheme provided under the plan. All the vacancies prevailing in different


8

institutions will have to be filled in against the non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan
as the burden of the expenditure will not be there.

XII. THE STATUS OF THE INSTITUTE

12.1 The Committee was informed that the National Institute of Ayurveda is a
registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It is an autonomous institution
with a Governing Body. As an autonomous body, the Institute functions independently vis-
a-vis the Department of ISM&H. The Director of the Institute, in a note submitted to the
Committee, pleaded that this autonomous status is not helping the Institute in any manner
and may be converted into an attached body of the Department of ISM&H on the pattern of
Jawaharlal Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education and Research, Pondicherry which
is functioning under the Department of Health. The Director stated that this would
effectively check the decay in the Institute and it will help in its progress. Since it is a policy
matter, the Commitee does not want to go into the merits and de-merits of the proposal.
The Committee desires that the Department of ISM&H may examine the proposal and take
the decision as quickly as possible.

XIII. CONCLUSION

The Committee trusts that the recommendations made in the preceding paragraphs
would be implemented in letter and spirit. The Department of ISM&H may send an Action
Taken note within two months.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1. National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences, popularly known as
NIMHANS is a premier research and training centre in the field of mental health and neuro
sciences. The University Grants Commission declared the Institute as a Deemed University in
1994. The important activities carried out in the Institute are manrower development, patient
care and research.

1.1 The Institute is the core centre for developing a national mental health policy, and to
propagate and monitor its implementation in the country. Efforts are made at all levels to
directly link the activities of the institute with the national health policies and goals. The
emphasis has been to evolve models of hospital and community based treatment programmes
not only in the area of mental health but also in respect of neurological disorders where such
community based programmes are feasible with special emphasis towards prevention.

Il. OBJECTIVES .
2. The main objectives of the Institute are as under:
1, To promote the growth and development of mental health and neuro sciences;

2. To develop the~institute into an advanced service, Post-graduate training and
research centre;

3. To provide and assist in the activities of research, evaluation, training, consultation
and guidance related to mental health including biological, psychological,
sociological and clinical aspects; i

4. To conduct experiments and develop patterns of teaching in under-graudate
education in all branches of mental health and neurological sciences by opening
training centres and instituting innovative schemes;

5. To develop courses and curricula in all branches of mental health and neuro-sciences
for under-graduate and post-graduate teaching and to attain self-sufficiency in post-
- graduate education in all branches of mental: health and neuro-sciences, in India;

6.:To develop community mental health models and programmes of services,
-demonstration, training and research in both urban and rural areas; and

7..To educate the public in mental health and neuro-sciences.
: EQUIPMENTS

3.:When the Committee sought to know as to whether the institute is equipped with latest
technology and sufficient equipments in all the departments, the Director stated that efforts
have always been made to equip all the departments with the advanced technology and
equipments. However, due to lack of funds they are not able to keep pace with latest
improvements in technology, he added. The committee was also informed that if a special
grant issmade available to the Institute then it would be possible to acquire the necessary
equipments. The Committee feels that the Institute is in need of sophisticated equipments for
diagnosis,.treatment & research and the department of Health may consider making available
sufficient:funds for the purpose.



IV. COLLABORATION WITH FOREIGN UNIVERSITIES

4. The Committee has noted that the Institute propose to have collaboration with foreign
universities and when asked as to how far they are able to finalise the proposals, the Director
informed the Committee that it has already developed collaboration with a renowned
University and for making further efforts in this direction the active support of the Ministry of
Human Resource Development is required. The Committee feels that it is a premier institute
of its kind, in the country and collaboration with eminent and renowned foreign universities
would further strengthen the Institute. The Committee therefore recommends that the
Department of Health should take up the matter with the Ministry of HRD in this regard.

ए. MANPOWER DEVELOPMENT

5. One of the three important objectives of the Institute is manpower development in the
field of mental health and neuro sciences. The Committee notes that the Institute offers Post
graduate courses including M.Phil. Post-certificate courses in nursing i.e. (Diploma in
Psychiatric Nusring DPN and Diploma in Neurological Nursing DNN) are also offered in the
Institute. Facilities to pursue Ph. D. Programmes are also available, it was added,

5.1. The Committee was informed by the Director that the courses conducted by the
Institute are always in great demand due to the limited in take capacity of the Institute. When
asked to explain the steps taken to meet the Demand, the director replied that recently it has
been proposed to increase the number of seat in the following courses:

MD — Psychiatry 8 to 14 seats
DM — Neurology 4 to 6 seats
M.CH Neurosurgery 4 to 6 seats
M.Phil Clin. Psychology 12 to 15 seats
M.Phil in PSW 12 to 15 seats

5.2. The Committee desires that this proposal may be finalised as early as possible. For
increasing the seats, the staff strength is also required to be increased. Necessary steps may,
therefore, be taken to sanction additional posts.

VI. STAFF POSITION

6. The Committee has noted that the Staff Position in the-Institute is as under:

Sanctioned Working Vacant
Teaching 143 122 21
Non-teaching 830 737 5

As regards the vacanies on teaching side it was stated that for five faculty posts inteviews
were already held. It was also stated that 14 posts are reserved for SCST and recruitment is
under process undes special recruitment drive, Action is being taken to fill up the remaining
posts, it was added. The Committee recommends that immediate steps may be taken to fill up
the posts reserved for SCSTs. The Committee also desires that the vacancies on the
non-teaching side also may be filled up ut the earliest. The Director also informed the
Committee that some posts have to be kept vacant due to paucity of funds. The Committee
views this with concern and strengly recommends that in future no posts should



—

be kept vacant just because of paucity of funds. The funds aspect has been dealt with
separately later in para 13.

VII. RESEARCH

7, Research activity encompass a large spectrum from cellular mechanisms to social
systems associated with various neurological and behavioural disorders. However, the
Committee learnt that it has not been possible to spend adequate time for research in the
neuro-Surgery Department. When the Committee sought to know the reasons for this, it was
stated that the Department's faculty are fully occupied with the operations and the follow up
of the neuro-surgical patients leaving them with very little time for research. This gap can be
bridged by increasing the staff strength, it was added. Neuro-Surgery Department is a very
important Department and research needs to be developed. The Department of Health may
take necessary action to ensure that research activities are not hampered in the Neuro-
Surgery Department.

VIII. DRUG DEPENDENCE UNIT

8. The Committee has learnt that a sixty bedded drug dependence unit is functioning in
the institute and funds are not being given for this by the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare while similar centres established in PGI Chandigarh, AIIMS Delhi etc. are funded
by the Govt. of India under the National Drug De-Addiction programme. The unique
feature of the Centre in this Institute is, it has been started with community based activity.
The Committee was also informed that the Ministry has been approached for providing
additional funds for De-Addiction programme. The Committee, however, feels that the
Institute should not over-burden itself with the Drug De-Addiction Programme particularly
when sufficient funds are not being received.

IX. NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR TREATMENT OF EPILEPSY

9. The Committee has noted that a survey conducted on more than one lakh population
on neurological disorders, showed that approximately 31 people out of 1000 suffer from
neurological disorders, the commonest being headache and epilepsy. Considering the gravity
of the situation, the Committee feels that there is need for evolving a national strategy on
epilepsy and other neurological disorders.

9.1 The Committee also learnt that basic research studies on Yoga have helped in the
application of Kriya Yoga in the successful treatment of patients with depression. Since
Yoga treatment does not require any medicines and is free from side effects, it needs to be
extensively used. The Committee therefore, recommends that steps should be taken by the
Institute to involve more Yoga experts in treating the patients who suffer from depression. *
The Yoga unit may be further developed.

X. PATIENT CARE

10. The Institute caters to the needs of Patients suffering from Psychiatric and
neurological disorders. The Institute has a bed capacity of 805. Besides this, the institute
also offers a combined neuro psychiatric out-patient service to impart better co-ordinated
patient care. When the Committee sought to know as to whether the bed capacity is
proposed to be increased, it was stated that they propose to increase the beds in casualty
unit by 50 beds. They also propose to increase bed capacity in head injury unit and stroke
unit, it was added. The Committee desires that necessary steps may be taken to increase the
beds at the earliest.

10.1. The Committee also learnt that people with even small accidents come from long



distances for treatment in the hospital. This would only increase the burden of the institute.
For this, some kind of screening should be done at the the local level General Hospital from
where a case should be referred to NIMHANS only if it requires specialised treatment: For
this, the Committee feels that the matter should be taken up with the State Governments
| requesting them to issue necessary circular to the General Hospitals stating that whenever
head injury cases come, they have to examine and admit unless it needs ४ special neuro-
surgical intervention. The Director assured the Committee that needful would be done in the
matter, The Committee desires that it should be pursued by the institute at regular intervals.

10.2. To save a number of lives from head injuries the Director apprised the Committee
that by making wearing of helmets compulsory for two wheeler drivers all over the country,
this problem can be solved to a large extent. The Committee feels that the suggestion is
good and it should be looked into.

10.3. The Committee has noted that the institute does not get sufficient kits for HIV
testing. The Director informed that National Aids Control Organisation (NACO) has been
requested to increase the number of HIV Kits supplied. That Committee feels that the
Institute is in need of HIV Kits and NACO may increase the supply of HIV Kits. The
Committee is, however, of the view that the Institute should not over burden itself with
treating HIV cases.

XI, PUBLIC AWARENESS

11. To overcome the problems occuring due to accidents and epilepsy, prevention is
\ required for which public awarness is essential. To a question as to whether the institute is
publishing any literature for the awareness of the common public on the mental health
related problems, the Director of the institute responded that they are planning in this
direction. One of the faculty members of the institute has published nearly forty books in
Kannada. The institute is also planning to publish them in the regional languages, he added.
The Director also stated that the health education bureau in the institute is working on it.
He also stated that the Institute is in a position to supply posters on mental health in case
any State is in need of it. The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need to publish
the materials about mental health and related problems in all the regional languages so that
people of all the regions/States can be benefited. Necessary steps may be taken in this
direction. The Department should take the responsibility of publishing the material in
various regional languages in a time bound manner.

XII. AYURVEDA CENTRE

12. There is a small unit under the control of Central Council of Ayurveda functioning in
the Institute which is not a part of NIMHANS. The Committee was informed by the
Director that there is a proposal to establish an udvanced centre of Ayurveda in the
Institute. The Committee is, however of the opinion that the opening of advanced centre of
Ayurveda is an additional burden for the Institute. Such a centre could be located elsewhere
in an Ayurvedic Institute and the patients requiring treatment in Ayurveda could be referred
there.

a XIII. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS

13. The Committee noted that NIMHANS has been provided with Rs. 21.08 crores for
1996-97. On being asked as to whether this amount is sufficient to meet the requirements of
the Institute, it was stated that a minimum of Rs. 30 crores was required. The Director also
informed the Committee that the main problem faced by the Institute is the lack of funds for
development. The Institute needs special grants for this purpose, he stated. Presently, the


हट

institute is not getting any grants from UGC and the Director requested that since it is a
Deemed University it may also be given development funds on the pattern of other
Universities. The Committee recommends that this may be considered. He further explained
that in the routine grants, every year 10% growth is there and due to escalation of costs,
they are not able to meet the demand. While the number of patients are increasing every
year, the non-plan expenditure is kept at the same level of 10% increase as per the
Government norms. Due to this, the Committee was told, the Institute has to keep some
posts vacant to have’some non-plan money to spend for patient care. The Committee is also
constrained to note that in view of this, it would be difficult to fill up all the posts and if all
the posts are filled up, there is no money for food for patients, drugs and other hospital
managements. The Committee a y.that this would only hamper the activities of the
Institute from doing good workéThe Committee, therefore, recommends that the full
requirements of the Institute may be taken care of by the Department of Health. The
Committee feels that NIMHANS, being the only National Institute of its kind, should not
starve for want of funds. The Ministry should plead the case properly with the Finance
Ministry and Planning Commission for providing adequate funds. at

fe The Committee was also informed that aid for development plans is received from
many foreign countries such as Germany, Japan, U.S.A etc. The Director pleaded that such
aid should be made available to NIMHANS also. The Committee recommends that the
Department of Health may look into the matter.

13.2 The Committee was surprised to find that different methods were being followed in
the case of committed expenditure of the previous plan. According to the understanding of
the Committee, committed expenditure will not get reflected in any shape or form in the
subsequent plan. What is termed as a non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan becomes
relevant only to the expenditure of new non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan period.
This applies in the case of both autonomous as well as deemed university institutions. In
order to get further clarification in the matter the Secretary and the Financial Adviser of the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare were specially called to clarify as to whether this
view of the Committee is correct or not. The Secretary could not come because of illness.
The Financial Adviser appeared before the Chairman and he confirmed that the non-plan
committed expenditure of the previous plan should not get reflected into the non-plan
expenditure of the subsequent plan. He also confirmed that they are not making any
distinction between the Government institution and other autonomous and deemed
university institutions which naturally means that the confusion which is prevailing in some
of institutions in treating committed expenditure as part of the new non-plan expenditure
should be clarified by the department concerned to all the institutions in the country so that
there should be uniformity in matters of procedure of not including the committed non-plan
expenditure in the subsequent plan’s non-plan expenditure.

13.3 The Committee also noticed that in some of the institutions where vacancies were
available, they were utilising the funds’ meant for vacancies, for the purpose of non-plan
expenditure, which according to the Committee is not a desirable feature. Plan money can
not be diverted for non-plan side or even the non-plan expenditure should not have any
element of the scheme provided under the plan. All the vacancies prevailing in different
institutions will have to be filled in against the non-plan expenditure of the subsequent plan
as the burden of the expenditure will not be there.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The All India Institute of Speech and Hearing was established in 1965 to meet the
long felt need to serve the Speech and Hearing Handicapped in India. The Foundation stone
of the AIISH building was laid by the then President of India, Dr. Sarvapalli
Radhakrishnan, on 25th July, 1966. The late Maharaja of Mysore, His Highness Sri
Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar, donated land for setting up the Institute. The present location
of AIISH is on the Manasagangothri campus, covering an area of 32 acres.

1.2. AIISH was made a registered Society in October 1966 and is governed by an
Executive Council. Since then AIISH has made rapid strides. New units, sections,
departments, have been added from time to time.

Il. AIMS and OBJECTIVES
2. The main aims and objectives of the Institute are as under:—

(a) To provide and assist in providing general, professional and technical education and
training in Speech and Hearing for graduate, post-graduate and doctorate courses;

(०) To provide and assist in providing general, professioua! and technical education and
training to various categories of personnel e.g., medical, paramedical, non-medical,
etc; >

(c) To provide and assist in providing facilities and encouragement to research in speech
and hearing, their disorders and the concerned diseases of ear, nose and throat;

(d) To provide and assist in providing clinical and surgical services for those with speech
and hearing handicaps and ear, nose and throat diseases;

(e) To assist in the development of speech and hearing clinics in hospitals and other
centres;

(f) To educate the public about persons with communicative disorders; and

(g) To stimulate interest in speech and hearing through publicity and mass
communication and to co-operate with other agencies and institutions or
ee professional associations.

Il. STAFF POSITION

3.1. When the Committee sought to know as to whether any vacancies are there in the

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The main function of the Department of Education is to evolve educational policy
and also to coordinate and determine standards in higher education, including research. The
Department mainly undertakes the Programmes relating to elementary education, Secondary
education, University and higher education, adult education and technical education. The
Department also coordinates various programmes of assistance and other activities with
UNESCO and other foreign agencies.

1.2. The literacy rate in the country as per-the 1950-51 census was 18%. While the Male
literacy was 27.2%, the Female literacy was just 9%. This showed that female literacy was
just one-third of the then male literacy indicating a wide gap between the two. In
comparison to 1950-51 census, the Census Report 1990-91 shows the literacy rate to be
52.2%. The male literacy is reported to be 64% whereas female literacy is 39.4%. This

~f shows that the wide gap between male and female literacy which was existing in 1950-51 is
bridged only marginally by 1990-91. This calls for a serious thinking in our planning and
implementation of various programmes to bridge the gap between male and female literacy.

1.3. The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992—97) had set the target of achieving 100% literacy
among the people of age group of 15 to 35 years. This involved changing the literacy status
of about 100 million people. The sector-wise plan outlay on education during eighth Five
Year Plan (Central) was Rs. 7,443 crores out of which Rs. 4148.75 crores was earmarked for
central Schemes and Rs. 3294.25 crores for Centrally Sponsored Schemes. The sector-wise
plan outlay on education during the Eighth Five Year Plan (States/UTs.) was Rs. 12,156.73
crores. Thus, the total sector-wise plan outlay on education during Eighth Five Year Plan
(Central+State/UTs.) was almost Rs. 19,600 crores. As against the initial outlay of Rs. 7443
crores (centre) for Eighth Five Year Plan, an amount of Rs. 5867.39 crores was already
utilised till March, 1996 leaving a balance of Rs. 1575.61 crores for the last Annual Plan of

4 Eighth Plan Period. However, the expenditure upto March, 1997 shows it to be Rs. 2058.07
a crores which confirms an increased expenditure (of Rs. 482.46 crores) i.e. Rs. 7925.46 crores
177 56 against the original estimate of Rs. 7,443 crores for the whole Eighth Five Year
Plan@The Eighth Plan aimed at Universal Primary Education through both full-time formal
| | Schools and part-time non-formal arrangements for working children and girls in particular.
1 | Special emphasis was also to be laid on tribal education with 00०6 regard to their social,
! economic and cultural disparities prevailing in the society for long. The physical target for
f the Eighth Plan is 3.5 lakh Non-Formal Education Centres. However, only 2.80 lakh have
| been sanctioned till 1996-97. Hence, the Committee feels that the progress in these areas is
| | still very less and recommends that efforts should continue in these areas with greater
concern.

॥ व 1.4. The Approach Papers on the Ninth Five Year Plan indicates apart from carrying
रे : out the directions given by National Policy on Education (NPE) (1992),-and keeping in view
the declaration of education as an aspect of fundamental human right to life, making the ©
nation fully literate by the year 2005 will be a committed goal. Around 6% of the GDP will
be earmarked for the education sector by the year 2000 A.D. and 50% of that will be spent
on primary education. Further subtantial funds will be earmarked for imparting technical

1.5. Committed Liability:-—The Committee has noted that the committed liability of the
plan schemes has not been reflected in the budgetary allocations for 1997-98 which ‘is the
first year of. the Ninth Plan. The Committed expenditure which is accounted in_ the
subsequent plan at the termination of the previous plan is taken out from the plan and
becomes a separate committed expenditure. If this is not done,.the Departments will be
handicapped by this amount of plan expenditure. The exercise of identifying committed
liability has not been done by any of the Departments for 1997-98. Committee in this
connection has considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed in this regard as under. -

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the “out-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan
scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan
scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such scheme till 1990-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans. of 1990-91 and 1991-92”.

The Committee was also given to understand that the Planning Commission issued
circular to all the Departments dated November’5, 1996 sending therewith guidelines for
classification of expenditure. The Ministries were also requested to make necessary provision
as committed non-plan expenditure for the upkeep of existing assets etc. Accordingly, all the
Ministries/Departments were asked to adopt the guidelines while submitting the plan
proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan and annual plan 1997-98. However, the Departments
have not done this exercise. The Committee in this connection heard the views of the
Secretary. Department of Expenditure to clarify the position. He informed the Committee
that even though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not
identify the committed expenditure in time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been
provided under Demand No. 31. The Department may approach the’ Department of
expenditure for their share. The Committee, also desires that the Department may complete
the exercise at the earliest so that they may not be handicapped on account of this. The

ek The Committee expressed its concern over the issue of literacy rate and stated that the
National Literacy Mission is a high priority area. As per the 1991 Census, the literacy rate
was 52% which is a shame. It compares unfavourably with other neighbouring countries such
as Myanmar and Sri Lanka and also vis-a-vis Thailand,Japan and Singapore. Hence the
Committee desired to know about the plan of the Department to achieve the commitment
made by the Government to make India Literate by 2005 A.D. The Department in its reply
stated that there is a greater need for involvement of the Panchayati Raj Institutions and
womens’ leadership in the literacy movement, and much higher allocations would be
necessary to achieve the goal of full literacy. The term full literacy does not signify coverage
of the entire non-literate population in’a district, but the non-literate population in age-
group of 15—35. The present literacy rate at India is based on 1991 Census. However, the
National Literacy Mission’s estimate is that the literacy rate of this point of time should be
around 60%. Out of about 13 crore non-literates so far accessed by National Literacy
Mission. 9 crore are currently enrolled, and 6 crore persons in the age-group 15—35 have
been made literate. If the current tempo of social mobilisation is maintained, the desired
level of literacy could be achieved by 2005 A.D. as indicated in the Common Minimum
Programme. Universalisation of Elementary Education, and compulsory primary education
will help ensure that accretions to the non-literate populace will be kept to a minimum. In
order to achieve the objective of full literacy by 2005 A.D., National Literacy Mission’s
thrust areas would be the following:—

1.0 One of the most psessing problems that is being faced today by the country is the
alarming rate of growth of population. The current high population growth rate is mainly
due to three major factors as enumerated below:

1, the large size of the population in the reproductive age group;
2. higher fertility due to unmet need for contraception; and
3. high wanted fertility due to prevailing high Infant Mortality Rate (IMR).

The all India average annual exponential growth rate during the last decade has been of
the order of 2.14% which is marginally lower than 2.22% during the previous decade, but it
is still very high when compared with the developed nations of the World. Similarly, the
female to male ratio is 927-1000 which acts against women. Reasons for this will have to be
found out and steps to arrest the trend should be taken.

1.1 With a view to check the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was
taken up with the introduction of Planning in the country. By implementing the Family
Welfare Programme the Country has been able to avert an estimated 197.39 million birth
upto March, 1996. This has brought down the exponential growth rate of population from
2.71% per annum to 2.14% in the 1991 census, 1.93% in 1995 as per sample Registration
Sy stem and the latest being 1.8% as per UNDP Report.

{e 1.2 The Committee is constrained to note that even though there are some States which
are doing very well such as Tripura—1.11%, Kerala-1.17%, Tamil Nadu—1.23%, etc., the
national growth rate is adversely affected by States such as Goa—7%, Rajasthan—2.41%,
U.P.—2.43% etc. (National rate 1.93% in 1995—source: Sample Registration System) The
Committee, therefore, strongly desires that effectives steps are required: to be taken in these

States.
