REPORT
1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The Kothari Commission focussed its attention on breaking the barrier between the
“World of Learning’ and the ‘World of Work’ and to bring one as close to the other as
possible. Recognising the importance of Vocational Education, the National Policy on
Education, 1986, launched a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Vocationalisation of Secondary
Education in February, 1988. The main objectives of the scheme are:—

(a) To bridge the gap between the ‘World of School’ and the ‘World of Work’;
(b) To enhance individual employability;

(c) To reduce mismatch between demand and supply of skilled man power by pre
qualified middle level man-power superior to skilled workers;

(d) To provide an alternative to those pursuing higher education without any aim or
purpose and to direct the energies of youth towards constructive purposes;

(e) To bring out the importance of working usefully with one’s hands and imbibe the
concept of dignity of labour; and

(f) To reduce the number of drop-outs, failures and frustration in students.

1.2 The National Policy on Education (NPE) — 1986 had fixed the target of diverting
10% of students at the +2 level to the Vocational stream by 1990 and 25% by 1995. The
revised policy i.e. programme of Action (POA) — 1992 revised the target of diversion to
10% by 1995 and 25% by 2000 AD. The Department in its reply stated that even though the
scheme was launched in February, 1988, it was operationalised in actual terms during
1989-90. Therefore the target was revised to 10% by 1995 and -5% by 2000 AD. The
Department further stated that the target was achieved in terms of capacity sanctioned for
diversion of students at +2 level. However the findings based on All India Evaluation
Report on Vocational Education states that about 5% diversjon of students at the +2 level
against the 10% of NPE target has been achieved.

1.3 The Committee while looking into the disbursal of funds of different States observed
that funding has been most irregular in certain cases. The statement showing year-wise and
State-wise details of funds released is at Annexure I. From the Statement, the Committce
has noticed that many States are not being released sufficient funds. Also some States show
little interest in claiming for more funds and for implementing the programme. The
Committee has also been given to understand that some States have not been released funds
because of non-submission of audit reports. The Committee was also given to understand
that the scheme has not been given proper attention in North-Eastern States as well.

1.4 The Committee during its visits was further informed that due to strict guidelines
given by the Centre on the mode of expenditure, there is limited autonomy to function in
regard to expenditure to be incurred. It was stated that sufficient autonomy was not given to
divert funds to other areas within Vocational Education which were of urgent necessity. The
Committee during its visit found that the Management structures have remained weak in
many areas.

1.5 The Department informed that there are about 150 Vocational Courses introduced
in six broad areas, namely, Agriculture, Business and Commerce, Engineering and
Technology, Health and Para-Medical Services, Home Science and Humanities and Others
(List at Annexure II). The Committee observed that the selection of schools for starting

1



Vocational Education is done on the basis of District Vocational Surveys. But the
Committee was constrained to note that till now (As per the information collected from the
Department in November, 1997) only 166 District Vocational Surveys have been conducted
in the Country and out of the 25 States of the Country, only 6 States, such as Andhra
Pradesh (23), Himachal Pradesh (12), Madhya Pradesh (45), Rajasthan (31), Tamil Nadu
(19) and Uttar Pradesh (31) and National Capital Territory of Delhi (5) have conducted the
District Vocational Surveys. However in rest of the States/UTs these surveys had not been
carried out as has been pointed out by the All India evaluation Report on Vocational
Education. Due to this the Schools were selected at random in both rural and urban areas.
The Committee was also informed that the number of courses listed is very less and is
required to be broad based. The Committee was further informed that there still remained a
wide gap between the enrolment of boys and girls, especially in the field of Engineering and
Technology and Health Courses.

1.6 The Committee was given to understand that the link between the Industry and
Vocational Education is the weakest one. There still existed a mismatch between the
industry’s need and the products of the educational institutions and Vocational Schools.
Educational inputs are mostly outdated and not relevant, not to speak of quality of
institutions and their outputs. Consequently, industry is unable to absorb the products of the
institutes and a large number of educated youths remain unemployed.

1.7 The representatives of the Industrial Associations informed the Committee that in
order to stimulate private sector participation, there is a need for adopting the “German
dual System” of Vocational Education. Under this system, firstly, Vocational training is
carried out simultaneously with school studies and secondly, every trainee is sponsored by an
industrial unit, with a contractual obligation by the student to work for that industrial unit
for a certain period after completion of training. This model could be operative in India also
with a close coordination between the industry and the institutes, they felt. The Committee
has also been given to understand that the courses have more of a theoretical base rather
than of the practical base.

1.8 The Committee during its visits was informed by some of the schools that the
Vocational training for certain specific courses need not have to be exclusively at the Higher
Secondary level. Instead of being taught after the 10th standard, it could be lowered down
to upper primary level. The trainees in the field of carpentry, plumbing etc. need not be
highly qualified. What is necessary here is perfection of skills. The Committee has also taken
note of the fact that the school drop-outs are an important chunk of student population who
remain out side schools. According to statistics, drop-out rates in 1995-96 was 38.95% in
classes I—V and 52.26% in classes I—VIII.

1.9 The Committee while getting the first hand information during its visits came to
know that the vocational courses are being used as launching pad for vertical mobility. The
Committee was given to understand that one of the weak areas of the Vocational Education
Programme is the shortage of trained teachers and field experts.

1.10 The Committee while discussing with the NGOs and others during its visits was
informed that special attention is required to be provided to women, handicapped children
and spastics and above all to rural people. It was also stated that there is a need for a
humanitarian consideration to be given for the orphans and street children while enrolling
them in the Vocational Education.

1.11 The Apprenticeship Act 1961 was amended in 1986 to include pass-outs of


3

vocational courses at the +2 level. The All India evaluation Report found that there is
limited interaction between Board of Apprenticeship Training (BOAT) and State
Directorates. This is leading to under utilisation of seats for apprenticeship training by
vocational passouts.

1.12 The Committee was informed that a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Pre-
Vocational Education was launched in 1993-94, with the objective of imparting training in
simple marketable skills to the students of classes IX & X. The Committee has however
been informed that many States are still taking preparatory actions and the results have not
started flowing in as yet.

Il. OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

2.1 The Committee emphasises that vocational education has very ancient roots in our
country. There used to be ‘craft schools’ in villages for training in crafts. The Committee
appreciates the emphasis given to vocational education by various Commissions and the
National Policy on Education 1986. Even though all these efforts culminated into launching
the scheme in 1988, yet the scheme has not made much headway so far. The‘Committee is
constrained to note that the scheme has not been given due weightage and has also not been
implemented to the extent it should have been done.

2.2 The Committee is deeply anguished to note that only 5% of the targets fixed has
been achieved. The Committee is of the view that even if this figure is to be relied on, there
remains another 20% to be covered by 2000 AD for diversion of students at +2 level which
stands as a tough task ahead. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that the
Department should make serious efforts to give a meaningful thrust to the Scheme. The
Committee also feels that the programme needs to be totally re-oriented.

2.3 The Committee is also not happy to note that inspite of 9 years of implementation
of the Programme, the need and area based approach has not yet been strictly followed. The
Committee recommends that community participation and need and area based approach
must be followed to accelerate the process of diversion of students at the +2 level so as to
achieve the target.

2.4 The Committee is pained to note that the programme has not received adequate
priority in most of the States. There is also a considerable time-lag between release of grants
from the Centre and its disbursement to the schools. The Committee is of the view that
when no response is received from State Governments on yearly basis, it should be followed
up and accountability fixed. The Committee was given to understand that funds are
generally released to reimburse the expenditure made, which is a major hurdle in the
successful implementation of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
funds be released in advance on six monthly basis.

2.5 The Committee finds that in many a cases, the Central assistance released to
Vocational education is used by the States as a ways and means expenses andr diverted for
the purposes other than the ones for which the assistance was released. The Committee feels
that this is not a healthy trend. The Committee is of the considered view that this problem
can be tackled if separate funds are earmarked for Vocational Education by the Planning
Commission and it is impressed upon the State Govts. that non-utilisation of funds for
Vocational Education would be treated as misappropriation for which the concerned State
Government would be held responsible. The Committee also recommends that for proper
monitoring, there should be a Joint Monitoring Mechanism which would have

4661/RS—4A



4

representatives from Central Government, State Government concerned, members of
Parliament of that particular State and MLAs of that area to ensure successful
implementation of the Scheme.

2.6 As the scheme of Vocational Education is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and funds
allocated depend on proposals received from the States, the Committee is of the view that
sufficient awareness is required to be created in this regard. The Committee is also of the
view that proper initiative is lacking on the part of the Central Government due to which the
problems are arising. The Committee stresses that the Department should take all necessary
steps to activate the State Directorates and increase awareness among the State about the
utility and importance of the Scheme.

2.7 The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the neglect of District Vocational
Surveys. These surveys are an important ingredient, because the need and are based
approach of the Programme depends mainly thereon. The yearly District Vocational Survey
should be made compulsory and community participation in it should be encouraged so that
assessment of man-power requirements of the area, range of available occuptions, trend of
emerging vocations etc, are properly recognised. Without this, it is difficult to introduce area
and need based courses,

2.8 The Committee finds that the courses that are offered are generally not very
popular in many of the States. If out dated courses are offered, the people would have very
limited choice. Similarly, if a course which is not suitable to an area is introduced, students
would not be attracted by such course. It is therefore, essential that the programme should
include the courses which are useful in the tertiary sector. The Committee, is however,
constrained to note that the approach of the Department is very peripheral in this regard.
There are many examples such as plumbing, carpentry, agriculture related skills, pump set
repairs, para medical course and many other new courses which can be introduced on
requirement. There is a tremendous scope and demand for such skills, particularly in the
tural areas. The Department should keep in mind the fact that the vocational education
programme is meant for improving the skills of the people who are not able to go for higher
education, rather than making people engineers/rchitectscientists etc.

2.9 The Committee is of the view that unless the gap is bridged in regards to enrolment
of girls and boys, the country would be losing the talent of the major chunk of its
population. Hence the Committee recommends that steps must be taken to encourage more
and more number of girls to be enrolled in Vocational Education in general and in
Engineering and Technology and health Courses in particular.

2.10 The Committee feels that there is a necessity on the part of the Vocational Schools
to formulate updated packages which must be multifunctional through tradesSpecialised skill
from secondary school levels. There is also necessity of a placement cell to establish,
maintain and disseminate placement status record at the school and provide a sense of
direction to the students. The Principals of the Vocational Schools and Heads of the
tespective Departments should’ be in constant liaison with sector specific industry personneY
representative deputed by the collaborating industry.

2.11 The Committee further recommends that industrial sector should be involved in
curriculum preparation and renewal. Demonstration of basic skills should be done by
industrial personnel also. Faculty visits to the industry for specialised skill training,
nominating an industrial representative for the monitoring and inspection team, deputation
of the external examiner from the industryinvolvement of industry in evaluating students
performance, on-the-job training provision for about 4—6 weeks, apprenticeship training for

4661/RS—4B


5

one year on completion of the course (based on selection criteria) by the collaborating
industry and above all a profile of job requirements by the industry for the purpose of
placement to be provided by the collaborating industries and their recommendation for
absorption in organisations located elsewhere, are the aspects which should be seriously
considered in collaboration with the industry. The Committee, however, feels that as there is
a lack of proper planning in this regard, there is an urgent need for Perspective Planning.
Not only this, efforts should also be made to assimilate the agro-based industries in the
curriculum of vocational education, so as to make the task of achieving the goals easier.

2.12 Looking at the present scenario, the Committee feels that there is a need to devise
a system of imparting vocational education which while building a sound theoretical base
could also ensure connectivity to the market and job security.

2.13 The Committee is of the opinion that since skill is a major requirement for
vocational education, the 10th standard as essential qualification can be brought down to
class 8th. The Committee is constrained to note that about 52.26% of the children drop out
in classes I—VIII (As per the 1995-96, figures). Many of those drop-outs are quite
vulnerable and indulge in undesirable activities. This manpower can be utilised for
constructive purpose if education is made attractive and relevant. Vocational education is the
best alternative. The parents will also be interested in sending their children to schools
because of the usefulness of courses. The Committee expresses its concern over the school
Drop-Outs who form a major chunk of the rural masses and urban poor and desires that
special courses and literature be developed for this target group. In the Rural Areas, there
can be greater need for multidisciplinary courses like agriculture-related Vocational subject
which include repairing of Pump sets, agricultural machinesimplements etc. Similarly
fisheries can also be given due attention. Small trades like TV Mechanic and Radio can also
generate employment in rural areas and these courses can also be incorporated under the
Scheme. The Committee is of the view that in Urban areas, there are greater number of
Industries and job facilities and the Industrial units should be linked to the courses offered
which'can take into account the requirements of the Industrial units. If this is done, larger
number of students including drop-outs can be accommodated after the completion of their
courses in the jobs of the Industrial units. The Committee therefore recommends that such
trades be considered for differential needs of Urban and Rural areas.

The Committee in this connection takes note of the Pre-Vocational Course which is
being implemented. But it is going at a snail’s pace and is required to be accelerated. This
scheme may also be slightly modified to establish proper linkage with the main scheme.

2.14 Similarly, many students who are good at practical and vocational courses may be
weak in the regular subjects such as language, mathematics, science etc. Such students may
not be able to pass out the regular examination to get the school certificate. It is therefore,
necessary that a separate certificate for vocational course is given to enable such students to
get gainful employment. In case a student could not complete the other subjects but secured
good marks in Vocational papers, another year of practical training may be given and a
certificate in vocational course could be given to him. There could also be two levels of
vocational certificate course. The lower level should cover the students who take up
Vocational Education after class VII or class VIII and Higher level certificate could be given
to those who take up Vocational Education after class X. The certificate from Vocational
Education centres would act as a proof of acquired knowledge and skill. There can be a
separate Institute or Board for issuing the certificate for vocational education. The certificate
can be a recognised one just like the ITI certificate.

“2.15 The Committee is also constrained to note that lack of trained teachers is one of



6

the weakest links. The Committee desires that the States should be asked to give priority to
teachers’ training as this programme cannot be successful without trained teachers. The
Committee is also concerned on the lack of willingness on the part of the old teaching staff to
accommodate new courses which stands as a stumbling block in the progress of Vocational
Education. Students would be attracted towards Vocational Education only when new and up-
to-date courses are offered. The Committee feels that there is an urgency of Re-oricntation
Training for existing teachers to adapt themselves to new courses and also induction of more
new teachers for updated courses. However, the Committee feels that an element of
indecisiveness with regard to continuance of this Scheme as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme
persists. This has created a sense of skepticism in the minds of the State authorities
implementing this scheme. That is why teachers taken under this scheme are given only an
adhoc appointment. In this respect, the Committee is of the view that once the teachers are
appointed on a permanent basis they would be actively involved in the training programmes
offered. In this way the Teachers training would be more meaningful. The Committee is of the
opinion that by this course of action, the unemployment problem can be solved to some
extent.

2.16 The Committee is constrained to note that even if seats are reserved for the Dalits
and other deprived sections in Vocational Institutes many of them are not in a position to
finally clear the courses offered. The Committee also observes that in Rural areas, due to poor
infrastructural facilities and lack of other developmental facilities many a students fail to
compete with the urban educated students. Hence, the Committee is of the view that unless
some sort of coaching classes are provided to these groups, it would be difficult to achieve the
desired goal. The Committee therefore recommends that coaching classes be arranged for the
disadvantaged sections of society.

2.17 The Committee is of the opinion that mentally and physically handicapped children
and other deprived section of the society need to be given special attention. A more
humanitarian approach should be followed while dealing with the neglected and disabled
section of society where output need not be judge by the adherence to law rather by the
number of people benefited and settled.

2.18 The Sub-Committee was informed during its visit to Chennai (24th to 26th
September, 1997) that in Tamil Nadu Vocational Education is being used as launching pad for
securing admission into Polytechnics. ‘Students who fail to qualify the entrance test of
Polytechnics, join Vocational Education and after one year of its completion, through the
quota fixed for Vocational Education, get admission in 2nd year of Polytechnics. In this way,
the basic aim of Vocational Education to espouse the concept of self employability goes into
the background. Steps should therefore be taken to see that Vocational Education fulfils its
objective like individual self employability, supplying skilled manpower and acting as an
alternative to those pursuing higher education without any aim. The Committee is, therefore,
of the view that only those students from Vocational Education who are very brilliant and
secure the qualifying standard for joining polytechnics should be allowed to go for it.

2.19 The Committee expresses concern over the under utilisation of seats for the
Apprenticeship training by vocational passouts. This has stood as a weak link and has
adversely affected the acceptability of the Vocational trainees. The Committee is of the
opinion that steps must be taken to encourage the students for going through Apprenticeship
Training after completing Vocational Education which would make the Vocational Trainees
more and more acceptable to the industries. There should be proper placement of students.
Hence the Committee is of the view that the placement of students under Apprenticeship
Training needs to be vigorously implemented. There should also be proper monitoring of it.


2.20 The Committee has been given to understand that many Institutions running the
vocational courses in the Private and Voluntary Sectors make use of the courses for
financial exploitation and exorbitant fees is charged from the students. Steps are therefore
required to be taken to stop such exploitation and misuse of Vocational Courses by the
managements.

2.21 The Committee is of the opinion that Voluntary Organisations must submit their
audited report year wise. The Committee desires that the evaluation by Joint Evaluation
Team be conducted every year and voluntary agencies must be made accountable to the
local community for their acts of omissions and commissions.

2.22 The Committee has come to know that in the Chief Ministers Conference held in
July, 1996, a decision was taken to transfer the scheme of Vocational Education at +2
stage to the States. However, as this decision has no endorsement of the National
Development Council, the implementation of the Scheme is presently held up. The
Committee feels that this State of indecisiveness has adversely affected the scheme. The
Committee finds that Rs.60 crores were allocated for this scheme in the BE of 1997-98.
However, in the light of the decision of the Planning Commission to transfer the scheme to
States, no funds were released to the StatesUTs. As a result, budget provision was
brought down to Rs.20 crores and actual expenditure was only Rs.4 crores during 1997-98.
Allocation for 1998-99 is Rs.10 crores only. The Committee is of the view that the drastic
cut in funds in the first two years of the ninth Five Year Plan has adversely affected the
scheme of Vocational Education in general. Not only this, the scheme functioning
somewhat satisfactorily in some of the States has suffered due to this. The Committee
expresses its dissatisfaction on this state of indecisiveness. It is of the considered view that
since the scheme of vocationalisation of secondary education is of special significance, it
should continue as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and drastic cuts in funds for this scheme
should not be effected.

2.23 The Committee was given to understand that under the Vocational Education
Scheme, Certificate is issued by the Board after the completion of two years course. The
Department, however clarified that there were some courses which did not require two
years to complete it. The Committee is of the view that the courses which can be
completed in less than two years should not be prolonged purposelessly and permitted to
be completed within the required period only. By putting a strict range of two years for
Vocational Education for a course which could be completed much earlier, the scheme
itself has created a barrier for the students. Hence, the Committee recommends that there
should be flexibility in the term of the courses and necessary changes in the Vocational
Education Scheme may be effected accordingly.

2.24 The Committee is of the considered view that the Vocational Education Scheme
is still continuing as a Pilot project. It has come to the notice of the Committee that four
external agenciesinstitutions were entrusted the work of conducting a region-wise
evaluation of the Vocational Education Scheme and the final report has been submitted by
Operation Research Group (ORG). The Committee recommends that in the light of the
findings of this report, the StatesUTs should be approached by the Department for taking
corrective measures for successful implementation of Vocational Education. Scheme.

2.25 The Committee finds that at present a number of Vocational Schemes are being
handled by different departments like Department of Education, Rural Employment and
Poverty Alleviation and Ministry of Labour. However, Committee feels that there being no

4661/RS—SA



8

coordination among these Departments, achievement rate of these schemes has not been
quite satisfactory. The Committee is, therefore, of the considered view that a common
strategy should be evolved so as to integrate all these Vocational Schemes and take the
maximum advantage of the facilities available with the different departments.

2.26 The Committee observes that there has been regional disparity so far as setting up
of ITIs is concerned. Eastern region, Jammu and Kashmir and also the Backward and Tribal
areas are the most neglected lot. The Committee feels that such areas need to be given
special assistance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be initiated for
provision of 100% Central Assistance for developing the institutional mechanism in these
areas. The Committee finds that the organised sector has been the major beneficiary of ITIs.
The unorganised sector comprising about 90% of population mainly from rural areas which
also includes large number of Drop-outs and Non-Formal Education students has been
totally left out. This is due to the fact that there is a mismatch between the labour market
requirement and the trades and skills being offered in ITIs. There being no proper outlet,
average students are left with no alternative but to opt for higher studies. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that urgent steps need to be taken for broad-basing the Vocational
education scheme by inducting area specific courses under ITIs.

2.27 The Committee finds that under the Training of Rural Youth for Self Employment
(TRYSEM) Scheme, there exists no exhaustive list of trades. The State Govts. have the
option to select their trades in accordance with the illustrative list of trades furnished by the
Central Govt. The Committee, however, feels that Area Specific and Need-Based approach
has to be developed to generate the interest of Rural Youth in these courses. The
Committee was given to udnerstand that in most of the cases funds were being released
divertly to the implementing agencies. Chances of diversion of funds by the States were thus
very less. i

2.28 The Committee is constrained to note that although physical achievements so far
as training aspect of both the schemes is concerned ‘ure quite satisfactory, this is not the
position if we look at the figures relating to number of Youths Self EmployedAvage
employed. The Committee would like to emphasise that generation of employment both self
and wage is the ultimate objective of both these schemes. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that some pilot projects should be started on trial basis where all kinds of
facilities are made available to trainees so as to make them gainfully employed.

2.29 The Committee finds that no recent evaluation of both the schemes of ITIs &
TRYSEM has been carried out. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the
Department should carry out surveys so as to find out the inherent lacunae in the schemes
and take necessary remedial action. The Committee would also like to point out that
effective monitoring mechanism should be evolved so as to carry out effective
implementation of the Vocational Schemes. This monitoring Committee may consist of
CentralWState Govt. Officials and M.P/MLA and other local representatives.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee notes that adequate measures have been taken by the Museum
authorities for scientific conservation of rare and invaluable artifacts in the possession of
Indian Museum.

The Committee is happy to note that attempts have been made by the Indian Museum
for arranging exhibition of a number of art objects by rotation. Thus, quite a few antiquities,
art objects, anthropological specimens lying in godowns till now could be displayed in
temporary exhibitions. The Committee also finds that permanent arrangements have been
made for display of a number of architectural fragments/sculptures hitherto kept in the
reserve.

’ The Committee is however, constrained to note that these measures alone are not
sufficient enough. The Committee finds that acute shortage of space in the Indian Museum
has acted as a barrier on the display of even 40 per cent of its entire collections. The
Committee has been informed that purchase of land and construction of suitable modern
buildings with specialised galleries, lightings and display arrangements are required for
housing the precious collection of Zoological and Botanical Surveys. Both the Surveys are
thus not in a position to vacate the space occupied by them in the Indian Museum Building.

During the course of evidence of Secretary, Department of Culture on the 24th
September, 1998, thé Committee had expressed its serious concern about the acute space
constraint prevailing in the Indian Museum, Calcutta and enquired about steps taken in this
regard. The Department in a subsequent note has explained the current position about the
construction of the New Annexe Building of Indian Museum as under:—

“The Department has been frequently, emphasising that Museums, including
Indian Museum, should improve their Galleries and displays by incorporating the
latest techniques and practices followed elsewhere in the world. The Indian
Museum has been facing the space shortage for display of its artefacts and
curiosities for quite some time. Initially, it was proposed that an Annexe Building


a

in the existing premises be constructed to overcome the space shortage. However,
this could not be pursued as it required filling up of existing pond and the
municipal permission may be difficult to obtain. The Department has accordingly
proposed a two proned strategy to improve the utilisation of existing space. One,
the Department would prevail upon other organisations occupying the space in the
indian Museum building to vacate the area and second, utilise the existing gallery
space more effectively. We expect the second strategy to yield results in the short
term. The Department has already written to the Indian Museum to prepare plans
atid blueprints by seeking the expertise, if need be from professionals in a time
bound manner.”

The Committee is perturbed to note that the proposed Project for construction of an,
Annexe Building has been shelved as it required filling up of existing pond and the
municipal permission may be difficult to obtain. The Committee would like to draw the
attention of the Department to its Action Taken Reply which states as under:

The Department is examining the proposal for taking up the matter before the
Expenditure Finance Committee taking cognizance of the revised estimate submit-
ted by the CPWD for these construction works. The estimated area which would
be raised by the proposed Annexe building when completed is tentatively at
approximately 8165 sq. metres.”

‘The Committee finds it very surprising and against all the norms that without going into
the feasibility of proposed site for Annexe building, the whole exercise as mentioned above
‘has been undertaken by the Department. The Committee takes note of the two pronged

occupying the space in the Indian Museum Building can be prevailed upon to vacate the
premises to some extent. There should be no difficulty in getting some space vacated by the
Aathropological Survey of India, which is under the administrative control of the
Department of Culture.

The Committee was earlier informed that although the foundation stone of Bhasa
Bhavan was laid as early as on 7th April, 1989, the actual construction work could be started
only in February, 1995. Originally, the estimated cost of the Project in February, 1989 was
Rs. 35.34 crores. However, the entire Project was expected to be completed by December,
2000 A.D. at a revised cost of Rs. 60.46 crores. As per the latest Action Taken Report
furnished by the Department, the Project has been delayed because of want of clearances
from authorities like Calcutta Municipal Corporation. The Committee found that from 1994-
95 onwards till 1998-99, Rs. 20.30 crores have been released by the Department. However,
till 1997-98 the work could not progress beyond the basement because the Calcutta
Municipal Corporation has not given the clearance for the construction of the super structure
of Bhasa Bhavan.

At its meeting held on the 24th September, 1998. the Committee sought clarifications
from the Secretary, Department of Culture in the matter. Subsequently, the Department has
submitted a status note on the construction of Bhasa Bhavan, National Library, Calcutta
which reads as follows:—

“Construction of Bhasa Bhavan for National Library, Calcutta has been undertaken to
accommodate collection of books in Indian Languages and major languages of the
World. The foundation stone for this building was laid in April, 1989 and the final
administrative and financial approval for the work was issued in January, 1993. The
budget allocations for construction of building was made through the budget of Ministry
of Urban Affairs and Employment as the work was entrusted to the CPWD. The
desired progress could not be made on the project as the necessary clearnaces for
superstructure from Calcutta Municipal Corporation could not be received. On
intervention by the Department, the Calcutta Municipal Corporation has issued a
provisional building permit in June, 1998 to Director, National Library, Calcutta,
stipulating certain conditions such as submission of architectural plans after making the
necessary corrections along with the structural plans. National Library, Calcutta has
been directed to expedite the clearance from the Calcutta Municipal Corporation.
Meanwhile, the preliminary works were started by CPWD and upto now around Rs. 17
crores approximately has been spent on the project and the basement work has almost
been completed. The original cost of the project was estimated to be Rs. 35 crores
(estimated in 1989). The latest estimates suggest the project cost to be around Rs. 72
crores. For 1998-99 Rs. 6 crores has been allocated in the Budget of Ministry of Urban
Affairs for this Project. All possible efforts are being made to persuade the CPWD to
spend the entire amount during the year. Further, we propose to get enhanced outlay
for the project in the following years. The latest assessment made by the Department
and the discussions held with concerned authorities in CPWD indicate that the project
would be completed by 2002. The mutter has already been taken up by the Secretary,
Department of Culture with his counterparts in Ministry of Urban Affairs and, if felt
necessary, a joint team from Department of Culture and Ministry of Urban Affairs
would be deputed to the site for monitoring the progress. In case the Department does
not receive adequate response from the Minisitry of Urban Affairs shortly, Secretary
(Culture), propose to hold a meeting with his counterpart. Thus. the matter is receiving
highest priority. However, it may be submitted that eventually, the work is to be
done by CPWD which is under the administrative contro! of Ministry of Urban
Affairs.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee express its serious concern over the tardy progress made in the
‘construction of Bhasa Bhavan. The Committee finds that even now only a provisional
building permit has been issued by the Calcutta Muncipal Corporation. The Committee
strongly recommends that concerted effort should be made by all concerned so that all the
conditions put forth by the Calcutta Municipal Corporation are fulfilled at the earliest.

The Committee is constrained to note that the original estimated cost of Rs. 35.34
crores of the ‘Bhasa Bhavan’ Project in February, 1989 was revised to Rs. 60.46 crores and
the Project was expected to be complete by December, 2002 AD. The Committee finds that
the latest estimates suggest the Project cost to be around Rs. 72 crores and the target date
for completion of the Project is now 2002. The Committee expresses its strong reservations
over this state of affairs. The Committee apprehends that in view of the prevailing situation,
the target date is likely to be revised yet again. The Committee feels that the Department
cannot escape from its responsibility by intimating that the responsibility for timely
completion of Bhasa Bhavan Project lies with the CPWD which is under the administrative
control of Ministry of Urban Affairs. The Committee, therefor, strongly recommends that
the Department should make concerted efforts so as to effectively resolve all the disputed
issues for completion of Bhasa Bhavan within the targeted time limit.

The origin of the National Library, Calcutta can be Matter of record. No com-

traced back to March, 1836 when the Calcutta Public ments.

Library was opened to the Public at 30, Esplanade,
Row, Calcutta. Subsequently the Calcutta Public
Library was merged with the Imperial Library and
offered to the Public in January, 1903. The National
Library came into being in 1948 with the passing of
the Imperial Library (Change of Name) Act, 1948.

The National Library, Calcutta is the biggest library
in the country with the collection of about 2.4 million
volumes, besides journals, periodicals and palm-leafs
etc. It was declared as an Institution of national
importance as enshrined in Article 62 of the 7th
Schedule of the Union List of the Constitution of
India. At present the National Library is housed in
three separate buildings with a separate preservation
laboratory, spread over 30 acres of land in the
compound namely “Belvedere”, a French name

- meaning beautiful garden within the heart of Calcutta

City.

The National Library serves as the permanent
repository of all reading and information material
produced in India as well as all printed material
written by Indians and concerning India written by
foreigners, wherever published and in whichever
language. The National Library is the recipient of all
material published in India, under the Delivery of
Books Act, 1954 as amended in 1956. The Library
has an Exchange Programme with 225 institutions in
95 countries under the Cultural Exchange Programme
of the Government of India.

The following are the basic aims and objectives of the
National Library:—

(i) Acquisition and conservation of all significant
printed material produced in the country to
the exclusion of ephemera;

(ii) Collection of printed material concerning the
country wherever it is published and also
acquisition of a photographic record of such
material that is not available within the
country;

(iii) Acquisition and conservation of manuscripts
of national importance;

(iv) Planned acquisition of foreign material
required by the country

(v) Rendering of bibliographical and documenta-
tion services of retrospective material, both
general and specialised

(vi) Acting as a referral centre purveying full and
accurate knowledge of all sources and bibliog-
raphical information and participation in inter-
national bibliographical activities;

(vii) Provision of photocopying and reprographic
services; and

(viii) Acting as the centre for international book
exchange and international loan.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-
seventh Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in its
Thirty-fourth Report on India's Performance in International Sports.

2. The Thirty-fourth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development was persented to Rajya Sabha on the 21st December, 1995 and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 22nd
December, 1995. Replies of the Government on the recommendations contained in the report, received from the
Department of Youth Affairs and Sports were considered by the Committee. Clarifications were also sought by the
Committee from the Secretary and other Officials of the Department.

3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same on the 27th August, 1998. The Committee
at its meeting held on 19th November, 1998 decided to present the Action Taken Report in the House during the
Winter Session of Parliament.

New DELHI, S.B. CHAVAN,
27th August, 1998 Chairman,
Bhadrapada 5, 1920 (Saka) Department-Related Parliamentary

Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development.

4736/ RS/ F—3-A


CHAPTER I
REPORT

The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained
in its Thirty-fourth Report on India's Performance in International Sports which was presented to Rajya Sabha on
21.12.1995 and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 22.12.1995.

2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained
in the Report. They have been categorised as follows:

(i) Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: 1, 6, 8, 9, 11, 14, 17, 18,
19, 20, 26, 28, 29, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 40, 41, 47, 48, 49, 50, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 59, 60, 63, 64, 65, 68, 69,
70, 71, 72, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85.

(ii) Recommendaions/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's
replies: 3, 4, 7, 10, 22, 23, 24, 25, 27, 30, 31, 38, 39, 61, 62.

(iii Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted
by the Committee: 2, 5, 12, 13, 15, 16, 21, 33, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 51, 52, 58, 66, 67, 73, 74, 80.
(iv) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been received -
Nil. ;
3. The Committee will now deal with some of its recommendations on the Action Taken Notes of the Government.
Recommendation No. 1

The Committee feels it should be our objective to see that every child takes part in sports and games that every
parent encourages the child to do so. It should also be our endeavour to see that as children grow, they do not lose
their enthusiasm for sports, not does the pressure of studies towards a bright career diminish their interest for
participating in sports and games.

Action taken

To promote sports and games amongst children a decision has already been tak~n to integrate physical education
and sports with the educational curriculum. The Central Advisory Board on Education (CABE) had recommended
to make sports and physical education a compulsory subject in schools and colleges. Following are the salient
recommendations of the CABE:—

(i) Physical education and sports should be made a compulsory part of curriculum and assigned at least 40
minutes everyday for all school going children;
(ii) Mass participation activities and sports competitions may be organised by the State Governments regularly
for schools and colleges;
(iii) Subject teachers may be trained as physical education teachers through pre-service and in-service training
courses;
(iv) Special weightage may be considered to be given to sportspersons who have excelled in school and
college admission; and
(v) State Governments may identify at least one school per district as a sports school for nurturing of talented
sportspersons.

These recommendations of the Sub-Committee have been accepted by the CABE, Deptt. of Education and
Deptt. of Youth Affairs & Sports. All the State Governments have been advised to implement the recommendations.
The progress of the implementation of the report was also discussed during the meeting of State Secretaries held
during October '96. Conference of Ministers and Secretaries of North East States held at Guwahati in
November, ’96 and Conference of Ministers of State for Youth Affairs & Sports held in February 97.


2

The Education Department has also set up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri A.K. Pandya, Ex-
Secretary, Deptt. of Youth Affairs & Sports, Government of India, to review the progress of implementation of the
Sub-Committee Report in the Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodaya Vidyalayas and the States. During the course of
these meetings it is seen that the Committee's report has been accepted by the managements of Kendriya Vidyalayas/
Navodaya Vidyalayas and these are being implemented in schools administered directly by the Government of
India. Also many of the States have already initiated action on implementation of recommendations of the
Committee.

Apart from the above, to provide encouragement to sportspersons at early stages of their career, the Department
provides monthly scholarship of Rs. 500 to talented children. The Department has also recently revised the scheme
of Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools which aims at encouraging effective participation in competitions at
inter-school, district, State and national levels. The scheme will provide an opportunity to a large number of
school children to participate in school level tournaments and will thereby give impetus to sports activities amongst
school: children. न

The Department has also proposed a new scheme as part of the IXth plan proposals called "National School
Fithess Programme”. It is proposed to formulate a batery of tests to judge the fitness level of school children in
High/Higher Secondary Schools and based on that stars and certificates will be provided to the students passing the
tests.

Comments of the Committee

1

The Committee desires that implementation of the recommendations of the CABE Sub-Committee should be
vigorously pursued with all the States. ‘National School Fitness Programme' proposed to be started by the Department
during IX plan is a welcome step. This new scheme is required to be finalised at the earliest. The Committee
recommends that the Department may take all necessary steps in this direction.

Recommendation No. 2

Our performance in creating a conducive environment for sports should also ensure that boys and girls with
high potential are encouraged to remain active in sports through a system which offers them due social recognition
and encouragement, as well financial benefit. This is very essential, if we are to become competitive internationally
as a nation.

Action Taken

The Department agrees with the observation of the Committee. At present, boys and girls with high potential are
being encouraged to continue with sports by providing them scholarship under the Scheme of Sports Talent Search
Scholarship. Further some of them are also being trained in the SAI Centres.

Due encouragement and Social recongnition is being provided to sportspersons for excelling in sports by
providing them with awards under the Schemes of Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award, Arjuna Award and Cash
Awards for winning medals in international sports events. In fact, Junior and sub-Junior's players are also entitled
to cash awards.

Besides, medal winners at Olympics and World Cup and World Championships are given a monthly pension of
Rs. 2,000 and gold medal winners at the Asian games are given a pension of Rs. 1500 per month.

While the Department is contributing its mite towards the objective of encouragement of sports, it is also
emphasised that unless the society recognises the sportspersons as achievers, little can be expected.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is not fully satisfied with the reply given by the Department. The social status is linked to
financial gains and financial position. Unless sports is financially viable, children and parents would not look
towards taking up sports as a career. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendations for developing
a system so as to ensure social recognition and encouragement as well as financial benefit to sportspersons.

Recommendation No. 5

There is also a need to develop at least one sports school, preferably residential, in each district with the
requisite playing facilities and equipments. These schools could ultimately be developed as centres of excellence
in sports, on the same pattern as is being done by China and East European countries.


Action Taken

Secretary, Department of YouthA ffairs & Sports has written to all Chief Secretaries of the States/UTs emphasising
the need to develop at least one sports school preferably residential in each district with appropriate facilities and
equipment.

It may be mentioned that the Deptt. is not in a position to set up such schools as setting up of such schools
would require substantial investment in terms of school building, sports infrastructure and recurring cost for
running of the school. With the limited budget of the Deptt. it is not possible to take up such a scheme.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee finds that very few sports schools in State like Rajasthan, Kerala, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh
have been set up till now. The Committee is of the firm view that a large number of sports schools spread throughout
the country is the ultimate requirement for producing world class sports persons successfully participating in
International events. Even if the Department does not have sufficient funds, corporate sector and private agencies
could be approached for funds. Besides this, the Committee feels that some of the schools in different states having
large play fields and sufficient infrastructure could be converted into sports schools. The Committee was informed
that in 14 districts of Maharashtra, under Kreeda Probodhini scheme, whereas children are enrolled in different
schools, they stay together and sports, nutritious food, exercise, physical education is taken care of under one roof.
The Committee recommends that the Maharashtra example should be brought to the notice of other States also so
that sports talent is identified at an early stage.

Recommendation No. 8

Coupled with the absence of sports consciousness and culture in the country, there is almost total Jack of sports
infrastructure at the grassroot level all over the country. The Committee found that the infrastructure, so far
created, is mainly confined to the metro cities, big industrial townships defence cantonments etc. and caters to the
needs of people living in the urban areas, whereas 80 percent of the population, which lives in the villages and
small towns, is generally deprived of this benefit. The tribal and rural areas, with their age old games, are devoid
of any sports infrastructure worth the name.

Action Taken

While agreeing with the recommendations of the Committee, it is submitted that the Working Group for the IXth
Plan set up by the Planning Commission has recommended that the Sports infrastructure at the grassroot level will
have to be developed by the State Governments. As a follow up measure, the Deptt. has already written to the
State Governments in this regard. The matter was also taken up during the Conference of State Secretaries held in
October "96 and State Ministers held in February 1997. States have been asked to provide greater funds for
development of sports infrastructure in their plans so as to meet the needs of villages, small towns, tehsil and
district headquarters. They have been asked to involve local bodies for creation of sports infrastructure at the
grassroot level.

On its part, the Deptt. is already administering a scheme of grants to State Sports Councils for creation of
sports infrastructure. The scheme provides for assistance to State Governments/UTs and registered voluntary
bodies for creation of sports infrastructure like playfields, indoor/outdoor stadia, swimming pool etc. in all areas
including small towns. Greater financial assistance is given under the scheme for hilly and tribal areas. However,
due to paucity of resources, the Department has not been able to meet the demands of sports infrastructure of the
country.

Recommendation No. 9

One of the reasons cited for the lack of sports infrastructure in the country is the non-availability of sufficient
funds for the promotion of sports. The amount provided for sports in the Central Government is less than 0.0001 per
cent of the Government's total budget. Even taking into consideration the States' provisions for sports, the percentage
of allocation does not improve either, which shows that sports is not a priority area.
Action Taken ;

Department of Youth Affairs and Sports is in agreement with the view that resources provided for development
of sports is totally inadequate. The Department has, on innumerable occasions, has brought this to the notice of

4736/ BS/ F—+A


4

the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance. In the Annual Plan provisions for the year 1997-98, the
allocation for sports has gone up from Rs. 55 Crore in 96-97 to Rs. 75.66 Crore. The recommendations of the
Committee have helped in obtaining this higher allocation. However, this increase is also insufficient.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee agrees with the resource constraints being faced in the field of sports. The Committee feels
that recognising the necessity of providing/strengthening sports infastructure, sufficient funds should be allocated
by Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance. Keeping in view India's dismal performance in various
international events, Planning Commission should atleast once make a realistic assessment of overall requirement
of funds for sports in the country. This is all the more necessary because India with second largest population in
the world and even after 50 years of Independence has not been able to produce world class sports-persons.

The Committee was informed that a small State like Manipur was spending quite a large amount on building
up sports infrastructure and other related activities. Not only Sports Department, other Departments in the state
were also contributing to a large extent. The Committee feels that this system under which different Departments
have coordinated and jointly contributed for one purpose should be studied so that other States are approached to
follow the Manipur example.

Recommendation No. 12

The Committee while visiting the Regional Centres of Sports Authority of India, LNCPEs, NIS and the important
stadia/sports complexes, found it distressing that barring the Bangalore, Calcutta and Gandhinagar Regional Centres,
the condition of most of the Sports complexes/stadia was far from satisfactory.

Recommendation No. 13

The Committee recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports should work out a proper plan and
schedule for maintenance of these buildings/stadia constructed at a huge cost. The Department should also introduce
a system of regular monitoring and inspection of these buildings by senior officials so as to ensure their proper
maintenance and upkeep.

Action Taken on Recommendations No. 12 and 13

There are five stadia in Delhi under the Sports Authority of India being looked after by'the Stadia Directorate of
SAI. The important details in regard to these stadia are summarised below:—

Sl. Name of the Maintenance
No. Stadia Agency
1. IN. Stadium cPWwD
2. National Stadium CPWD
3. Talkatora Swimming Pool NDMC
4. LG. Stadium
Cycling Velodrome SAI
$. Dr. Karni Singh
Shooting Ranges DDA

There are also 4 Regional Centre, (Bangalore, Calcutta, Gandhinagar, Imphal), 2 Sub-Centres (Aurangabad,
Guwahati), NIS Patiala, LNCPE, Trivandrum and a number of SPDAS, Sports Hostels & SAG Centres.

Earlier, maintenance schedules were being drawn up by SAI from time to time for the above complexes till 1992
and these were being reviewed in a meeting with the engineers of the maintenance agencies at a periodic interval
for necessary follow-up action. However, with the drastic cut in budgetary allocation this practice could not be
scrupulously adhered to as the maintenance agencies were left with no option but to attend to the urgent work
only.

The annual maintenance cost of SAI stadia at Delhi and the infrastructure created at various SAI Centres all over
India works out to approximately Rs. 5 crores per annum.

4736/ RS/ F—4-B


5

Since no regular maintenance could be taken up due to paucity of resources, now in addition to regular
maintenance, SAI needs Rs. 16.00 crores for special repairs of various stadia at Delhi and Rs. 2.52 crores for
infrastructure at SAI Regional Centres. The entire special repair programme can be taken up immediately provided
funds are available.

The non plan budget of SAI has been reduced from Rs. 11.63 crores in 1994-95 to Rs. 6.00 crores in 1997-98.
Ministry of Finance has opined that SAI should generate its own resources to take care of the Non Plan expenditure.
The generation of resources by SAI, though, has gradually increased from Rs. 1.83 crore in 1992-93 to Rs. 6.18
crores in 1995-96 to approximately Rs. 8 crore in 1996-97, is not enough to take care of the maintenance requirement.
As such a planned programme of maintenance cannot be taken up unless suitable budgetary support is provided to
SAI under Non-Plan. However, whatever is possible within the existing resources is being done after prioritising
the works.

As regards monitoring and inspections of these buildings, SAI and the Department are taking necessary action.
Further Comments

The Secretary stated that all the five stadia in Delhi are maintained by different organisations but the Department
has very little resources and within that they have to meet the expenditure. The maintenance agencies do not pay
for the maintenance and only SAI provides funds for this purpose, it was clarified. While agreeing that the
maintenance is not properly done, the Secretary informed the Committee that alteast Rs. 16 to 20 crores are
required for bringing these stadia up to the required level. The Secretary stated that sufficient funds should be
made available to the Department for major repairs since for the last twenty years there had been no proper
maintenance of these stadia for want of money. The Secretary further informed the Committee that for the last two
and a half years, all new schemes have been put on hold so that all the funds could be spent in completing the
unfinished stadia.

On the question as to whether the stadia should be handed over to local bodies for maintenance or not, the
Secretary agreed that they should be handed over to the local bodies.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is very constrained to note the pathetic condition in which the stadia are existing now. The
Committee strongly feels that the Department should approach the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission
without delay for providing a one time grant for immediate and necessary maintenance of all the stadia. The
Committee is of the view that new schemes should also be initiated side by side. The Committee feels that efforts
should be made to transfer all the stadia to the local bodies for their regular maintenance.

The Committee is of the view that a big stadium instead of being used only for the event for which it was built,
may be divided into 4 or 5 sub-divisions so that it can be used for different events. Not only this, infrastructure
available in big stadium can be made available to nearby schools, sports clubs, sports bodies etc.

Recommendation No. 15

The Government has erected huge and massive sports infrastrucutre in the metro cities and big towns. These
structures are used only when national or international tournaments take place. For the rest of the period, they are
just lying idle or under-utilised. Some of them are rented out for cultural programmes and other shows. There is
a problem of their maintenance as well. A plan should be drawn up for utilisation of the infrastructure.

Action Taken

The stadia which were built by the Central Government directly are under the management control of SAI.
Sports Authority of India, after its coming into existence, had also undertaken construction of several facilities of
very high standards. As has already been pointed out that due to budgetary cut of SAI and the insistance that SAI
should raise resources for its survival, increasingly the facilitiés will have to be rented out for raising resources.
The Department agrees that playing facilities should primarily be used for sports and games only. In fact the SAI
has already initiated a dialogue with the Govt of NCT Delhi for using the playing facilities for school children.
Renting out for other activities will, however, have to be continued for generating resources.

Recommendation No. 16

The Committee feels that instead of organising the games at the State Capitals, many of the games could be
held in other places in the State so that the sports infrasturcutre is not concentrated in one particular area.


Action Taken

National tournaments as also the international ones need to be held in such places, where good facilities are
available. At the same time, such facilities, once created, need to be utilised on a regular basis. In many small
places, such facilities of international quality are nor available, nor are they required. In fact, in small places what
is needed is decent playing facilities.

The matter has already been taken up with the Indian Olympic Association. In fact the latest trends are also in
favour of holding tournaments in places other than State Capitals. In the last national games events took place
both in Pune and Bombay. In the Karnataka National Games also, some of the events are taking place in Mysore.

Further Comments:

The Secretary further stated that school education being a state subject, the State Governments were primarily
responsible for starting sports activities right from the beginning or at the local level. Although attention of State
Governments had been repeatedly drawn by the Department they did not have suffcient funds for doing that. The
situation was so bad that a large number of schools in the States were continuing without adequate play grounds.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is pained to note that a large number of schools in the country do not have adequate playgrounds.
Immediate action is required to be taken for improving the situation and Department should impress upon all the
State Governments to make efforts for providing adequate playground for every school. The Committee feels that
sports appears to be a neglected subject. For the youth of the country, it is necessary that sports facilities are
provided everywhere. International meets come once in a while. If we do not start from the beginning, the
performance of our sports-persons is not going to improve. The Department should formulate schemes whereunder
sports activities can be started by the State Governments in every school of the country.

Recommendation No. 21

The Committee desires that, as an incentive, sportspersons who have participated in the state, national and
international events should be allotted houses or plots by Housing Boards and Urban Development Authorities on
priority basis at concessional rates. They may also be given house building loans by Banks and other Financial
institutions at low interest. Eminent sportspersons, who, after retirement, intend to start their own industry/
business, etc. may be given licenses for purpose, alongwith bank loans and land, if necessary.

Action Taken

The recommendation of the Committee has been brought to the notice of the concerned agencies like State
Governments etc.Although, there are cases in which individuals, companies, State Governments have given cash
awards or awards in other forms to a few sportspoersons, who have achieved excellence in international arena, till
today, no formal scheme or even a pattern has emerged. In certain games like cricket or tennis, the achievers have
been given gifts or cash awards. However, in other games, which do not have high spectator value or have not been
able to catch the imagination of the people in a big way, the lot of even international achievers is quite dismal.
However, as has been mentioned, the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports have been giving cash awards to those
who win medals in World level tournaments.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to note that no formal scheme has emerged so far to provide for loans, financial
incentives to the sports persons. The Department’s acceding to this fact is not going to take away its responsibility.
The Committee strongly feels that even though no other agency or State Government has evolved any such
scheme it is for the Department to take an initiative in this direction.

Recommendation No. 29

The Committee recommends that one of the outstanding sportpersons may be nominated to the Rajya Sahba in
recognition of his/her distinguished service to country.
Action Taken

The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, who in turn took it up with the Ministry of
Home Affairs. No final decision has been communicated to the Department in this regard.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is of the view that even the revised rates are very insufficient and the charges should be increased

Recommendation No. 44.

The various federations/associations in the country are alleged to be the weakest link in the chain of sports

The guidelines are proposed to be revised, defining the roles and responsibilities of national sports federations

4736/ RS / F—S-B


Further Comments

It is essential that the national federations organise competitions, tournaments and championships on a regular

Recommendation No. 51
» There is no coordination or. cooperation between various agencies engaged in promotion of sports. There is no
accountability and responsiblity for poor performance in sports in international events. The Committee emphasises

the need for clearly demarcating the duties and responsibilities of each one of the agencies so that the accountability
could be fixed for their lapses.

Action Taken

For having propoer coordination and cooperation on structured ‘and orgat ised lines, it is felt that-suitable
legislation and rules and regulations under such legislation is necessary. While by and large, attempts at effective
coordination and cooperation are being made by the Department constantly with the IOA, national sports federations
and the State Governments, the results are not always commensurate with the efforts. Accountability and
responsiblity for performance in sports in international events can also be appropriately apportioned if there is
legislation, rules and regulations. However, it may be pointed out that in matters such as sports, where international
standards are constantly changing, normally upwards, and many other factors such as the state of development of

Comments of the Committee

The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Department that it is not easy to fix accountability for
lapses. If the Department cannot fix responsibility for poor performance and for lapses in the international events:

Recommendation No. 52

It is often seen that teams are selected virtually almost on the last day and at times had reported after the events
had already started. The Committee feels that this state of affairs is highly deplorable and has to be stopped forthwith

environment.

Action Taken

The recommendation has been brought to the notice of the national federations. The primary responsibility of
selecting the team well in time lies with the federations only. On the part of the Government, the procedure for

teams.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to note the Department’s acceptance that sometimes due to various factors, selection
of team is done at a late stage which delays the final clearnace of teams. The Committee is of the firm view that if the
federations make advance preparations and select the teams sufficiently in advance then this problem will not arise.
The Government should, therefore, not clear the teams which are not selected sufficiently in advance. Unless this
condition is made mandatory by the Government, the federations will never fall in line.

The Committee noticed that neither the sports psychology nor the sports medicine was being given any priority

In India, only SAI has made a beginning in setting up facilities for sports sciences support. Practichlly no

National Sports Federations. The Committee is of the view that in such cases, the Government should not give

14

Camps, Coaches-Indian and Foreign, Programme of Scientific Support and the list of probables. The Junior and

Recommendation No. 75

The Committee feels that unless sports is also brought under the “Concurrent List” of the Constitution, sports
activities in the country cannot be uniformly regulated in an effective and coordinated manner.

Action Taken

In 1988 the Government approved a proposal to bring sports on to the councurrent list of the Constitution and a
bill was introduced accordingly, in the Rajya Sabha 24th November’88. However, it was decided that further
consultation with the States be undertaken.

The Prime Minister addressed a letter to all Chief Ministers on 3rd November’90. This resulted in 12 States
agreeing to the proposal and 12 opposed with no response from Manipur. Subsequently, letters were addressed by
the MOS/HRM to these 13 States. Out of these States, 4 have further conveyed their concurrence to the proposal.
Thus, 16 States have now agreed to the proposal. Out of the remaining 9 States, the State Governments of Rajasthan,
» & 8, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have not agreed to the proposal which State Governments of Karnataka,
Gujarat and West Bengal have stated that they are examining the proposal. Comments from Assam and Punjab are
yet to come.

This matter was again placed before the Cabinet and it was decided that this should be discussed under the
Chairmanship of Minister of Parliamentary Affairs with leaders of all political parties in the Parliament. Accordingly,
a meeting was held on 28th November 1996 to consider the proposal.

The matter was also discussed with the State Secretaries in the Conference held in October ’96 and with the
State Ministers in the Conference held in February’ 97. It was mentioned clearly that the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on HRD had also made recommendation that sports should be brought under Concurrent list of the
Constitution and a comprehensive legislation enacted by the Central Government. However it was seen that the
States which have not given their agreement to the proposal are still opposed to bringing the sports on to the
conurrent list of the Constitution even though the Department has very clearly stated that the proposal will not in”
any way affect the autonomy of the States. It has also been clarified that it was only an enabling provision which
will allow the Central Government to legislate so as to define the role and responsbilities of the various agencies,
especially in the context of our performance in important international events. It has also been mentioned that our
experience with regard to other sectors which figure on the concurrent list has been that the Central Government
and State Governments have worked in unison to achieve better results.


15

Further Comments

The Secretary informed the Committee that 2 majority of the States have agreed to the proposal. In a recent
conference of all the State Ministers of Sports, State Government of West Bengal which has been opposed all
along has also come around.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee desires that discussions should be continued with the States that have not agreed with the
proposal. The Committee however feels that merely bringing Sports under the jurisdiction of Concurrent List
would not serve the purpose. The Department would have to make concerted efforts to involve the State Governments
in giving Sports its due place.

“The Committee recommends that necessary funds may be provided for shifting Central Regional Centre to
Lucknow and to strengthen the sub-centres.

Recommendation No. 1

The Committee feels it should be our objective to see that every child takes part in sports and games that every
Parent encourages the child to do so. It should also be our endeavour to see that as children grow, they do not lose
their enthusiasm for sports, nor does the pressure of studies towards a bright career diminish their interest. for
Participating in Sports and Games.

Action taken

To promote sports and games amongst children a decision has already been taken to integrate physical education
and sports with the educational curriculum. The Central Advisory Board on Education (CABE) had recommended
to make sports and physical education a compulsory subject in schools and colleges. Followng are the salient
recommedations of the CABE:-

(i) Physical education and sports should be made a compulsory part of curriculum and assigned at least 40
minutes everyday for all school going children;
(ii) Mass participation activities and sports competitions may be organised by the State Government regularly
for schools and colleges;
(iii) Subject teacher may be trained as physical education teachers through pre-service and in-servce training
courses;
(iv) Special weightage may be considered to be given to sportspersons who have excelled in school and
college admission; and
(v) State Government may identify at least one school per district as a sports school for nurturing of
talented sportspersons.

These recommendations of the Sub-Committee have been accepted by the CABE, Deptt. of Education
and Deptt. of Youth Affairs and Sports. All the State Governments have been advised to implement the
recommendations. The progress of the implementation of the report was also discussed during the meeting of State
Secretaries held during October’ 96, Conference of Ministers and Secretaries of North East States held at Guwahati in
November "96 and Conference of Ministers of State for Youth Affairs and Sports held in February '97.

The Education Department has also set up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri A.K. Pandya, ex-
Secretary, Deptt. of Youth Affairs and Sports, Government of India, to review the progress of implémentation of
the Sub-Commitiee Report in the Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodya Vidyalayas and the States. During the course of
these meetings it is seen that the Committee’s report has been accepted by the managements of Kendriya
Vidyalayas\Navodaya Vidyalayas and these are being implemented in schools administered directly by the
Government of India. Also many of States have already initiated action on implementation of recommendations
of the Committee.

Apart from the above, to provide encouragment to sportspersons at early stages of their career, the Department
provides monthly scholarship of Rs. 500 to talented children. The Department has also recently revised the scheme
of Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools which aims at encouraging effective participation in competitions
at inter-school, district, State and National levels. The scheme will provide an opportunity to a large number of
school children to participate in school level tournaments and will thereby give impetus to sports activities amongst
school children.

The Department has also proposed a new scheme as part of the IXth Plan proposals called “National Schools
Fitness Programme.” It is proposed to formulate a battery of test to judge the fitness level of school children in
High\Higher Secondary Schools and based on that stars and certificates will be provided to the students passing
the tests.
