12. There has been an increase of Rs. 1.90 crores this year, as against the revised estimates of the 
last year, which, in view of price esclation, is negligible. Therefore, the Committee feels that allocation 
for ASI should be adequately increased because a large number of monuments are in dilapidated 
condit ions and need urgent repairs and a great number of monuments and sites remain unidentified 
an d unprotected. Out of around 8,000 monuments, about 3,500 are centrally prot ected . The Committee 
expresses its concern over the fact that even the centrally protected monum ents do not have proper 
maintenance and foolpr oof protectioq. Cases of larceny of artefacts, idols etc. have been occuring from 
time to tim e. During the course of evidence the Committee came to know that the number of staff 
engaged in preservations and maintenance of monuments is so small that the ratio works out to 1lfz 
staff per monument. Therefore, the Committee recommend s that staff strength of the ASI engaged for 
protection and preservation of monumenrs be adequately increa sed and all other necessary mea sure s be 
taken to check the increasing menace of pilferage. Some amount from the propo sed National Cultural 
Fund may also be utilised for the purp ose. 
The Committee is also of the view that , as envisaged in the Eighth Plan document related to the 
Department of Culture, voluntary organi sations should be attracted and encouraged to take up the task 
of preservation atid prot ection of monu'mcnt s. 
13. Even after one hundred and twenty five years of its existence, ASI has not been able to cover 
all parts of the country as far as excavation and exploration of ancient historical sites are concerned. 
Nor it has been able to deciphe r all the inscriptions. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
network of ASI should have been exten sively expanded and enlarged. It should also be well equipped. 
The scheme of village to village survev should also be undertaken and expanded. 
Anthropological Survey of India 
14. Researches in anthropology and allied disciplines and study of customs and traditions are 
some of the major functions undertaken by the Anthropological Survey of India. In the Eighth Five 
Year Plan document it was proposed to salvage and document those specimens of the tribal and folk 
art which face the threat of extincti on. It was also proposed to study inherent socio-religious 
disabilities of the tri bals, nature of tran sforma tion and mobilisation of their specia l skills in arts, dance 
and tnusic an d mastery over musical instruments. But , no follow-up action on these lines is found in 
the Annual Plans of the Departme nt. Therefore, the Committee urges upon the Government to pursue 
vigorously those objectives. Reasons for decrease in the plan allocation of Rs. 140.00 lakhs from Rs. 
150.00 lakhs (Plan Expenditure Revised) of the year 1993;94 are not tenable. Hence the Committ ee 
recommends that the provision should be increased. Study and research in the field of conservation of 
environment, welfare of women and children, nutritional status of Indian population, etc. have also 
been added to its activities, recently. 

15. In keeping with its aims and objectives, the Anthropologi cal Survey of India took up a 
national project called 'People of India' to analyse Indian population on the bas is of bio-cultural 
variables and socio-cultural determinents like marriage , kinship , region, language etc. Out of the 
proposed 43 volumes of the prestigious National Project 'People of India'- three under national and 
two under State series have so far been published. The remaining work should be expedited. 
Museums 
16. Museums play a vital role in the preservation of documents and objects of cultur al antiquity. 
In this field, at present, there are ten premier institutions under Govt. of India , includin g the 
National Reserach Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural proper ty located at Lucknow. Out of the 
ten institutions, three each are located at New D elhi and Calcutta and one each at Lucknow , 
Allahabad, Hydcrabad and Bombay, all situated in major cities. To provide representation to cultural 
aspects of othe r states of Indian Union, a new scheme for Promotion and Stre ngthening of Reg ional 
and Local Museums has been mooted and is env isaged to be ope rationlised during the Eighth Five 
Year Plan period. Govt. is also providi ng assistance for open ing private museums. Govt. proposes to 
intensify this scheme through a Committee which will look after them. But for this well conce ived 
scheme a meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs has been provided for the year 1994-95. There has been no 
change in the allocations for the last three years. In such a situation the Committee wonders how the 
scheme contemplated for the Eighth Plan could be implemented within the time-frame with this 
insignificant budget allocation. As the Eighth Five Year Plan is left with only two financial years, the 
Committee strongly recommends enhancement of financial allocation to speed up the implementation of 
the scheme. 
National Council of Science Museums (NCSM), Calcutta 
17. It is an autonomous organisation engaged primarily in the task of popularising science and 
technology among the studen ts in particular and the masses in general thr ough a variety of interactive 
and innovative programmes and activities like science exhib itions, schoo l centre s, portable 
planetarium and national science seminars etc. and setting up of a Science City in Calcutt a, is the 
highlight of the activities of the National Cou ncil of Science Museums. In the Eighth Plan docume nt it 
was proposed to create 1000 science centres to reach the common man, five new regional centres, 20 
district science centres and 203 school science centres in the under privileged rural schoo ls, 20 new 
mobile science exhibition buses, a science train, etc. The total outlay for the 8th Plan period of Rs. 
4500.00 lakhs for these ambitious proposals is too littfe. Slight increase in the allocatio n for this year, 
as against the last year's Budget Estimates, of around Rs. 161 lakhs and of Rs. 111 lakh s in Revised 
Estimates may not be said to be adequate in view of the rising prices. The implementation of the 
scheme has made very little progress and should be speeded up. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
_that additional grant be given for this scheme to increase scientific temper among the people. 
National Museum, New Delhi 
18. During 1994-95, the National Museum , New Delhi, proposes to organise exhibitions of 
Persian manuscripts in Teheran, an exhibition of Indian Art at Singapore and of miniature paintings 
at Tashkent. Apart from this, it is also proposed to introduce such new programmes as developing 
software for physically handicapped persons, lending consultancy services to the State and other 
museums, introduction of disc system for documentation of its huge collect ion , microfilming of 
manuscripts and computerisation of its library, etc. 
19. The provisions made for this year, as against last year, remain more or less the same. Plan 
provision has fallen from Rs. 200.00 lakhs to Rs. 190.00 lakhs and Non-P lan provisions has increa sed 
by only Rs. 7 lakhs in compariso n to the Revised Estimat es of the last year. Thus, there has been a 
decrease of Rs. 3 lakhs this year. The Committee is surprised to know as to how with this small 
allocation. It would be possible to ach ieve the targets set for this year. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that the allocation for National Museum be increased appropriately. 
Indian Museum , Calcutta 
20. The total provisions made this year for Indian Museum, Calcutta, arc less by 1.45 lakhs as 
agianst the Revised Estimates (both Plan and Non-Plan) of the last year. In this situat ion, apart from 

carrying out on-going functions the proposal to construct a new building for display of valuable 
artefacts may find itself in rough weather. It was also envisaged in the Eighth Plan document to set 
up new galleries on textiles, folk arts, gems and jewelleries. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that sufficient grant should . be provided to the Museum so that these schemes are completed. 
Institutes and Organisations of Tibetan and Buddhist studies 
21. There are. four autonomous institutes, namely, the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan 
Studies, VaranasC the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Leh; the Sikkim Research Institute of 
Tibetology and the Library of Tibetan Works & Archives, Dharamsala, which are engaged in 
preservation and propagations of Tibetan culture and tradition, restoration of ancient Indian literature 
preserved in Tibetan language, imparting higher education in Buddhist philosophy and literature, etc. 
The Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi, enjoys the status of a 'Deemed 
University'. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the encouragement given to these 
institutes feels that they should be allowed to pursue their academic interest without any extraneous 
influences. 
22. The Committee feels that due attention is not being paid in these institutes to promotion and 
development of Pali, one of ancient language of India and, therefore, recommends suitable steps in this 
regard. 
Libraries 
23. The Committee feels that the reading habi!S of the general masses are on the wane, partly 
owing to revolutionary changes in electronic media, partly due to the shift in social values titled more 
to materialism, and partly because of high prices of books. In this situation, libraries have to be 
opened on a large scale with even distribution in urban and rural areas. 
24. There are six major libraries under the Department of Culture. The total budgetary provision 
(lOth Plan and Non-Plan) for the year 1994-95 under this _head is Rs. 13.36 crores a tot"al increase of 
Rs. 2.38 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimates (Both Plan & Non Plan) of the last year. In 
view of the rising prices of books and other allied items, maintenance cost of buildings etc. this 
increase of Rs. 2.38 crores in not enough. 
25. The tendency of centralisation is perceptible in the scheme of libraries also. The Committee 
feels that suitable scheme be devised to spread the network of libraries to District Headquarters and 
small towns. There is also a need to interlink the major libraries with computer network. It will 
facilitate the research scholars and other persons desiring any information sitting in one library to 
gather additional information from all the connected libraries. 
26. The Delhi Public Library, established in 1951 with the assistance of UNESCO to provide free 
library service to the citizens of Delhi, has also now developed into a Metropolitan Public Library. A 
major portion of its activities is located in the affluent localities of Delhi and the rural and 
underdeveloped areas are being neglected. Therefore, ·the Committee, recommends that Govt. should 
take adequate steps to spread it~ network of libraries and reading rooms In the slum and 
underdeveloped areas of the National Capital. More and more mobile library vans should also be made 
available. In view of all these, the Committee recommends that the budget allocation for Delhi Public 
Library be enhanced appropriately. 
Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation, Calcutta 
27. Established in 1972-, it is an autonomous organisation fully funded by the Deptt: of Culture. 
The · main aim of the library is to support and promote library services. in the country. 
28. Increase in its budget provision this year is welcome. However, some irregularities in the 
fuqctioning of the library have come to the notice of the Committee. Guideliues on book purchasing are 
not being adhered to and books are allegedly being purchased at higher rl}tes than the market rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that these matters be looked into. 

Rural Library Scheme 
29. The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Culture has decided to focus its 
attention on the rural populace by deciding to set up rural libraries in villages. A teacher from the 
local school is proposed to be made in-charge of the library which will, in the incipient,have around 
300 books. The Committee is of the view that these libraries should also ~ave such books which may be 
used by neo-Iiterates in the post-literacy stage. It is, undoubtedly a well conceived scheme and generous 
funds should be provided for it. The Committee recommends that this scheme be made a pilot project 
so that about five and half lakh villages could be covered within a stipulated time-frame. The 
Committee also recommends that separate allocation be made for individual states. In consultation with 
the Ministry of Rural Development, the assistance of Panchayats may be sought to ensure speedy and 
effective implementation of this scheme. The Committee also recommends that the modalities for the 
implementation of this scheme be worked out as early as possible so that the scheme implemented in 
right earnest.

/. Sahitya Akademi

1956 with the objective of working actively for development of literature and to foster- and coordinate 
literary activities in all the Indian languages and to promote through them the cultural unity of the· 
country. To achieve these objectives, the Akademi is running programmes such as granting literary 
awards, translation and publication of books in different languages, etc. The Akademi also provides 
assistance to State Akademies. 
31. The Committee is not happy with the budgetary allocation made for the Akademi this year, 
which is only Rs. 57 lakhs more than the Revised Estimates of the last year :-

Sahitya Akademi is made ·to curtail its activities due to lack of funds. Therefore, the Committee

development of regional languages, in addition to Hindi. 
II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged 
in promotion and preservation of performing arts, extending financial assistance to cultural institution 
for training and production, undertaki~g inter-state cultural exchange programmes etc. Although 
there is an increase of around Rs. 27 lakhs this year, as compared to the last year's Revised Estimates 
(both Plan and Non-Plan) this is negligible in view of the price escalation. The Committee is of the 
view that the outlay for the Akademi may be appropriately increased. 
Ill. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major 
activities of the Akademi are to organise exhibitions (in and outside the country), artists' camps, 
bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the 
allocation appropriately. 

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, ~hich is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objective 's vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training , set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre 's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The niain 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by State Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be &voided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultural Centre spends on the propagation of 
the living folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

'he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note tha t the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes for. which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
.time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro,gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpose cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extendep....to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn areas. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans -Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under .privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asiatic Societ~, Calcutta 
49. The A~iatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
SO. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this Is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government sho11ld expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Culture the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations · engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There· has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abu! Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. S lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that there should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was estaolished in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years of 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations. are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started In the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that steps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the

From the above, it is very clear that the Institute is running without even a single

September, 1994 there were 39 vacancies on teaching side and they continued to remain

Comments of the Committee

The Committee takes note of the fact that as a result of the concerted efforts made by
the Department, there has been a significant improvement in the filling up of both teaching
and non-teaching posts of the Institute lying vacant since long. However, the Committee is
constrained to note that the ban on the revival of posts lying vacant for more than a year is
applicable in the case of teaching institutions also. The Committee takes a strong exception
to such a rule being followed by the Ministry of Finance. The Committee feels that such a
ban should not be made applicable to teaching institutions. The Committee feels that the
tule should be suitably modified to exclude all educational institutions otherwise the students
will suffer in their studies. The Department should take up this issue strongly with the
Ministry of Finance.

The Committee is of the opinion that the Department should continue their efforts for
creation of teaching posts. If possible, non-teaching posts may be reduced, but only after
adequately taking care of the CCIM norms.

The Committee had the impression that neither the pay scales of the Institute have been
referred to the 5th Pay Commission nor there has been any success in getting the pay scales
enhanced. The Secretary clarified that the ISM doctors in CGHS had been put on par with

However, NIA being an autonomous body, its pay scales are at par with that of Lady
Hardinge College and JIPMER. This was applicable in the case of all Government
Ayurvedic Institutions, it was informed.

JIPMER are applicable to NIA should be made known to all concerned through a circular.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Eighty-first Report of the Committee on Value Based Education.
2. The Committee in this connection appointed a Sub-Committee under my convernorship in its meeting held on 16th January, 1997 to look into the various aspects of the Value-Based Education for making an in-depth study on the subject and to present a report thereon to the Committee at an early date.
2. The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development. The Sub-Committee held discussions with a number of State Governments. The Sub-Committee also visited a few educational institutions where special efforts are being made to inculcate values in the students. The Sub-Committee also heard the views of eminent persons/educationists in this regard.
3. The Committee considered and adopted the report submitted by the Sub-Committee at its meeting held on 22nd January, 1999. The Committee decided to present the Report in the House during the Budget Session of Parliament. 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                                                S.B. CHAVAN
JANUARY 22, 1999
                                                                                                                        CHAIRMAN,
MAGHA 2, 1920 (Saka) Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Human Resource Development
REPORT
1. Values are principles which are consistent and universal and which direct our action and activities. They are in-built in our society, common to not only all the communities but also to all religions at all times. Values are, in other words, virtues in an individual. These values, if deteriorated, will hasten or accelerate the break-down of family, society and nation as a whole. India has age-old tradition of values interwoven in the national fabric. Although there has been great advancement in science and technology, there has been a gradual erosion of values which is reflected in the day-to-day life of a large section of our present society. Our young generation under the growing influence of negative aspects of Western culture, is stranded on the cross-roads, not able to decide which direction to take.
2. Education should aim at multi-faceted development of a human being – his intellectual, physical, spiritual and ethical development. Youth is the mirror in which future of a nation is fully reflected. In order to preserve, maintain and advance the position of our country in the world, it is imperative that there should be a comprehensive programme of value-education starting from the pre-primary level, embracing the entire spectrum of educational process. The minds, hearts and hands of children are to be engaged in forming their own character to know what is `good’, love `good’ and do `good’.
3. The Committee is aware that since independence, a number of high-powered Commissions and Committees on Education, namely the Radhakrishnan Commission (1948-49), Kothari Commission (1964-66), National Policy on Education (1986), Ramamurti Committee (1990), Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) Committee on Policy (1992), Planning Commission Core Group on Value Orientation of Education (1992) have highlighted the urgent need for making our educational system value-based. However, the Committee finds it very disappointing to observe that such well-concerted efforts during the last four decades have failed to achieve the desired results. Well-chalked out plans and strategies for making education value-oriented still remain on paper. The Committee feels that lack of co-ordinated effort on the part of all the implementing agencies may be held responsible for this sort of affairs.
4. Against this background, the Committee decided to re-examine the entire gamut of value-orientation of our educational system so as to come up with some effective suggestions for bringing about a much-awaited change. Realising that a smaller group would be in a better position to make an in-depth analysis of the subject, a Sub-Committee on Value Based Education was constituted on 16th January, 1997, which was subsequently re-constituted on 6th August, 1997. However, as the work allocated to the Sub-Committee could not be completed during the term of the previous main Committee, a new Sub-Committee came into being on 6th August, 1998.
5. The Committee invited suggestions from noted educationists on various aspects of value-based education, at what stage it should be introduced, whether both Govt. and NGOs should be involved in this task and in what manner it should be introduced. In order to have an over-all idea about the state-run value based education programmes, the Committee held discussions with representatives of a number of State Governments. The Committee was also benefited by views of quite a few eminent experts/NGOs, doing pioneering work in this area. Besides that, the Committee also held interactions with representatives of various Government Organisations. An encouraging response from individuals/organisations was received from all parts of the country. This showed the public concern with this vital aspect – the building up of our national character.
6. It was generally felt that ours is a vast and diverse ancient country historically, geographically and socially. Traditions are different, the ways of thinking and living are also different. But there are certain common elements which unite the country in its diversity. This country has a long tradition. Here from ancient times, there have been great saints and thinkers from different religions and sects who have talked about some eternal values. These values are to be inculcated by our young generation.
7. In ancient times in Gurukuls, emphasis used to be primarily on building the character of a student. Today, right from the schools upto the professional colleges, emphasis is on acquiring techniques and not values. We seem to have forgotten that skills acquired on computers tend to become outdated after sometime but values remain for ever. In other words, present day education is nothing but an information transmission process. Our educational system aims at only information based knowledge and the holistic view of turning the student into a perfect human being and a useful member of society has been completely set aside. Swami Vivekananda aptly said,
"Education is not the amount of information that is put in your brain and runs riot there, undigested, all your life. We must have life-building, man-making, character-making assimilation of ideas. If education is identical with information, libraries are the greatest sages of the world and encyclopedias are rishis."
8. Truth (Satya), Righteous Conduct (Dharma), Peace (Shanti), Love (Prema) and Non-violence (Ahimsa) are the core universal values which can be identified as the foundation-stone on which the value-based education programme can be built up. These five are indeed universal values and respectively represent the five domains of human personality: intellectual, physical, emotional, psychological and spiritual. They also are correspondingly co-related with the five major objectives of education, namely, knowledge, skill, balance, vision and identity.
9. Primary school stage is the period in child’s life when seed of value-education can be implanted in his/her impressionable mind in a very subtle way. If this seed is nurtured by the capable hands of dedicated teachers in school, if they insert values at appropriate intervals during a child’s school life, it can be easily said that half the battle in building up national character has been won.
10. It is very essential that at the school level right from primary stage, deliberate, planned and sustained efforts are made to inculcate basic human values among the students. Values are best initiated by a mother to her small child under her tender care in the secure atmosphere of home. However, nowadays, children are enrolled in school as early as at the age of four. At this impressionable stage, values like respect for parents, elders and teachers, truth, punctuality, cleanliness and courtesy can be easily inculcated in small children. They can also be sensitised regarding gender equality.
11. Besides the personal values, there are certain social values which ought to be imbibed by the young mind. These are the values which concern the whole community: concern for the aged and the handicapped, for the deprived sections of the society etc. Sincere belief in the dignity of labour is generally found to be lacking in our young generation. Values of self-dependence and insistence on doing manual labour are thus required to be impressed upon small children.
12. In view of the diverse character of our country, it is essential that certain National Values are also imbibed by our young students. They should be acquainted with the history of India’s freedom struggle, cultural heritage, constitutional obligations and the features comprising our national identity. The Committee feels that some of these national values can be imparted indirectly at the primary stage while at the middle and secondary level, these can be included in the curriculum.
13. Another aspect that must be given some thought is religion, which is the most misused and misunderstood concept. The process of making the students acquainted with the basics of all religions, the values inherent therein and also a comparative study of the philosophy of all religions should begin at the middle stage in schools and continue up to the university level. Students have to be made aware that the basic concept behind every religion is common, only the practices differ. Even if there are differences of opinion in certain areas, people have to learn to co-exist and carry no hatred against any religion.
14. One should never forget that all the values are derived from ultimate reality – supreme power or self-consciousness – to which man orients himself. Once faith in that reality is lost, then values lose their meaning. To believe that we have the divine spark in each one of us is the most important eternal value to be inculcated by the small children even before starting their school life. It is acknowledged now the world over that ultimate goal of education is realisation of the treasure within.
15. There has to be developed in students a feeling of respect for all languages of the country, if the concept of unity in diversity is to be effectively imbibed. Not only this, students also have to make a conscious effort to learn at least one regional language alongwith their own mother tongue. The Committee understands that at present mother tongue is not being taught in all the schools in the country. The issue whether it can be started in all the schools may be examined by the Department of Education. At the secondary stage, at least one foreign language may be learnt by the students with a view to know the advantages of international achievements in science and technology and other fields of human development.
16. A great deal of responsibility for evolving an educational system akin to our own civilisation and our own tradition rests on teachers. Children enter the school at a very tender age. Right through the primary and upper primary stage the teacher remains the role model for them. They have blind faith in him/her. The teacher is the key person who can inculcate all the required values in small children, in spite of many odds. This task would become easier if the teacher through his personality, character and actions sets an example before his students.
17. The present day concept of an efficient teacher is that he is a person who can teach mathematics well, or who can speak English well. Ideally, the transactional process should emphasise the hidden values in each lesson. But unfortunately, most teachers emphasise only the outer, superficial content in terms of knowledge and examine/evaluate only – whether the child has been able to memorise and has the capacity to reproduce what is memorised. Their behavioural aspects are seldom measured by teachers nor brought out during the transactional process.
18. The Committee feels that teachers cannot be held wholly responsible for the prevailing situation. Inadequacies exist in the teacher training system which does not prepare the teachers to either assimilate or disseminate values in their teaching. Therefore, the most important intervention that has to be made is in the area of teacher education. The Committee is of the view that value- education should be a part of curriculum for teacher training programme. Prospective teachers should be introduced to the concept of value-education. All methods and techniques – both direct and indirect for inculcating values in students in tune with the different stages of their psychological development should be an essential component of teacher training programme.
Re-orientation of teachers is also equally important. They need to be re-oriented, so that they may impart higher values to their pupils through example and through precept. Periodic value-orientation camps and workshops, brain-storming sessions etc. may, therefore, be essential components of inservice training for teachers.
19. Our educational system, which is too structured to allow for innovations and experimentation, is also to be blamed for the erosion of values. At the national/State level, a decision needs to be taken as to what are the core inputs which need to be incorporated in the curriculum and it should be left to the schools and colleges to innovate and experiment. The Committee feels that the teachers ought to have freedom, within the broad parameters of prescribed curriculum to decide what is to be imparted to children and the manner in which it is to be imparted.
20. During the course of its interaction with experts, the Committee was given to understand that at the school level, it would not be advisable to introduce value education as a separate component. School curriculum being very heavy, introducing another component would be increasing that load further. The Committee is of the view that as at the primary level, the syllabus is not rigidly written down, there is enough scope for the interested teachers to innovate things and teach in their own style. Therefore, instead of a separate value-education class or a prescribed text for it, a primary school teacher can integrate values in his students through teaching – learning methods, instructional materials and co-curricular activities. A system thus needs to be developed wherein various values can be identified and integrated in the curriculum.
21. Nobody can deny the fact that education itself is value-inherent. There cannot be a single teacher in a school who can be categorised as a teacher for values. The ideal situation would be that various aspects of value education are suitably incorporated in all subjects of school education. Thus, every subject teacher would be a teacher of values. Science and technology can be used as levers for inculcating tremendous values in students. For example, through Physics the concept of order, symmetry, supreme symmetry, equilibrium etc. can be imparted. Similarly, a new world-view can be portrayed by Social Sciences focussing on higher values like the principles of democracy, of tolerance and co-existence, respect for other people’s views, collective wisdom etc.
22. The Committee is not in agreement with the view that value-education should be taught as a separate subject and that students should be assessed through an examination only because otherwise the students and the teachers do not take the subject seriously. The Committee feels that such a procedure would no doubt encourage the student to have theoretical knowledge of values for securing marks in the examination. But it is doubtful as to how much values in true sense would be imbibed by them.
23. School environment is to be consciously organised to expose students to values formally as well as informally. It has to be so congenial that a child is able to enjoy it and also pick up some ideas which can remain with him as habits.
24. Morning assembly is a very effective medium of imparting values in students. Prayers sung in chorus are bound to create faith in a supreme power in the young minds. Patriotic songs sung in chorus help to inculcate belief in secularism and patriotism in the students. They are much more influential in forming the thought process. Special emphasis can be focussed on a particular value every day during the morning assembly.
25. In the morning assembly, students may also be encouraged to make presentation on different subjects with special focus on patriotism, national integration, humanism, cultural unity in diversity, service and sacrifice, secularism and the prevailing social problems. It is likely to have an impact on all students.
26. Meditation can also play a key role. Students can sit silently and reflect about their conduct and behaviour; they can learn to develop concentration and they can be made aware of the quiet strength lying within one's own body and mind. Meditation before exams is also bound to develop their concentration leading to better results.
27. At primary level, values can be imparted through stories/folk songs/ folklores/skits/flip charts/film strips. Story-telling is a very effective and practical means of transmitting values. Through this medium, small children can be made acquainted with the lives of great men who have achieved great heights in whatever sphere – be it science, religion, literature, industry, politics or sports.28. The Committee would like to emphasise that values are to be projected in such a manner that they relate to down to earth reality. Young students are fascinated by stories of great leaders like Swami Vivekananda but they tend to have a feeling that they are too high a role model and it is virtually impossible for them to follow their ideals. Here the role of the teacher becomes very crucial. He has to project the life story of great leaders in such a way that innocent minds are able to connect them with ordinary human beings who rose to such heights by sticking to great values.
29. The Committee feels that plays/dramas constitute another means for inculcating values in young students. When children are directly involved in the production of dramas and when they themselves conceptualise the theme, they are surely affected by the values inherent in such plays.
30. The Committee finds that the NCC, Scouting or Guiding which earlier used to be a major activity in most schools now seem to have almost disappeared. Besides that, due to heavy burden of studies, students are not generally inclined to participate in sports activities. There is a need for promoting these activities which can prove to be effective in promoting discipline, co-operation and creating a healthy attitude towards life.
31. At high school level, reading habits can be promoted by having compulsory library periods. Debates, discussions on specific subjects, symposia would develop in students values of compassion, respect for others and familiarity with and tolerance of the view-points of others.
32. The Committee is in agreement with the widely-accepted view that value-based education should be introduced at the school level and extended to college and university level. In the secondary stage, some advanced values which are of vital importance for national integration should be integrated into the syllabus.
33. The Committee is of the view that in the advanced stage, i.e. at the college and university level, values like human rights, co-existence and also ethical values in science and technology and comparative study of all religions – need to be taught by prescribing special books. Literature with special emphasis on co-existence and non-imposition of fundamentalist ideas will have to be produced.
34. Sex education is a tricky subject demanding our careful attention and thinking. At what stage it should be introduced, should it be introduced at all? According to the expert opinion, it should be introduced as a component of curriculum at the appropriate stage. The Committee agrees that it has become necessary to expose our young students to this education in view of ever-increasing prevalence of diseases like AIDS and Hepatitis B. However, a very cautious and objective approach is required on the part of teachers. The maturity level of students has to be properly assessed before starting such a programme.
35. The Committee is of the opinion that incentives including awards can be given to teachers successfully integrating values in their normal lessons. Similarly, those students who through their actions have been able to bring forth before the student community certain commendable human values like cooperation, honesty, bravery and integrity can be given awards and merit scholarships. Such incentives would certainly go a long way in inculcating values in children.
36. The Committee feels that history needs to be presented to the students in the right perspective. This has nothing to do with any ideology. Education has a lasting impression on young minds and distortion of history should not be allowed. Value of tolerance against the backdrop of culturally plural society of our country should be prominently brought out specially while writing history books.
37. The Committee finds that most works on the subject of value-based education are heavily loaded with urban values, urban attitude of the middle class and to some extent of the neo-rich in rural areas. Values representing rural and tribal background should certainly find a place in the value education programme of the country as a whole. The Committee is, therefore, of the considered opinion that special efforts in this regard ought to be made. One attempt can be that dedicated teachers willing to work in rural and tribal areas should be given preference in every possible way. In this regard, successful implementation of ‘Shiksha Karmi’ Scheme in Rajasthan can be cited as an example.
38. With the advancement in information technology, audio-visual media has dominated the information/knowledge system of our country. Under the invasion of Western culture penetrating into India through the media, the young are being literally moved away from our age-old traditions and values. Any attempt to instil indigenous values in students in schools, colleges are over-shadowed by the over-whelming impact of Western culture. The Committee is of the considered view that stringent efforts are required on the part of the Govt. to monitor the programmes being aired/telecast through its media. Similar steps need to be taken so as to have a mechanism of quality control of programmes under the control of private agencies too.
39. The Committee is aware that some good programmes are shown on the national TV but their message somehow is not reaching the young minds. Initiatives to make our own programmes attractive and meaningful need to be taken and that requires Government encouragement and Government patronage.
40. Divergent views were put across to the Committee as to the necessity of having a national programme on value-based education. One view was that a centralised programme should be formulated and the role of States should be restricted to the implementation thereof; otherwise there was every likelihood of different States taking different directions. The other viewpoint was that there should be an element of both centralisation and decentralisation. Certain universal core values which have an all-India applicability should be incorporated in the national programme to be adopted by all States. However, flexibility should be there so that States have the option to include values in their respective education programmes. The Committee is of the opinion that Central initiative is important. But too much centralisation tends to make the system regimented and rigid. States should also have a say in the matter.
41. The development of human resource, strongly anchored on value based education, is a stupendous task. The present educational system is faced with complex problems. In India, a country of enormous size and diversity, the implementation of any policy demands coordinated efforts by the Central Govt., the State Govts. and the Civil Societies actively involved in the implementation of value-based education. The Committee, however, feels that only those NGOs with proven track records and who are specially engaged in tribal, rural and backward areas need to be identified. An effective monitoring mechanism needs to be evolved so as to have a proper feedback of the work done by the NGOs.

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1. Education is the key to all processes of development, especially human development. Having regard to
the size of the population, diversity and economic frailties prevailing in the country, the challenges in the
path of providing Education for All are too many and enormous. Education being in the Concurrent List,
its meaningful development implies an effective partnership between the Union Govt. and the states. While
the role and responsibility of states to provide education continues to remain essentially unchanged, the
Union Department of Education has assumed a larger responsibility to reinforce the national and integrated
character of education, to look after the international aspects of Education and in general, to promote
excellence in all sectors of education throughout the country.
The Ninth Plan treats education as the most crucial investment in human development. Approach Paper to
the Ninth Plan indicates that "apart from carrying out the directions given by the National Policy on
Education, 1986 and NPA, 1992, making the nation fully literate by the year 2005 will be a committed
goal. Priorities, therefore, include universalisation of elementary education, raising the quality of education
at all levels, upliftment of the educational status of disadvantaged groups like SCs/STs/girls/disabled,
equality and removal of regional imbalances, vocationalisation of education and setting up of centres of
excellence".
1.3. The Secretary, Department of Education informed the Committee that an allocation of Rs. 20,381
crores has been made in the 9th Plan in the Central Sector as against an outlay of Rs.7,443 crores in the 8th

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
Plan, which represents an increase of more than two and a half times : 66.1% of the total allocation has
been earmarked for Elementary Education during the 9th Plan as compared to 38.7 % in the 8th Plan .
Attention of the Committee was, however, drawn to the fact that total allocation for Education both in the
Central and State Sector if taken together is less than 4% of GDP. Suitable budgetary provision in the 9th
Plan period is required if it is to be raised to the tune of 6% of GDP by 2000 AD. The Secretary explained
that the Approach Paper to the 9
th Plan had indicated that GDP at market prices would grow from
Rs.12,40,000 crore in 1996-97 to Rs. 17,50,000 crore in 20001-2002. Six per cent of that would be
Rs.1,05,000 crore in 2001-2002. The current year’s allocation should thus have been about Rs. 15,500
crore . The Committee is of the view that greater budgetary support is needed if 6% of GDP for
Education is to be made a reality.
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1. The budgetary allocation for 1999-2000 is Rs. 7936.74 crores of which Rs. 4699.04 crore is on the
Plan side and Rs. 3237.70 crore is on the Non-Plan side. Compared to last year’s Plan allocation of
Rs.4244.18 crores at BE which was reduced to Rs. 4044.18 crore at RE stage due to economic
considerations and also under-utilisation in some of the schemes, the plan allocation for 1999-2000
Rs.4699.04 crore shows some increase. The Secretary explained that allocation for 1999-2000 although at
an enhanced level still falls short of the requirements.
2.2. The Committee, however, observes that against a total allocation of BE Rs.4244.18 crore in
1998-99 reduced to Rs. 4044.18 crore at RE stage, expenditure upto 26.2.99 shows an amount of only
Rs.2650.29 crore. There are little chances of full utilisation of funds at this stage. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that Department should take all appropriate steps for maximum utilisation
of allocation made for 1999-2000. The Committee would like to be informed about the States where
funds could not be utilised fully. The Committee apprehends that in some of the States, there may be
instances where funds allocated by the centre for a particular scheme are being diverted for other
purposes. If that be so the Committee recommends that the Department should take up this matter
with the concerned States.
III. Literacy
3.1. The Secretary informed the Committee that as a result of concerted efforts made in the area of primary
education, non-formal education and adult education, there has been some increase in the literacy rate
prevailing in the country. Results of the 53
rd round of the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO)
indicate that against the literacy rate of 52.2% in 1991, this rate stands at 62% at the end of December,
1997 and has been projected to touch 64% at the end of 1998.
3.2. Male literacy rates have risen from 64.1% in 1991 to 73% in 1997 and the female literacy rates in the
corresponding period have risen from 39.3% to 50% . Thus, the gender gap in literacy rates is being
narrowed in overall terms. Another encouraging trend is acceleration of literacy rates in rural areas. While
in 1991, the urban literacy rate was 73.1% and the rural literacy rate was 44.7%, in 1997, as per the NSSO
Survey, urban literacy rate was 80% and the rural literacy rate was 56%.
3.3. In terms of performance in literacy, Mizoram leads the country with a literacy rate of 95%. Kerala
now occupies the second place with a literacy rate of 93%. Almost all the educationally backward states
have also shown reasonable improvement.

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
IV Elementary Education
4.1. Universal access, universal retention and universal achievements are the broad parameters to achieve
UEE. Meticulously formulated strategies have been adopted in the form of Operation Blackboard (OB),
Non-Formal Education (NFE), Teachers’ Education, District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) to
address the specific problem areas, gender and regional disparities. Out of the total budget of Rs. 7936.72
crore for the Department for 1999-2000, Rs. 3034.95 crore have been allocated for Elementary Education
alone. This is a considerable enhancement when compared to allocation of Rs.2780.03 crore for
Elementary Education in 1998-99.
4.2. The number of teachers which was 7.51 lakhs in gross terms in 1950-51 has risen to 47.57 lakhs in
1996-97, showing a substantial increase in the number of female teachers from 1.15 lakh to 16.52 lakhs.
However, the Committee views with serious concern that despite the increase in infrastructural facilities
and the concomitant increase in the number of teachers, the teacher-pupil ratio (TPR) has increased from
1:24 to 1:42 at the primary stage and 1:20 to 1:37 at the upper primary level. The Committee is in
agreement with Department’s observation that increase in TPR indicates that demand for
elementary education has increased and justifies the need for opening more educational institutions
to meet the demand of the school going population . However, simultaneous efforts are also required
to be made for creation of required number of posts of teachers specially in the Rural areas.
3. Drop-Out Rates
4.3.1. The progress in universalisation of elementary education during 8th Plan has not been
insignificant. Declining trend in drop-out rates is one of the parameters in this direction. The
decline is from 42% in 1991-92 (First year of 8th Plan) to 39% in 1996-97 (last year of 8th
Plan), showing an overall decrease of 3% at the primary level. At the upper primary stage, the
drop out rate was 58.7% in 1991-92 and it declined to 52.3% in 1996-97, showing an overall
decrease of 6.4%. The 9th Plan envisaged UEE to mean universalising access, retention and
achievement.
4.3.2. Target set out for Universal retention for 9th Plan is reduction of drop out rates between
classes I to V and classes I to VIII from the existing 36.3 % and 56.5% to 20% and 40%
respectively. The Committee however, notes that figures for drop-out rates on completion of
1997-98 (1st year of 9th Plan) stand at 39.58% and 54.14% for primary and upper primary
level respectively. Very vigorous efforts are required if targets set out for 9th Plan for control
of drop out rates are to be achieved. The Committee also observes that there has been no
marked improvement in respect of educationally backward states. Drop-out rates in classes I
to V for the year 1997-98 in respect of Bihar are as high as 59.65% Meghalaya has the
highest figures of drop-out rates 62.44% in classes I to V in the country. Situation is more
grim in classes I to VIII. Bihar has the highest drop-out rate of 77.11% with girls having a
dropout rate of 80.48%.
4.3.3. The Committee notes that for increasing the retention rate at primary and upper
primary level there are a number of interventions through a variety of schemes in which
active participation of both state govts. and NGOs is evident with funding provided by

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
the Govt. and also foreign agencies. However, drop-out rates have not shown an
appreciable declining trend. The Committee is of the firm view that concerted efforts in
a mission mode by all the implementing agencies are required to be made without any
delay, failing which targets set out for 9th Plan would remain on paper only. The
Department has to take an initiative in the right direction by targeting the weak areas in
different states and taking necessary remedial steps.
4. Operation Blackboard
4.4.1. The Department informed that under ‘Operation Blackboard’, 5.23 lakh primary schools and 0.76
lakh upper primary schools have been provided funds for development of academic infrastructure
(teaching learning material). On a specific query as to the exact number of teachers appointed against the
sanctioned posts, the Committee was informed that against 55,951 posts sanctioned for 3
rd teacher in
primary schools, 47,081 have been appointed so far. Against 45,089 posts of additional teachers sanctioned
in upper primary schools, 32,662 teachers have been appointed. Further, against the target of 47,000 posts
during 1998-99, only 24,369 posts have been sanctioned in primary/upper primary schools to date.
4.4.2. The Secretary informed the Committee that reluctance on the part of most of the states to create
additional posts of teachers was primarily responsible for large amount of funds either remaining
unutilised or not being released. The Committee views with serious concern utilisation of only Rs. 80.26
crores upto 26.2.99 against an allocation of Rs. 304 crores in 1998-99. The Committee was given to
understand that states were generally apprehensive about sharing extra burden under non plan due to
creation of additional posts once the plan period was over. There was a tendency on the part of State
Govts. to redeploy teachers against plan posts. The Committee feels that it is an undesirable activity. The
Committee is of the opinion that the State Govts. have a primary role to play for the successful
implementation of `Operation Blackboard’. They cannot shirk away from their responsibility.
4.4.3. Difficulties were also there due to procedural delays in centralised system of procurement of
teaching-learning material. As a result, approximately Rs. 365 crores were lying as unspent balance with
the state govts. Procurement level was as low as 38.63% in the case of Nagaland, 45% in respect of
Gujarat and 55.32% in MP. The Committee feels that there is a need for decentralisation of the system of
procurement of teaching learning material. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department
should take appropriate action in this regard.
4.4.4. While appreciating the fact that funds are now being released only on the basis of creation of
posts, the Committee strongly feels that there is a need for chalking out a well-planned strategy in
active coordination with state govts. so as to assess the actual requirement of teachers before
sanction of posts under ‘Operation Blackboard’. In view of the enhanced allocation of Rs.400 crores
for ‘Operation Blackboard’ in 1999-2000, the Committee is of the view that a meeting of all the State
Education Ministers with the representatives of the Central Govt. would be an ideal venue where
issues like non-utilisation of funds, difficulties being faced in implementing programmes etc. can be
discussed at length with possible remedies for the problem.
5. Teachers’ Training Programme
4.5.1. The Committee was informed that significant progress has been made so far as Teachers’ training
programme was concerned. About 448 District Institutes of Education and Training (DIETS) to provide
pre-service and in-service training to elementary school teachers and for adult education and non-formal
education personnel have been created. 110 Secondary Teachers Education Institutes have been upgraded

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
into Colleges of Teacher Education (CTEs)/Institutions of Advanced Study in Education (IASEs). In
addition, 20 State Councils of Educational Research & Training (SCERTs) have also been strengthened.
About 10 lakh teachers have been covered under the special Orientation Programme of primary teachers.
4.5.2. On a specific query as to the reasons for enhanced allocation of Rs.219.00 crores in 1999-2000 as
compared to only Rs.159.00 crores being provided in 1998-99, the Committee was given to understand
that the same was meant for meeting the requirements of revised norms and also for setting up 20 new
DIETs. 5 CTEs/IASEs, 10 BRCs and 20 CRCs during 1999-2000.
4.5.3. The Committee hopes that the exercise of revision of norms for grant of central assistance for
setting up of DIETs/CTEs/IASEs and strengthening of SCERTs would be completed during 1999-
2000. The Committee notes that an evaluation study for assessing quantitative and qualitative
progress of Teaches’ Training Programme with special focus on the performance of DIETs has been
initiated. The Committee hopes that this evaluation would result in strengthening the capacity of
Teachers’ Training Institutes.
 
  
 
4.6 Externally-aided Projects
4.6.1. District Primary Education Programme (DPEP), an externally aided programme aims at
operationalising the strategies for achieving UPE/UEE through district specific planning and disaggregated
target setting in 1ow female literacy districts and builds on successful TLC campaigns. The Department
informed that the Programme is under implementation in 163 low female literacy districts in 14 states.
Expansion of the project to another 30-35 districts in UP, 10 districts in Rajasthan, 8 districts in Orissa and
5 districts in West Bengal is in the pipeline, the Committee was informed. The Committee notes that
against a projected requirement of Rs. 950.00 crores, an allocation of Rs. 750 crore has been made for
DPEP for 1999-2000. However, as per the decision of the Planning Commission, funds for externally
aided projects like DPEP would be provided based on the requirements of ongoing projects as well as
those in the pipeline. The Committee finds that against an allocation of Rs.550 crores for DPEP in 1998-
99, utilisation figures stand at Rs.340 crores as on 26.2.99. DPEP is a very important intervention for
achieving UEE. The Committee would like to point out that there is an urgent need for utilising the
funds without delay but in a judicious manner. Provision of Rs. 10 crores in 1999-2000 as a
‘Domestic Component’ so that DPEP could reach those States/districts where external funding may
not be available is a welcome step.
2. The Committee was given to understand that certain problems were arising in the
implementation of DPEP in Kerala where very few districts have been covered under
this programme. The Committee desires that the Department may look into it
4.6.3. The other externally aided projects are the Lok Jumbish Project and Rajasthan Shiksha Karmi
Project which are also innovative projects aimed at universalising of elementary education together with
qualitative improvement in remote and socially backward villages in Rajasthan with a primary focus on
gender. The Department informed that LJP has undertaken environment building activities in 5,683
villages and has completed school mapping exercises in 4,006 villages. 383 new schools have been opened
while 227 primary schools have been upgraded. 2697 villages in 146 blocks in Rajasthan have been
covered under the Shiksha Karmi Project. 6285 Shiksha Karmis provide primary education to 2.01 lakh
children in day schools and Prehar Pathshalas.

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/82edreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:09:27]
4.6.4. The Committee views with serious concern that in view of the post-Pokhran developments,
fundings for Phase III of both the Programmes which were to start from 1st July, 1998 has been
withdrawn by Swedish International Development Authority (SIDA). As a result, against an
allocation of Rs.37.50 crores and 16.17 crores for LJP and SKP respectively in 1998-99, to only
Rs.4.5 crores and 5.2 crores could be utilised. The Committee was informed that UK’s Department
for International Development (DFID) has come forward provide alternate funds for Phase III of
both these programmes. The Committee hopes that enhanced allocation proposed for SKP and LJP
in 1999-2000 in anticipation of DFID Funding would be fully utilised and the work accomplished so
far under these two projects would not suffer a further setback.
7. Mid-day Meal Scheme
4.7.1. Mid-day Meal Scheme launched in August, 1995 covers all the children studying in primary classes
in all Govt., local body and Govt.-aided schools in the country. As per the 1998-99 figures, 9.75 crore
children in about 6.88 lakh schools were beneficiaries of this Scheme. The State Govts are to supplement
the Central efforts by providing the conversion costs for serving cooked meals for which financial
assistance is available to them under the JRY/EAS funds. However, the Committee was informed that only
5 states and 1 UT, i.e. Gujarat, Kerala, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh (in 174 Tribal blocks only)
and Pondicherry serve cooked meals. What is more surprising is that two states, Haryana and J&K which
used to, had to revert to the distribution of the food-grains in 1996-97 due to resource constraints,
inadequate cooking arrangements and resentment among teachers. Non-serving of cooked meals defeats
the very objective of the Scheme. The Committee views with serious concern the total lack of state
initiative in the implementation of a scheme designed to give a boost to the universalisation of
primary education. The Committee strongly feels that successful implementation of Mid-day Meal
Scheme by 5 states and 1 UT can well be followed by the remaining states of the country. The
Committee is of the view that there should be supply of food grains to the States only on the
condition of serving of cooked meals to the children.
4.7.2. The Committee was informed that the Mid day Meal Scheme was facing a severe resource crunch.
During 1998-99, there has been disruption in supply of foodgrains due to paucity of funds and non-
reconciliation of lifting figures between states and FCI. As a result, lifting of foodgrains during the current
year has been lower than the average of 70-75% allocation during the last three years. The Committee was
given to understand that allocations for 1997-98 and 1998-99 were much below the requirements under
this scheme. The proposed allocation of Rs. 1031.10 crore for 1999-2000 would be too meagre to meet the
requirement of approximately Rs. 3000 crores to continue coverage of all the children of primary classes in
the country. Consequently, FCI may again resort to suspension of supply of foodgrains. This is an
alarming position which warrants urgent action on the part of the Govt. for augmentation of allocation of
funds under this scheme.
4.7.3. The Committee views with serious concern the proposed move of the Govt. to restrict the Mid
day Meal Scheme to Girls, SCs/STs only. Instead of restricting this scheme to a limited category, the
Department should explore all the possibilities for removing the bottlenecks – both physical and
financial – in close coordination with state govts. and implementing agencies. The Committee hopes
that findings of the evaluation study of Mid day Meal Scheme presently being conducted by the
Operation Research Group in 10 states would prove to be useful in taking a decision in the right
direction.

4.8 Non-Formal Education
4.8.1. The implementing agencies for this Programme are both State Govts. and NGOs. During 1997-98,
the number of NFE Centres being run in the State Sector was 2.41 lakh which remained the same in 1998-
99 too. However, there was increase in the number of centres being run by NGOs. Against 49,000 centres
run by 740 NGOs in 1997-98, there were 58,000 centres managed by 825 NGOs during 1998-99.
However, enhanced provision ;of Rs. 309.21 crores in BE 1998-99, in view of the revision of NFE Scheme
with enhanced cost parameters had to be reduced to Rs. 160 crores at the RE stage. The Committee has
been given to understand that unspent balance of Rs. 61.88 crore lying with State Govts and delay in the
finalisation of revised NFE Scheme were the two factors responsible for drastic reduction at the RE stage.
However, the Committee finds that even this reduced allocation is not likely to be utilised fully as there
has been an expenditure of only Rs. 108.61 crores upto 26.2.99.
4.8.2. The Committee views with serious concern the conclusion arrived at by the evaluation study
conducted in 6 states by the Planning Commission that NFE Programme has not made any notable
contribution. Some of its major findings as detailed below are very disturbing :-
o        erratic and much less than required flow of funds to NFE centres in the State
Sector.
o        Acute shortage of teaching /learning material in NFE Centres;
o        Attendance and enrolment in girl centres are low. Large number of girl centres
have male instructors;
o        Lack of coordination between State Govts and NGOs; and
o        Very weak supervision and monitoring of NFE Programme.
4.8.3. The Committee has been informed that proposed revision of the NFE Scheme incorporating the
modifications as suggested by the Planning Commission, views of experts and NFE practitioners and State
Govts.is at an advanced stage of preparation for consideration by EFC. The Committee strongly feels
that Department should make concerted efforts for finalisation of revised NFE Scheme without any
further delay and full and judicious utilisation of enhanced allocation of Rs. 350.00 crores proposed
in BE 1999-2000.
4. The NFE Programme initiated way back in 1979 on an experimental basis, was scaled up
in 1987 into a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for educationally backward States and was
further expanded during the 8th Plan period. It took 20 years to arrive at the conclusion
that NFE Programme has been perceived as a low cost, inferior and ineffective alternative
for full-time school meant for the poor people. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the revised NFE Programme should have an effective in-built
mechanism for monitoring with full coordination between implementing agencies
i.e.. State Govt/NGOs and the Central Government.
V. Grants-in-aid to Voluntary Organisations
Under the `Scheme of Assistance to Voluntary agencies under National Literacy Mission’ grants are
released to voluntary agencies and Resource Centres (State and Regional). The Committee finds that the
major portion of assistance is being given to State Resource Centres. The Committee would like to have an
idea about the composition of these resource centres and their functionings.
